**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 1:**

**Surat al-Ra'd (13)**

It has been transmitted through Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah that it is Makkiyyah (Meccan). The same is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Sa'id ibn Mansur said in his Sunan: Abu 'Awanah narrated to us from Abu Bishr, who said: I asked Ibn Jubayr about the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾, whether it refers to 'Abdullah ibn Salam. He said: How could it, when this surah is Meccan?

Mujahid transmitted from Ibn al-Zubayr, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and through Ibn Jurayj and 'Uthman from 'Ata' from him, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Qatadah, that it is Madaniyyah (Medinan). However, in the narration of the last, there is an exception of the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they have done﴾, up to the end of the verse, for it is Meccan. It is also reported that its beginning, up to the verse ﴿And if there were a Qur'an﴾, is Medinan, and the rest is Meccan.

In support of the view that it is Medinan, al-Itqan mentions what al-Tabarani and others transmitted from Anas: that the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Allah knows what every female carries﴾, up to His words, glorified is He, ﴿and He is severe in might﴾, were revealed concerning the story of Arbad ibn Qays and 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl when they came to Medina to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Then he said: What reconciles the differences is that it is Makkiyyah except for some verses within it, which are forty-three verses according to the Kufan count, four according to the Medinan count, five according to the Basran count, and seven according to the Syrian count.

The connection of this surah with what precedes it is that He, glorified is He, said earlier: ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by while they turn away from it﴾. He then summarized the heavenly and earthly signs, and here He, mighty and majestic is He, detailed that in the most complete detail. Also, He has brought here, in what indicates His Oneness, mighty and majestic is He, what serves as an explanation of what He related about Yusuf, peace be upon him, from his words: ﴿Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ Also, in each of the two surahs there is consolation for him (ﷺ), along with the shared content at the end of that surah and the beginning of this one concerning the description of the Qur'an, as is not hidden.

Concerning its virtue, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Marwazi in al-Jana'iz transmitted that he (ﷺ) used to recommend that when a dying person is present, Surat al-Ra'd be recited beside him, for that lightens the matter for the dying person, makes his soul's extraction easier, and eases his condition. Other reports concerning this have been transmitted, but scholars have stated that they are fabricated. And Allah knows best.

**(Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. Al-Mar.)** Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning of this is: "Ana Allahu a'lamu wa ara" (I am Allah, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing). This is one of the well-known opinions regarding such letters.

**﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾.** Many have taken al-Kitab (the Book) to mean the surah, and in the sense of "what is written," it truly applies to it without any need for figurative usage. The pointing to its verses (with "these") is on the basis that they are, for the recitation of some of them and the others being in the course of recitation, like things present. Or it is on the basis of their being preserved on the Preserved Tablet, or with the angel. The meaning is: "These verses are the complete, wondrous surah in its genre." This is said to be derived from the lam (the definite article "al-") in "al-Kitab," because the idafah (genitive construction) is explicative (bayaniyyah), so the sense is "that Book." When a predicate is defined by the lam of genus, it conveys hyperbole, and that the subject of judgment has acquired from excellence what makes it the very essence of the genus, and not merely one of its kinds. Since this appears impossible, that is what is intended.

It is also permissible that al-Kitab means the Qur'an, and "these" is a pointing to the verses of the surah. The meaning is: "The verses of this surah are the verses of the Qur'an, which is the wondrous, complete Book, independent of description by that, known among books, deserving of being specifically called 'the Book.'" The apparent meaning is that all of it is intended. It is also permissible that it refers to what was revealed at that time. However, the interpretation of the Qur'an is preferred because it is what comes first to mind from the unqualified "Book," which needs no adjective. By this, all that is intended from describing the verses with the perfections of what they are attributed to becomes clear. This is unlike when it is taken as a reference to the surah, for it does not have the same prominence in being described by that, which would make an explicit description unnecessary. There is a discussion on this, but in any case there is no objection to interpreting "the verses of the Book" as "those," as is not hidden.

It was also said: "These" refers to what Allah the Exalted related to him, peace be upon him, of the reports of the prophets, peace be upon them, which were indicated at the end of the previous surah in His words: ﴿That is from the news of the unseen﴾. On this view, it is permissible that al-Kitab means what includes the Torah and the Gospel. Ibn Jarir transmitted this from Mujahid and Qatadah.

Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted this on the assumption that "al-Mar" is intended to refer to the letters of the alphabet, and he made that the first subject, with "tilka" as a second subject, "ayat" as its predicate, and the whole clause as the predicate of the first subject, with the pronoun (rabit) being the demonstrative. As for His words, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth﴾, the apparent reading is that the relative pronoun (alladhi) is the subject; the clause "unzila" (was revealed), with its subject, is its relative clause; "min rabbika" (from your Lord) is related to "unzila"; and "al-haqq" (the truth) is the predicate. The relative pronoun is, according to many, intended to mean the entire Qur'an. The statement is an addition (istidrak) to the description of the surah only with perfection. In its style is the saying of Fatimah al-Anmariyyah, when she was asked: "Which of your sons is best: Rabi', or 'Imarah, or Qays, or Anas?" She said: "May they be bereaved of me! If I knew which of them is best, by Allah, they are like a hollow ring, and one does not know where its ends are."

This is like how she denied preference at the end by affirming perfection for each one, indicating that the perfection of each is not encompassed by description. It is a summary after detail for this purpose. Likewise, when He, glorified is He, affirmed perfection for this surah in particular, He followed it with the addition that every revealed text is like that, and no single surah is singled out by it, for the reason mentioned. This, it is said, is a wondrous meaning and an eloquent aspect, mentioned by the author of al-Kashshaf. It was also said that it is for confirming what precedes it and for providing proof for it, because if all that was revealed to him is true, then that revealed part is also true, since it is from all that was revealed. Thus it is perfect, for there is nothing more perfect than truth and sincerity. Because the argument is hidden, al-'Allamah al-Baydawi said that it is like a proof for what precedes it. Yet the first is better, though even this is not free from some obscurity. If it were said that the perfection mentioned earlier means the perfection relating to eloquence and rhetoric, and that this is a description of the one pointed to with inimitability in respect of that, and that this is a description specifically of it, on the assumption that the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, or of what includes it and other things, on the assumption that the apparent noun is not placed there, by being the truth that corresponds to reality (since eloquence and rhetoric do not require truth), as is shown by consulting the Hariri maqamat, it would not be far off at all. So reflect.

Al-Hawfi permitted that "min rabbika" is the predicate and "al-haqq" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is the truth," or it is a predicate after a predicate, or both are one predicate, as is said in "al-rummanu hulwun hamid" (the pomegranate is sweet, sour). This is a strained i'rab (grammatical analysis). It is also permitted that the relative clause is in the genitive position, in coordination with "al-Kitab," and "al-haqq" in that case is the predicate of an omitted subject, and nothing else.

It was said: The coordination is either coordination of the general over the specific, or one of two adjectives over the other, as they said in His words: "He is the king, the lord, and son of the valiant..." (the verse continues).

Some make it coordination of the whole over the part, or coordination of one of two synonyms over the other. Each has its direction. If by al-Kitab what was transmitted from Mujahid and Qatadah is intended, then the matter of coordination is clear.

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "alladhi" is an adjective (na't) of al-Kitab, with the addition of a waw in the adjective, as in "atani kitabu Abi Hafs wal-Faruq wal-nazilin wal-tayyibin" (the letter of Abu Hafs came to me, and [of] al-Faruq, and the descenders, and the good ones). This was criticized on the basis that what was mentioned about the addition of the waw for attachment, Sahib al-Mughni restricted to the case when the adjective is a clause, and we have not seen anyone mention it in the case of a single word.

Al-Hawfi also permitted that the relative clause is coordinated with "ayat" and that "al-haqq" is made an adjective of it, and this, as you see, is far-fetched. Then, on the assumption that "al-haqq" is the predicate of a mentioned or omitted subject, the intended meaning restricts truthfulness to what was revealed, because of its prestige in it. Nothing in that indicates that what is other than it is not true at all. Moreover, its truthfulness entails the truthfulness of the rest of the heavenly books, since it confirms what is before it and is a guardian over it.

Some opponents of qiyas (analogical reasoning) cited this verse, on the basis that it contains a restriction in the context of evidence for negating that. They said: The ruling deduced by qiyas is not revealed from Allah the Exalted, for otherwise whoever judges by it would be a disbeliever, according to His words: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾. And whatever is not revealed from Allah the Exalted is not true, by this verse, because it indicates that there is no truth except what Allah the Exalted has revealed.

Those who uphold qiyas refuted their premise in two ways: that the intended meaning of "not judging" is denial and not affirming (of truth), or that the intended meaning is one who does not judge by anything at all of what Allah the Exalted revealed, and there is no doubt that this is the attitude of disbelievers. Or the intended meaning of "what He revealed" there is the Torah, by the evidence of what precedes it, and we are not bound by it, so it is specific to the Jews, and the intended meaning is the ruling of their disbelief, since they did not judge by their own Book. We say in accordance with that, as explained in the commentary on al-Mawaqif. As for their premise in the second part, that the intended meaning of "revealed from Allah the Exalted" is what includes the explicit and other than it, so that qiyas enters into it, we do not include the analogue in the ruling of the original text revealed from Him, glorified is He. Yet an explicit revealed text has come: ﴿So take warning, O people of insight﴾, and this indicates, as has been verified in its proper place, the goodness of following qiyas. Moreover, you have come to know the purpose of the restriction.

It is also possible, as has been said, that the intended meaning is "the truth," not any other of the books that were not revealed, or that were revealed to others, on the basis of their distortion and abrogation. It may be said that their argument is refuted by the sunnah (prophetic practice) and ijma' (scholarly consensus), and the answer is the same answer. The significance of expressing the Qur'an by the relative pronoun, attributing the revelation to it with the passive form, and mentioning the attribute of lordship as a pronoun-suffix referring to him (peace be upon him), is not hidden: it indicates the grandeur of what was revealed, the honouring of what was revealed, and an allusion to the reason for the predicate's construction.

**﴿But most of the people do not believe﴾.** It was said they are the disbelievers of Makkah, and it was said they are the Jews and Christians. The better view is that it refers to most of them in general. **﴿Do not believe﴾** (1) in that manifest truth, because they neglect looking at it and reflecting upon it. Their non-belief, as Shaykh al-Islam said, is connected to the description of its truthfulness, because that is the basis for affirmation and denial, and not to the description of its being revealed, as some have said. And because it comes by way of description and not

﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see.﴾ That is, He created them raised high, in the manner of the saying "Glory be to He who made the elephant large and the gnat small," not that He raised them after they had not been so. ﴿Without pillars﴾: that is, supports. ʿAmad (عَمَد) is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) according to most scholars, and its singular is ʿimad (عِمَاد), like ihab (إِهَاب) and uhub (أُهُب). It is said: "ʿamadtu al-ḥāʾiṭa aʿmiduhu ʿamdan" when I shored up the wall, so it leaned and rested. It was also said that the singular is ʿamud (عَمُود). Forms such as adim (أَدِيم) and udum (أُدُم), and qasim (قَصِيم) and qusum (قُصُم), have come, and faʿil (فَعِيل) and faʿul (فَعُول) share many rulings. It was also said that it is a plural, but the first view is preferred for reasons we will point out shortly, if Allah the Exalted wills.

[Page 88]

Abu Ḥaywa and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read ʿumud (عُمُد) with two ḍammas, which is the plural of ʿimad, as shihab (شِهَاب) and shuhub (شُهُب), or of ʿamud, as rasul (رَسُول) and rusul (رُسُل). Both may take the paucal plural aʿmida (أَعْمِدَة). The plural here agrees with the plural "the heavens," not because the negation applies to each heaven as regards ʿumud rather than ʿimad. The prepositional phrase (al-jārr wa al-majrūr) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: He raised them free of pillars.

﴿You see them﴾ is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) with no place in i'rab. It is brought in to confirm that the heavens are raised in this way, as if it were said: "What is the proof of that?" and the answer was: "Your seeing them without pillars." It is like your saying: "I am without sword or spear, do you see me?"

It is possible that the resumption is grammatical without an implied question and answer, but the first is better. It is also permitted that the clause be in the position of a circumstantial clause from "the heavens," meaning: He raised them visible to you without pillars. This is a future-anticipated circumstance (ḥāl muqaddara), since those addressed did not yet exist when they were raised. In either case the object pronoun refers to the heavens.

It is also permitted that the clause be an attribute of "pillars," so the pronoun refers to them. Support for this is drawn from Ubayy's reading ﴿tarawnahu﴾ (you see it, masculine), since the apparent sense is that the pronoun refers to ʿamad, and its masculine form then is clearly appropriate, because it is a collective noun and its root in the singular was considered. Its return to "raising" is contrary to the apparent sense. On the reading as an attribute, it is possible that the negation applies to both the attribute and the qualified noun, along the lines of the verse:

"And you do not see the lizard burrowing in it,"

because if they had pillars they would be visible. This is in meaning like the resumption. It is also possible that the negation applies only to the attribute, which indicates that they have pillars but these are not visible. This was reported from Mujahid and others. What is meant by the pillars is the power of Allah the Exalted, who holds the sky from falling upon the earth, so ʿamad on this view is a metaphor (istiʿara).

Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "The sky rests on four angels, with an angel entrusted to each corner." Some claimed that the pillars are Mount Qaf, since it surrounds the earth and the sky is upon it like a dome. The Imam (al-Razi) criticised this as utterly baseless, and what may be meant by it will come, if Allah the Exalted wills. I do not find that what preceded from Ibn ʿAbbās is authentic. So the truth is that the pillars are the power of Allah the Exalted. This is evidence for the existence of the Wise Creator, exalted is His majesty, because the raising of the heavens above the other bodies equal to them in corporeality (jirmiyya), as established in its place, and their being specified by what requires that raising, must have a specifier that is neither a body nor corporeal, which prefers some possibilities over others by His will.

[Page 89]

Al-Kashshaf (the Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari) preferred the resumption, arguing that proof by the raising of these bodies without pillars is sufficient, and that the appeal to their being observed and perceived is a confirmation of the verification. Then it is not hidden that when the object pronoun in ﴿you see them﴾ refers to the raised heavens, the apparent sense of the verse requires that the thing seen is the sky. The philosophers have stated that what is seen is the sphere of vapour and its thickness, as the author of al-Tuḥfa (the Tuhfa) said: fifty-one miles and fifty-nine minutes, the total being approximately seventeen and a third farsakhs. They mentioned that the reason it appears blue is that it is always illuminated by the rays of the stars, while what lies beyond it, not accepting light, is like darkness relative to it. When the sight's light passes from the parts illuminated by the rays to the parts that are like darkness, the viewer sees what is above it, dark, mixed with the earthly and stellar light, as an intermediate colour between darkness and light, namely the azure colour. This is like when we look from a translucent red body at a green body, where a mixed colour appears to us made of red and green. They agreed that the heavens, which are the spheres, are not seen, because they are transparent and have no colour, since they do not block the eyes from seeing what lies beyond them of the stars, and everything coloured is blocked from that. The Imam al-Razi criticised this, saying: "We do not grant that every coloured thing is an obstruction, since water and glass are coloured, because they are seen, and yet they do not block. If it is said that they do obstruct perfect sight, we say: how do you know that you perceived these stars with complete perception?" End of quotation. Moreover, what they mentioned does not apply to the outermost sphere (al-muḥaddad), since there is nothing beyond it to be seen, nor to the sphere they call the sphere of the fixed stars (falak al-thawabit), since there is no visible star above it. Nor may they say: "If each of them were coloured, its colour would have to be seen." For we say: its colour may be weak, like the colour of glass, so it is not seen from afar. And even if we grant that its colour must be seen, we say: why is it not possible that this clear azure which is seen is its colour, and that what was mentioned first concerning it, excluding its affirmation, is the sphere of fire? As for what is said, that it is a matter that is pleasing in the transparent when its depth is great, as in the sea water, which is seen blue with varying blueness according to the varying depth, near and far, then the mentioned blueness is a colour imagined in the air between the sky and the earth, since it is transparent, and the greatness of its depth profits nothing, because blueness, though it may be an imagined colour, may also be a real colour inherent in bodies. What proof is there that it does not arise except by that imagined way? So it is possible that the seen blueness is a real colour of one of the two spheres. Thus said some verifiers.

You know that there is no obstacle, according to the Muslims, to the seen thing being the lowest heaven, called the sphere of the moon by the philosophers. Indeed, this is what the apparent texts require. We do not grant that what they mention of the layers of air is an obstacle. This blueness may be a real colour of that heaven, which Allah the Exalted coloured it with as His wisdom required, and the traditionalists (al-Athariyyun) hold this, as al-Qastallani said. It is supported by the apparent sense of what is authentically transmitted from the saying of the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace: "The green (sky) has not overshadowed, nor has the dusty earth carried, anyone more truthful in speech than Abu Dharr." In another narration: "from the earth." It is possible that it is an imagined colour in one of the layers of the transparent air which Allah filled between the sky and the earth, and that it has in itself a real colour whose manner Allah the Exalted knows best. There is no distance in its being white, and this is what some reports indicate. But we see it from behind that air in this manner, just as we see a white thing from behind a green glass as green, and from behind a blue glass as blue, and so on. It was reported in some narrations that this is the reflection of the colour of Mount Qaf upon it.

It has been objected that Mount Qaf does not exist, and this has been refuted by proof that repels it, as al-ʿAllama Ibn Ḥajar said: what came from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, through chains collected by the memorisers (ḥuffaz) and a group among those who committed themselves to collecting the authentic, and the statement of a Companion of this kind, in which there is no room for personal opinion, has the ruling of what is raised to the Prophet (ﷺ). Among these reports: that beyond our earth is an encompassing sea, then a mountain called Qaf, then an earth, then a sea, then a mountain, and so on, until he counted seven of each. Some of those transmitters reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn Buraydah that it is a mountain of emerald encompassing the world, upon which are the two wings of the sky. The same was reported from Mujahid. The author of Ḥall al-Rumuz (Ḥall al-Rumuz) relates that it has seven branches, and that each heaven has one branch. There is doubt in the heart about the soundness of this. Indeed I am certain that the sky is not carried except upon the shoulder of power, and the apparent sense is that it encompasses the earth from all its directions, as was reported from al-Ḥasan. As for the blueness, the two possibilities remain.

The discussion of the seeing of the remaining heavens remains. The apparent sense of the verse requires it, and I suppose you do not see that, while some verses support you. So you need to say that the remaining heavens, even if they are not truly seen, are in the status of the seen, because if this one has no pillar, it cannot be conceived that what lies beyond it has a pillar upon which it stands in any way. This returns to the meaning that "you see them" is either literally or by ruling, "without pillars." It is permitted that the meaning is "you see their raising," that is, the heavens altogether, without that. Al-Kashshaf indicates this. If the pronoun is taken to refer to the pillars, the matter is clear, so reflect. Among the remote views that we do not accept is that of some who claimed that ﴿you see them﴾ is a statement in form but its meaning is a command: "See them, and look whether they have any pillars."

﴿Then He established Himself﴾ — Glory be to Him — with an establishment befitting His essence ﴿upon the Throne﴾, which is the outermost sphere in the language of the philosophers. Reports have come concerning its greatness that dazzle the minds. Many of the later scholars (al-Khalaf) made the wording a figurative expression (istiʿara tamthiliyya) for protection and governance. Some interpreted "established" as "took dominion" (istawla). The position of the early scholars (al-Salaf) on this is well known, yet we have already discussed it. Whatever the case, it does not mean the intention to create the Throne, as they said regarding His saying: ﴿Then He turned to the sky and made them seven heavens﴾, because its creation was before the creation of the heavens. There is no need to take it as intention while maintaining the precedence of creation. The ﴿then﴾ is taken as a delay in rank. Yes, some said: it is for a delay in rank, not because establishing has the meaning of intention mentioned, which precedes, but because it is an eternal attribute befitting Him, the Exalted in majesty, which also precedes the raising of the heavens, and between them there is a delay in rank.

﴿He subjected the sun and the moon﴾: He made them submissive and made them obedient to what was intended from them. ﴿Each﴾ of the sun and the moon ﴿runs﴾: moves through the stations and degrees ﴿for a term specified﴾: that is, a fixed time. The sun completes the orbit in a year and the moon in a month, and the running of each of them does not differ, in His saying: ﴿And the sun runs to its appointed resting place﴾.

The moon—We have measured it in stations.” This is what is related from Ibn ‘Abbas. It has also been said: each of them runs toward a set term, beyond which its course does not extend, and that term is ﴿When the sun is wound up﴾ and ﴿And when the stars fall, scattered﴾. This is the meaning Mujahid gave to the phrase “the appointed term” (al-ajal al-musamma) as “the world.” It has been said: the correct interpretation is what is related from the learned man (al-Habr, a title of Ibn ‘Abbas). As for the second view, it does not fit the separation between the subjugation (al-taskhir) and the governance (al-tadbir). Moreover, their end is one and the same. The expression “each runs” is explicit in plurality, and what marks the end is ‘ila (“to”), not al-lam. It was objected that if he meant that this expression is explicit in the plurality of the one who has the end, then that is granted, but it is of no use. If he meant its explicitness in the plurality of the end, then that is not granted; al-lam comes with the meaning of ila, as in the sense and elsewhere, and you know that this yields no more than the soundness of the second interpretation, so understand. What we have indicated regarding the meaning of “each” is the apparent one. Ibn ‘Atiyyah claimed that the mention of the sun and the moon includes the mention of the stars, so the meaning of “each of them” includes what is like them among the stars. The truth is what you have learned.

﴿He governs the affair﴾, that is, the affair of the upper and lower worlds. The meaning is that He, glory be to Him, decrees, determines, and disposes of these things in the most perfect manner. Otherwise, tadbir in its lexical sense implies reflecting on the “back” (dubur) of matters, which cannot be attributed to Him, exalted is He.

﴿He details the signs﴾, that is, He sends them down and makes them clear in detail. By “the signs” is meant the verses of the revealed books, or the Qur’an, as is appropriate to what precedes. Or by them is meant the proofs indicated earlier, and “detailing” them means making them clear. It has also been said that it means producing them, as is appropriate to what follows.

Both sentences may be considered resumptive, or they may be circumstantial clauses (ahwal) from the pronoun in istawa and sakhkhara, being part of its completion, on the basis that it was brought to establish and clarify the meaning of istiwa’. Or they may be a clause explaining it. It is also permitted that ﴿He governs﴾ be a circumstantial clause from the subject of sakhkhara, and ﴿He details﴾ a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿He governs﴾, and “Allah, who…” and what follows be, on all these readings, a subject and predicate. It is also permitted that the glorious Name be the subject, the relative clause its qualifier, the clause ﴿He governs﴾ its predicate, and the clause ﴿He details﴾ a predicate after a predicate. The reading that this is a subject and predicate was preferred in al-Kashshaf, because His saying, exalted is He, which comes later, ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾, is joined to it in the manner of contrast between the heavenly things and the earthly things. In the counterpart, the predicative reading is required, so this one is likewise, so that the two correspond. Also, it indicates that His being such is the object intended by the judgment, not that it is a means toward establishing the predicate and magnifying it, as in the other view. Then he said: On this view, it is a clause confirming His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth﴾. He turned away from the pronoun of the Lord to the explicit, comprehensive Name, to emphasize the confirmation, as if it were said: how could the one whose acts are these not be the sender of the truth, than which there is no greater truth? In bringing the subject and predicate both as definite, there is what establishes that these acts are His alone, without partnership. This is especially so since they have been made relative clauses (silat) for the relative pronoun, and this is more fitting to the context than making it a descriptive clause, which would establish His being the one who governs and details, while also magnifying the status of both, as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Indeed He who raised the heaven built for us
a house whose pillars are mightier and loftier.

The mention of the signs being an inferior support is weak, because the signs in the two places have different meanings, and because the appropriate arrangement would then be for it to come after His words: ﴿And it is He who stretched out the earth﴾ ... etc. Moreover, the attributes in question, namely the raising of the heavens and what follows it, are for the stated purpose, while their counterparts are for a different and incompatible purpose. In the first case there is a subtle point, in that the first items are followed by His words, glorified is He: (yudabbiru, yufassilu) [the verbs in the singular, "He arranges, He details"], for certainty. The second are followed by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾, that is, from the excellence of the preceding items, because they give certainty, while the following items are means to attaining it, since reflection (fikr) is its instrument. The indication of placing the second items first is relative to us, despite their being later in rank, and that is lost on the other reading. End quote. This is very good in my view. As al-Shihab said, there is no contradiction between the two readings, on the basis that the descriptive reading (wasfiyya) requires that the matter be known, while the reading as a predicate (khabariyya) requires otherwise, because knowledge is required in both. The purpose of the statement is His words: ﴿so that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord﴾. (2) That is, so that you may reflect and verify the perfection of His power, glorified is He, and thereby know that whoever has power over that has power over the resurrection and the recompense. Its summary is that He, glorified is He, did all of that for this purpose. On the other reading, He did the last two for this purpose, although the whole belongs to Him. Then he said: This also favours the first reading, just as it is favoured by the fact that He mentioned the clarification of the signs, which is the raising and what follows it, for He mentioned them so that they might be used as evidence of His power and knowledge, and they can only be used as evidence if they are known, so this requires that they be descriptive.

If it is objected: the relative clause must be known, whether it is a descriptive or a predicate. It is said: if that is a relative clause, it indicates the attribution of the signs to God, the Exalted; and if it is a predicate, it indicates their attribution to an unspecified existent, which is insufficient for the inference. So consider this carefully.

Al-Nakha'i, Abu Razin, and Aban ibn Taghlib, on the authority of Qatada, read (nudabbiru, nufassilu) with the "nun" in both. Similarly, Abu 'Amr al-Dani narrated it on the authority of al-Hasan. Al-Khaffaf and 'Abd al-Wahhab on the authority of Abu 'Amr, and Hubayra on the authority of Hafs, agreed on (nufassilu) with the "nun". The author of al-Lawami' said: it came from al-Hasan and al-A'mash as (nufassilu) with the "nun". Al-Mahdawi said: there is no difference of reading regarding (yudabbiru), but this is not as he said, as you have heard.

Then, when He, exalted is He, mentioned from the heavenly signs what He mentioned, He followed them with mention of the earthly proofs, so He, exalted is His majesty, said: ﴿And it is He who stretched out the earth﴾, that is, spread it out in length and breadth. Al-Asamm said: the spreading is the stretching out to a point whose end cannot be seen, so there is in it an indication of the vastness of its extent and the breadth of its regions. It was said: it was gathered together, and then He spread it out from Mecca, from beneath the House. It was also said: it was gathered together at Bayt al-Maqdis, then He spread it out and said to it: "Go here and there," and that is what is meant by the stretching. It is not hidden that this is contrary to what the context requires.

The verse has been used as evidence that the earth is flat, not spherical. The philosophers differ on this. A group among them held that it is not spherical, and these are two sects. One says it is convex on top and flat on the bottom, so it is like a bowl turned over upon the surface of the water. The other says the opposite. Most of them held that it is spherical. As for its length, that is because the lands that share the same latitude, or have no latitude, whenever they are nearer the west, the rising of the sun and of the other stars over them is delayed by the same proportion, and this cannot be conceived except in a sphere. As for its latitude, that is because the traveller going into the north, whenever he proceeds further into it, the pole rises higher above him in proportion to his advance, at a uniform rate, so that he sees it near the zenith of his head. Likewise the northern stars appear to him and the southern stars become hidden from him. The traveller going far into the south has the opposite experience. As for the places between these, it is because of the combination of the two matters.

The visible unevenness of its surface was raised as an objection against them. They answered that this does not impair the basic sphericity, which is known by sensory observation through what has been mentioned, for the ratio of the height of the greatest mountains, according to what their induction has established and what their opinions have arrived at, namely Mount Damavand between al-Rayy and Tabaristan, or a mountain in Serendib, to the radius of the earth is like the ratio of a seventh of the width of a barleycorn to a cubit.

This was objected to: suppose what you have said is so; what is your view of what is submerged in water? If they say: when the visible part is spherical, the remainder is also, because it is one nature, we reply: then the matter returns to simplicity, and its requirement is true sphericity, and there is no doubt that the unevenness prevents this, even if it is not apparent to the senses because it is extremely small. But you know that the teachers are content with sensory sphericity on the visible surface, so the question about the submerged part does not apply to them, and it is not fitting for them to answer by appealing to simplicity. The truth, which none denies except an ignorant person or one who feigns ignorance, is that what appears of it is spherical to the senses. That is why the sphere of the heavens differs, and the times of the prayers differ in the lands. Noon may occur in one land and not in another, and likewise sunrise and sunset and other things. As for the sphericity of what lies beyond what has been mentioned, no one knows it except God, the Exalted. Yes, because of its great visible mass, every piece and region of it is seen as if it were flat, and likewise every great circle. By this it is known that there is no contradiction between the spreading and its being spherical.

Ibn 'Atiyya claimed that the apparent meaning of the Sharia requires that it be flat, and it seems he holds that view, which is contrary to what the evidence requires. According to them, it consists of three layers: the pure layer surrounding the centre, then the clayey layer, then the mixed layer in which minerals and many plants and animals come to be. The pure layer, according to some of them, is not coloured. Ibn Sina inclined to the view that it is coloured. He argued against this: the earth that exists with us, although mixed with other things, is such that we find in it what is predominantly earthy. So if the basic earth were transparent, then we should see, in some part of the earth that is not formed by mineral formation, something that has transparency. The earth would be in this respect like water and air, for although they are mixed, they have not entirely lost transparency.

Those who held that it is coloured differed. Some said its colour is greyness (ghabara), and others claimed it is blackness. The one who claimed blackness said that greyness only occurs when earthy particles are mixed with airy particles, and by them the matter fractures and greyness results. But when those particles gather such that no many airy particles mix with them, blackness becomes intense, as with charcoal before it turns to ash. Fire has no action except in separating mixed things. So when it dissolved the airiness in the wood and the earthy particles gathered without any foreign thing intervening, the colour of its particles appeared, which is black. Then when it turns to ash, airy particles mix with those particles, so they become white again. For this reason it is correct in the report, and the term "the grey land" (al-ghabra') has already been applied to the earth, and it is possible that all its layers are like that, and possible that its upper face is like that. Yes, in some reports it is related that beneath the earth there is white dust. What has been mentioned of the layers does not contradict any sound report on this. As for the claim that there are seven layers, with between each layer and another the distance that is between each heaven and another, five hundred years, and in each there is a creation not among Muslims, and of the earth the like of them, this is not established, as you will know, God willing. The report on this is also not established as sound. Similar to this, in my view, is what is related from Ka'b, who said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him: God, exalted is He, made the distance between east and west five hundred years' journey: a hundred years in the east where nothing of animals dwells, neither jinn nor humans nor beasts, and no tree is there; a hundred years in the west likewise; and three hundred years between east and west where animals dwell. Likewise what Ibn Abi Hatim related on the authority of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, that the world is a journey of five hundred years: four hundred years are ruin and one hundred years are inhabited.

[Page 92]

The established view among the experts in geometry and astronomy is other than this. The early ones among them mentioned that the circumference of the circle of the earth parallel to the meridian circle is eight thousand farsakhs, obtained by multiplying the farsakhs of one degree, which they say is twenty-two and nine farsakhs, by three hundred and sixty, the circumference of the great circle on the earth. The later ones say that this is six thousand eight hundred farsakhs, obtained by multiplying the farsakhs of one degree, which they say is nineteen farsakhs minus nine farsakhs, by the aforementioned circumference. On both views, the discrepancy between what the geometers and their companions say and what is attributed to others from earlier times is a great matter, and the truth in this is with the geometers.

They claimed that the natural place is the centre of the sphere, and that by its nature the earth requires that it be submerged in water, still at the very centre of it. But because hills, mountains and high places came to be in one side of it, and the opposite in another side, for reasons you will hear later, God willing, and because it is in the nature of water to flow from high places to low places, the raised side of the earth was uncovered and the water flowed to its low sides. The stars, in their view, have an influence on this according to the conjunctions which change with their movements, especially the fixed stars and the apogees and perigees, which vary in their positions. The astronomers judged that the length of the uncovered land is half the earth's circumference, and its breadth is one quarter of it, toward the north. As to which of the two northern quarters is uncovered, its determination is impossible or difficult, as the author of al-Tuhfa said. As for what is other than that, al-Imam said: there is no proof that it is submerged in water, but it is more likely that it is, since water exceeds the earth many times over. For every element must be such that if it were entirely transformed into another similar element, and water diminishes in volume when it turns into earth, then, in addition, if there were in some places of the three remaining quarters a small inhabitation that is not counted, then beneath the two poles there cannot be habitation because of the intensity of the cold.

They judged that the inhabited part is a quarter because they did not find, in the observations of celestial events such as eclipses and conjunctions of stars that have no difference in aspect, a difference in the hours of those who are in the east regarding those events beyond the hours of those in the west, exceeding twelve equal hours, which is half the cycle. For each hour is fifteen degrees of the equator, approximately, and multiplying fifteen by twelve gives one hundred and eighty. We say that ruin exists and that it is much more than the inhabited part, and most of the inhabited part is northern, and in the south there is only a small amount of it. But we say: what they claimed as the cause of the uncovering is not granted. We attribute the fact that the earth is such that it was found suitable for the dwelling of animals and the growth of plants to the power and choice of God, glorified is He. Otherwise, the most just of knowledge is that there is no way for reason to know the cause of that with certainty. He said: He, exalted is He, did that to the earth merely by His will, which accords with wisdom.

[Page 92]

﴿And He placed within it firm mountains﴾, meaning mountains that are fixed in their places, from *rusuw* (steadiness), which is the stability of heavy bodies. The qualified noun is not mentioned, because the dominance of the attribute with these words makes it unnecessary. *Fawa'il* is the plural of *fa'il* when the latter is an attribute of a feminine noun, as in *ha'id* (menstruating), or an attribute of a masculine noun that does not denote a rational being, as in *jul' bazil* (a camel in its ninth year) and *bawazil*, or when it is a non-derived noun or one that functions like one, as in *ha'it* (wall) and *ha'ith*. The restriction of this plural pattern to *fawaris*, *hawalik* and *nawakis* applies only to attributes of rational beings, not absolutely. The plural here is used for an attribute of a non-rational being. It has been said: then there is no need to make the singular *rasiya* here an attribute of the paucity plural *ajbul*. It is also said that in the plural of abundance, *jibal*, one considers that it incorporates a group of paucity plurals, each of which is treated as its singular. However, it has been said in response that there is no room for this, because the pluralness of each of the two plural forms is only in the sense of covering the singular, not in the sense that the paucity plural covers the singular while the abundance plural covers the paucity plurals. Thus each of them is a plural of *jabal* (mountain), and *jibal* is not a plural of *ajbul*. End of quotation. It has been objected to this that whoever said that *rawasi* here is the plural of *rasiya*, an attribute of *ajbul*, is not bound by what they mentioned. If it is valid to apply *ajbul rasiya* to the mountains of a particular region, for example, then it is valid to apply *jibal* to the mountains of all regions without considering *jibal* as the plural of the paucity plurals. Yes, it is not valid for *jibal* to be the plural of *ajbul*, because then it would be a plural of a plural, which contradicts what the lexicographers have explicitly stated. Making *rasiya* an attribute of *jabal* rather than *ajbul*, with the *ta'* in it being for emphasis (*mubalagha*) and not for feminization, as in *allama* (very learned), is also possible. It is objected to this that the *ta'* of emphasis in the pattern *fa'ila* is not consistent.

Abu Hayyan said: the description of mountains as *rawasi* has become dominant, and for this reason they have dispensed with the qualified noun by means of the attribute. The plural of a plural of a noun is like *ha'it* and *hawa'it*, and this is something for which there is no need, given what you have heard. It has also been objected to this that dominance comes through frequency of usage, and the question of its validity is from the outset, so his argument is circular. It has been answered that the frequent use of *rawasi* is not applied to a qualified noun, which is sufficient for his claim. There is room for reflection on this. Likewise, there is no need for what has been said: that it is the plural of *rasiya*, an attribute of *jabal*, feminine in consideration of the area. All of this arises from heedlessness toward what the research scholars of the Arabic sciences have mentioned.

Furthermore, the expression of mountains by this title is to show that the earth's settledness branches from their stability. In a report: "When God Most High created the earth, it began to sway, so God Most High created the mountains upon it, and it settled. The angels said: 'Our Lord, You have created a creation greater than the mountains.' He said: 'Yes, iron.' They said: 'Our Lord, You have created a creation greater than iron.' He said: 'Yes, fire.' They said: 'Our Lord, You have created a creation greater than fire.' He said: 'Yes, water.' They said: 'Our Lord, You have created a creation greater than water.' He said: 'Yes, wind.' They said: 'Our Lord, You have created a creation greater than wind.' He said: 'Yes, the son of Adam who gives charity with his right hand and conceals it from his left.'"

The first mountain placed on the earth, as Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ata', was Abu Qubays. The total of the mountains visible on it is one hundred and eighty-seven mountains.

The philosophers denied that the earth's stability is due to the mountains, and they differed about the cause of this. Among those who hold the sphericity of the earth (*kurriyya*), some considered it to be the attraction of the celestial sphere toward it from all sides, which requires that it remain in the middle, as is related of an iron piece in a box with magnets on all sides: it stands in the middle because the attraction from every side is equal. This was rejected: the smaller object is quicker to be drawn to the attracting body than the larger one, so what is the matter with the clod of earth that is not drawn to the celestial sphere but rather flees from it toward the center? Also, the nearer object has a stronger claim to be attracted than the farther one, so a clod thrown upward is closer to the sphere by their principle, and it should therefore not return. Others considered it to be the repulsion of the celestial sphere by its motion from all sides, as when a bit of dust is placed in a spherical flask which is then spun rapidly around its two poles, and the dust happens to stand in the middle because the repulsion is equal from every side. This was rejected: if the repulsion has this strength, why is it not perceived? Also, what is the matter with this repulsion that it does not direct the motion of the winds and clouds toward one specific direction? Also, why did it not make our movement toward the west easier than our movement toward the east? Also, the motion of a heavy body should be greater the larger it is, because the larger body is slower to be pushed off by the pusher than the smaller one. Also, the motion of a heavy body falling from the beginning should be quicker than its motion at the end, because at the beginning it is closer to the sphere.

Those who do not hold this view said that the earth extends infinitely downward, and the reason for its rest according to them is that it has no lower place to descend into. This is refuted by the proof that bodies are finite. Others said that it is finite and that the cause is its floating on water, with its convex side upward and flat side downward, or the reverse. This was rejected: mere floating does not require rest, and in any case this view is remote from the philosophers' principles.

Their research scholars held that its rest is due to its essence, not to a separate cause. In *al-Mabahith al-Mashriqiyya* [Eastern Investigations] it is said: "The common argument in refuting what they said about the cause of rest is to say: everything you have mentioned, of attraction, repulsion and other things, consists of accidental and non-natural matters, not necessary to the quiddity. So it is valid to assume the quiddity of the earth devoid of them. When we suppose the occurrence of this possible matter, either it will be located in a specific place or it will not be located in it. In that case, either it will be located in all places or in none of them. The last two are clearly false, so the first is determined: that it is specifically located in a determinate place, and this is due to its particular nature. In that case its rest in the place is due to its essence, not to a separate cause. If this is understood, then let its being specifically located at the center be understood in the same way." Then he mentioned several investigations concerning the formation of mountains. The first: a large rock is formed because great heat encounters sticky clay, either all at once or gradually.

As for elevation, it has a cause in itself and a cause by accident. The first is like when the wind that causes an earthquake lifts a portion of the earth and makes it a hill among hills. The second is when the clay, after hardening, varies in the softness and hardness of its parts, and strong-flowing waters or violently blowing winds coincide, so they dig out the soft parts and leave the hard ones. Then the torrents and winds continue to act on those hollows until they are deeply excavated, and what they have turned away from remains lofty. It is most likely that this inhabited land was in ancient times submerged in seas, so abundant sticky clay settled there. Afterward it was uncovered and mountains formed. A supporting consideration for this assumption is that when we break many stones, we find within them parts of sea animals such as shells. Then, when the mountains came into being and the seas moved, rising occurred, either because torrents dug out what lies between the mountains, or because what was uncovered of these was more firmly hardened and of harder clay, so when what lies beneath it collapsed, it remained higher and loftier. However, these are matters that cannot be completed within a period that history can record.

The second: the cause of the veins of clay in the mountains may be that some of what crumbles from them becomes dust, is moistened by water, or is mixed with good clay. It may also be due to the fact that ancient sea clay is not uniform in substance: some of it hardens strongly and some becomes weak. It may also be that the sea happens to overflow gradually onto a plain and a mountain, so the plain becomes sticky clay ready for strong hardening, and the mountain crumbles, as when you soak a brick and dust in water, then expose the brick and the clay to fire: the brick crumbles and the clay remains hardened.

The third: we sometimes see some mountains stacked in layers, one stratum after another. This is likely because its clay was arranged in this manner: one stratum was first deposited, and then after a period another stratum formed and was deposited. Each stratum had been flowing with substance different from the other, so it became a barrier between it and the other stratum. When the material hardened, the barrier became disintegrated from between the two strata.

Yet the causes they have mentioned for formation have been criticized: it is not hidden that the specific hardness of some parts of the earth and the softness of others, while the relation of all those parts to the celestial bodies, which they claim are their preparatory causes, is equal, requires a determining cause, because of the contiguity and adjacency between the soft and hard parts. At this point the intellect stops and attributes this specificity to an external cause, namely the Chooser, the Agent, may His majesty be exalted. So I wonder why He did not do it first, without the burden. Yes, it is not far-fetched that this may be among the causes of their formation by the will of God Most High, according to those among the followers of revealed religions and others who speak of intermediaries, but not according to the Ash'aris, since everything for them is directly attributed to Him, glorified is He. Thus an actual intermediary is inconceivable on their view. The causes mentioned are matters that yield only weak conjecture. As for the observation of parts of sea animals such as shells, it is likewise: we often see such things in places of rainfall, and someone I trust has told me that he witnessed frogs that had fallen in rain. Moreover, this does not hold if the uncovered part of the earth was uncovered at the beginning of creation and was not submerged in water, and then became uncovered. This is also what some research philosophers have held. They raised objections against those who say that uncovering occurred later, arguing that the strongest of their proofs is that the sun's perihelion lies in the southern direction, so the sun is nearer to the earth there than on the northern side by the thickness of the complement of its equator. Therefore the heat is intensified there, and water is drawn from the north to the south, since heat attracts moisture. For this reason the northern quarter was uncovered. When the perihelion shifts to the northern side, the matter is reversed. This is refuted by the argument that if this were so, the other northern quarter would also be uncovered, since there is no difference between the two quarters in this respect. To commit to this is remote, and no one has committed to it.

Then, the existence of mountains in the submerged part, which is their existence in the inhabited part, requires that it was once inhabited and that the lowland was in a direction other than its present one. This is a statement that land continues to be sea and sea continues to be land through the alternation of the directions of the apogee and perigee, so that what is uncovered is at times the northern side and at other times the southern side. Since this occurs gradually, it would require that today we should observe some of the southern side uncovered and some of the northern side submerged. Do not suppose that this exists; for if it did, it would be well known. Indeed, the apogee of the sun today is at the tenth degree of Cancer, and its movement each year is about one minute. Thus, from the time it moved from the northern side until today, there have been many thousands of years, during which much was submerged and much was inhabited. Yes, it is related that the island of Cyprus was once connected to the mainland, then the sea came between them. But even if this is established, it is not what we are discussing, and we do not grant that the world is one that has been uncovered by what has occurred, since it may have been uncovered before. Therefore the truth is that this land, after it came into existence, did not become sea, and this ocean, after it encompassed, did not become land. This is what the divine reports and the prophetic traditions require. Yes, some reports have come whose apparent meaning is that the inhabited earth was uncovered at the beginning of creation, like the report of the ruby; and in others their apparent meaning is that it was submerged, like the report of Ibn Abbas that when God Most High wished to create the creation, He commanded the wind, and it uncovered a foam-like substance (hashafa), and from it the earth was spread out to the extent God willed in length and breadth, and it began to sway, so He placed upon it the firm mountains. In the Torah there is a text to this effect: at the beginning of the Book of Genesis, God first created the heaven and the earth, and the earth was submerged and vast, and there was darkness, and the winds of God were blowing over the face of the waters. God willed that there should be light, and there was light. Then it is mentioned in it that when a second day had passed, God willed that the water beneath the heaven should gather into one place and the dry land should appear, and it was so. God named the dry land "earth" and the gathering of the waters "seas." It also states in it that the creation of the two luminaries was on the third day. It is averse to making the cause of the uncovering what you have heard about the proximity of the sun, and to what this verse indicates and other verses declare, namely that the mountains are a cause of the earth's stability, and that without them it would sway. This is a matter for which no evidence on our principles stands, which is why we believe it even if we do not know its precise wisdom with certainty. It may be that its wisdom is that God Most High created the earth, as His wisdom required, small in comparison with the other spheres, and gave it a determined measure of weight, and placed it in the place where He placed it within the water, and made some of it appear. This is not due to anything inherent in its essence, but only to His will, which follows His wisdom, glorified is He. So it began to sway because of the agitation of the waves of the ocean surrounding it, and He placed upon it mountains by which it became heavy, such that the waves no longer had power over it. This is like what is seen in ships, where they place in them what weighs them down, such as stones and other things, for such a purpose. That the ratio of the height of the greatest mountains to it is the earlier ratio does not harm us in this context, for volume is one matter and weight is another; a small-volume thing may be far heavier than a large-volume thing. And it should not be said: it was possible to create it from the outset in such a way that the waves would not move it, so why did He not do that, but instead created it such that the waves move it, and then placed mountains upon it to counter that? For we say: glorified is He, He did so because of the wisdoms in it, which He, exalted is His majesty, knows best. This question is like asking: it was possible to create man from the outset such that hunger and thirst would have no effect on him, for example, so why did He not do that, but instead created him such that they affect him, and then created for him what repels them so that he may repel them with it? There are many similar examples. This is nothing but the result of heedlessness regarding the wisdoms that follow from what God Most High has done. Perhaps the wisdom in what we are discussing is to display the greater magnificence of His majesty to the angels, peace be upon them, for that awakens the eye of awe. Do you not see how they said, when they saw what they saw: "Our Lord, You have created a creation greater than the mountains..." etc.

It is said to one who does not believe in this: explain to us a wisdom that makes some things precede others in creation, whatever the ordering may be; and likewise the wisdom of creating man and the like in need, and creating what removes his need, rather than creating him without need in a manner requiring nothing further. If he explains something, we say the same regarding what we are discussing. Then we say: the wisdom of creating the mountains is not confined to their being pegs for the earth and a cause of its stability; rather there are many wisdoms that none knows but God Most High.

The philosophers have mentioned many benefits of the mountains. They said: the material of clouds, springs and mineral things is vapour, so they form only in mountains or what is near them. As for springs, when the earth is loose the vapours dissipate from it, so no appreciable quantity gathers; hence they gather only in solid earth, and mountains are the hardest of lands, so they are naturally the strongest in holding back the vapour until what is suitable to be the material of springs gathers. It is likely that the bed of the mountain is filled with water, and the mountain, in retaining the vapours, is like a solid alembic prepared for distillation that lets none of the vapour escape; the earth beneath it is like the cucurbit, the springs are like the tails in alembics, and the valleys and vapour are like the receivers. For this reason most springs burst forth from mountains, and fewest in deserts; and this too occurs only when the earth is solid. As for the fact that most clouds form over mountains, there are several reasons. The first is that within mountains there are moistures not found within loose lands. The second is that mountains, because of their height, are cooler, so there remains on their surfaces dews and snows that do not remain on the surfaces of lands. The third is that the rising vapours gather over mountains. When this is established, it becomes clear that the causes of the accumulation of clouds are greater over mountains, because the material there, outwardly and inwardly, is greater, the retention is stronger, and the dissolving cause, which is heat, is less. As for mineral things that need vapours, their mixture with earthy matter is greater, and they remain in places where they are not scattered longer; and nothing in this sense is like mountains. Whoever reflects will know that mountains have benefits beyond these that cannot be counted. So it does no harm that some people, beyond this, deny some of what has been mentioned. I have heard from some contemporary people that among their benefits is that they are a cause for the uncovering of this amount of land that is seen, owing to the retention of the vapours that seek the direction of height in them. This requires that the earth before them was submerged, which is contrary to what the apparent meaning of his statement, peace be upon him, implies: "When God Most High created the earth, it began to sway, so He placed mountains upon it and it became stable." It appears that there is a conflict between their being pegs, as stated in the verses, and their being a force drawing the earth towards the direction of height. There is no objection to what has been said regarding their being a cause of the earth's stability: that their being in it like a keel in a ship contradicts it, since that would require the earth to move against the direction of the blowing wind, because we are beyond preventing the occurrence of wind in a manner that moves it by its cause in that way.

All of this is when we apply reason to what is apparent and restrict ourselves to customary matters. But if we attribute all of that to the power of the Doer who chooses, exalted is His majesty, and say: He, glorified is He, created the earth spread out, placed mountains upon it, and preserved it from swaying for wisdoms He knows, in which thoughts are bewildered and which none encompasses except those given knowledge from His presence among those with insight, then all burdens are lifted from us and all trials removed. Nor does it follow for us on this basis that the earth is the centre of the world, as is the opinion of most earlier and later philosophers.

Only a small group of the ancients disagreed, claiming that the sphere of fire is at the centre because it is more noble than the earth, being luminous, subtle and of fine colour, while the earth is dense, dark and of ugly colour, and the place of the noble must be the noblest place, which is the centre; so it is at the centre. This is one of the weak persuasions. Even so, it is answered that we do not grant the nobility of fire over the earth absolutely. If it is preferred in subtlety and what goes with it, the earth is preferred in several respects. The first is that fire in excessive quality is corrupting, and the earth is not so. The second is that it does not remain in a foreign place as the earth does. The third is that the earth is the sphere of life and growth, and fire is not so. What is mentioned of the visual sense's appreciation of fire is countered by the tactile sense's appreciation of the earth in relation to it. Moreover, even if we grant its nobility, it requires only a central place of honour, not a central place of quantity, since there is no honour in that; and that is nothing other than its place which most earlier thinkers claim for it, because it lies between the elemental bodies and the celestial bodies. Among the later thinkers, only a small group disagreed: Herschel and his companions, who claimed that the sun is at rest in the centre of the world and everything else moves around it, because it is a very great body, and all bodies are below it, especially the earth, which relative to it is as nothing; and the wisdom is that the greater rests and the smaller moves. This too is one of the weak persuasions. Even so, it is answered that the rest of the smaller, especially amid waves and winds, and the motion of the greater, especially the kind of motion that most people attribute to the sun, is more forceful in power; and their justification of this by saying that we do not see the sun deviating from what is called the zodiac belt, so it should be at rest unlike others, is not without its problems. What many people incline to is that beneath the earth there is water, and that it is in it like a green watermelon in a basin. It has come in some reports that the earth is on the back of an ox, the ox on the back of a fish, and the fish in the water, and none knows what is under the water except He who created it. Many have mentioned that the caudate lobe of that fish's liver is what will be the first food of the people of Paradise. They took the fish, based on what is authentically reported from his saying ﷺ: "The first thing the people of Paradise will eat is the caudate lobe of the fish's liver," as referring to that fish, and explained the wisdom of that eating as an indication of the ruin of the world and a good tiding of the corruption of its foundation and the safety of returning to it, since the earth they used to inhabit was resting upon it. The eating was specified as the caudate lobe because physicians have explained that if the disease falls on the liver but not on the caudate lobe, recovery is hoped for, whereas if it falls on the caudate lobe the patient perishes; so their eating of that is more emphatic as a tiding. Some denied the soundness of reports indicating that it is not directly upon the water, especially the long report which

Al-Baghawi mentioned it in Surah "Nun" (al-Qalam) and did not deny the authenticity of the report that "the first thing the people of Paradise will eat is the caudate lobe of the fish's liver." He said, however, that by "fish" (ḥūt) in it is meant a single fish. The evidence for this is what Sultan al-Muhaddithin al-Bukhari narrated: "The first thing the people of Paradise will eat is the extra piece of the liver of a fish, from which seventy thousand will eat," with the word *ḥūt* in indefinite form.

A parallel to this is in Sahih Muslim, where it is mentioned that on the Day of Resurrection the earth will be a single loaf which the Almighty will turn over with His hand, as one of you turns his loaf on a journey, as a provision (nuzul) for the people of Paradise. Their condiment will be an ox and a nun (fish), from the extra piece of whose liver seventy thousand will eat. Mention of the state of the earth in it does not specify the intent of the opponent, for it is possible that the combination of these is to indicate the ruin of this world, the cessation of the matter of preparing for livelihood, and the termination of the elemental, watery life. As for the indication of the first, it is evident. As for the indication of the second, it is by seizing the ox and eating the extra piece of its liver, for it is the mainstay of the plowman (ḥārith), who is concerned with his livelihood. And in the report: "Each of you is a plowman, and each of you is ambitious (humām)." As for the indication of the third, it is by seizing the fish and eating the extra piece of its liver as well, for it is an elemental, aquatic animal that cannot survive even a moment when separated from water. By this the complete correspondence between what the report contains becomes clear.

It is not far-fetched that the manifestation of worldly life may be in the form of a fish, and what is necessary for it of the essential means of tillage for the matter of livelihood in the form of an ox, and that all hunting is in the belly of the wild ass (al-Fara'). This would be among the kinds of the manifestation of death in the form of the white-speckled ram on that Day.

Some of the gnostics (al-'arifin) said, concerning the secret of singling out the liver: it is the house of blood, and it is the house of life, and from it its distribution occurs in the body to the heart and other things. The vapor of that blood is the soul, which is expressed as the animal spirit. So in its being food for the people of Paradise there is good news that they are living and will not die.

It is also mentioned that from the ox is extracted the spleen (ṭiḥāl), which in animals is in the position of the filth in the body, for the filth of the body gathers in it from the corrupt blood that the body gives it. It is given to the people of the Fire, who eat it. And this comes from the ox because it is cold and dry, like the nature of death. Jahannam is in the form of a buffalo, and the food of the people of the Fire from its spleen is more appropriate to it. Because of the bloodiness in it, the people of the Fire do not die; and because it is from the filth of the body and from corrupt, painful blood, they do not live and do not enjoy. So its eating increases them only in sickness and ailment.

It is reported from al-Ghazali, though responsibility for the report lies with the one who transmits it, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked on one occasion what is beneath the earth, and he said: "The fish." On another occasion he was asked and said: "The ox." By this (ﷺ) he meant the two constellations which are among the twelve well-known zodiacal signs (burūj). Each of them was the peg (watad) of the earth at the time of the question. If the peg at that time had been, for example, the scorpion, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have said: "The scorpion is beneath the earth." You know that this is far removed from the aims of the Lawgiver (ﷺ).

It is not complete, according to what I have come to know, that the earth is on the back of the ox, the ox on the back of the fish, and the fish on the water. The statement that what is meant is that the earth is above the ox, in consideration that it is its peg at the time of the report; and the ox is above the fish, in consideration that it is among the northern zodiacal signs, while the fish is among the southern ones; and that the northern signs in most of the inhabited world are counted above the southern signs; and that the fish is above the water, in consideration that there is no visible barrier between it and the water, and that none approaches it except an ox or an ass. [This is what is said], but it does not hold.

Some scholars interpret the report about the order (tartīb) by saying that what is meant by it is an indication that the cultivation of the earth depends on tillage, and tillage depends on striving and agitation. That ox is among the beginnings of tillage, and the fish hardly ever stops moving in the water. This is, as you see, weak.

What should be relied upon is belief in what has come from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), if it is authentic, for there is nothing beyond it, (ﷺ), of wisdom. As for the order which the philosophers mention, they have not brought any clear proof for it, and they have nothing in it except what yields conjecture (ẓann). In that case, it is possible to say [another] order.

Yes, one should not say [anything] of an order which sense contradicts and clear reason rejects. And if the like of this comes from the Lawgiver, it is obligatory to interpret it, as is not hidden.

Some of the learned scholars (fuḍalā') mentioned that no account came from the Lawgiver (ﷺ) concerning the order of the celestial and terrestrial bodies and the explanation of their states, as the philosophers did, because that is not among the important matters in his view (ﷺ). The important thing is only reflection upon them and inference from them to the oneness of the Creator and His perfection (jalla sha'nuh). This is achieved through what is perceived of them. Glory be to Him who raised the heaven without pillars (ʿamad), and spread the earth and placed in it firm mountains and ﴿rivers﴾.

"Rivers" (anhār) is the plural of *nahr*, which is the course of abundant water. It is also pluralized as *nuhur*, *nuhūr*, and *anhur*, and it is applied to flowing waters on the earth. [The verse] joined them to the mountains and attached to both one verb, in that the mountains are a cause of their formation, as has been said. It has been objected that this is based on what some philosophers held: that mountains, because they are composed of hard stones, when vapors rise to them they are retained in them and mature, and then they turn into water, and sometimes they break through and come out. It is mentioned that what the traces indicate is that they descend from the sky, but since their descent upon the mountains is greater, rivers often come forth from them. This suffices for making the two partners in one agent and making them one sentence.

It seems that by the descent from the sky upon the mountains they meant the descent of rain-water from the sky, which is one of the celestial bodies, upon them. Most say that the descent is from the clouds, and that by "sky" is meant the direction of height, which is what observation judges. We have already put before you what relates to this at the beginning of the book, so remember it.

The rivers which Allah the Exalted placed in the earth are many. Some mentioned that they are one hundred and ninety-six rivers. It has been said that they are more than that. In four of them it has come that they are from Paradise. In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Sayhan, Jayhan, the Euphrates and the Nile—each of them is among the rivers of Paradise." The first two are written with an *alif* after the *ḥā'*, and they are two rivers in the land of Urdunn. Jayhan is the river of al-Maṣīṣa, and Sayhan is the river of Adana.

As for al-Jawhari's statement in his Ṣiḥāḥ that Jayhan is a river in Syria, it is an error, or he meant it figuratively, in that it is in the lands of the Armenians, which border Syria. These two are other than Sayhun and Jayhun with a *wāw*, for Sayhun is the river of India. It flows from mountains at its far reaches, on the side facing the spring, until it empties into the Abyssinian sea on the side facing the coast of India. Its course is four hundred farsakhs. Jayhun is the river of Balkh. It flows from ʿAyn until it reaches Khwarazm, where part of it disperses into places and the remainder goes on to the lake on which is the well-known village of al-Jurjaniyya, below Khwarazm. Ships sail on it from it to there; their length is a month's journey and their breadth is about the same.

As for the statement of al-Qadi ʿIyad: "These four rivers are the greatest rivers of the lands of Islam: the Nile in Egypt, the Euphrates in Iraq, and Sayhan and Jayhan, also called Sayhun and Jayhun, in the lands of Khurasan." al-Nawawi said that in it there are objections from several aspects. The first is his saying "the Euphrates is in Iraq," whereas it is not in Iraq; it only separates Syria and al-Jazira. The second is his saying "Sayhan and Jayhan, also called Sayhun and Jayhun," thus making the names synonymous, whereas that is not so; rather Sayhan is other than Sayhun, and Jayhan is other than Jayhun, by the agreement of people. The third is his saying "in the lands of Khurasan." Sayhan and Jayhan are in the lands of the Armenians near Syria. End of quotation.

It may be answered concerning the first in a manner similar to what was answered concerning al-Jawhari. It is not hidden that after assuming synonymy, it is correct to rule that both are in the lands of Khurasan, just as it is correct to rule that both are in the lands of the Armenians.

Concerning these rivers being from Paradise, there are two interpretations. The first is that what is meant is the comparison of their waters with the waters of Paradise, and the information of their distinction over others; the like of this is common in speech. The second is what al-Qadi ʿIyad mentioned: that faith has encompassed their lands, and that the bodies nourished by them are destined for Paradise. This is nothing; but if it were referred back to considering the comparison, meaning that they are like the rivers of Paradise in that those nourished by their waters are believers, it would be more correct.

Al-Nawawi said: "The more correct view is that the statement is on its apparent sense, and that they have a source from Paradise, and it exists today according to the People of the Sunna."
