The first interpretation is rejected also by what is in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of the Night Journey (Isra'), where the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) narrated: "He saw four rivers coming out from its root: two apparent rivers and two hidden rivers. I said: 'O Jibril, what are these rivers?' He said: 'As for the two hidden rivers, they are two rivers in Paradise. As for the two apparent ones, they are the Euphrates and the Nile.'" The pronoun in "its root" refers to the Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary), as is explained in Sahih al-Bukhari and elsewhere.

Al-Qadi ʿIyad said here that this hadith indicates that the root of the Sidrat al-Muntaha is in the earth, since the Nile and the Euphrates come out from its root. al-Nawawi objected to him that this is not necessary; rather its meaning is that the rivers come out from its root, then flow wherever Allah the Exalted wills, until they emerge from the earth and flow in it. This is not prevented by reason or by the Law, and it is the apparent sense of the hadith, so it is obligatory to adopt it.

It was said: Perhaps Allah the Exalted conveys the waters of those rivers, by His overpowering power, to their places where their emergence is observed, from a place no one sees. That is not difficult for Allah. The apparent meaning is that what is meant is the source of their waters emerging from their places, not the rivers themselves and what is joined to them of torrents and others.

It seems to me that some people, such as Lisna, commit to this for everything that does not flow in those rivers. Some of them also make the reports on this matter indications only of inner matters, which is not what sound souls accept. Yet I do not forbid interpretation while the matter remains external (afāqī), and not believing the apparent sense does not harm the religion, as is not hidden to one who has no bigotry.

The Akhbaris have a lengthy discourse on these rivers which the ears of people of intellect loathe, and which does not flow in the rivers of their hearts, and I do not think it fit for anything but being cast into the sea.

There came in some reports, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Two rivers are believing and two rivers are disbelieving. As for the two believing ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates; as for the two disbelieving ones, they are the Tigris (Dijla) and Jayhun." This is taken to mean that the Prophet (ﷺ) likened the first two rivers, for their benefit with ease, to the believer, and the last two to the disbeliever, for they do not benefit in that way, since their waters mostly come out only with machinery and hardship. Otherwise, describing these with belief and disbelief in the true sense is not evident.

Furthermore, the most excellent of the rivers, as more than one has said, is the Nile, and the rest are equal. Some added the Tigris to those counted as from Paradise, and narrated a report on that from Muqatil, from Ikrima, from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is not something to be relied upon. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

﴿And of all the fruits﴾ is connected to *ja'ala* in the Exalted's saying: ﴿He made in it two spouses, two﴾. That is, two in a true duality, and they are the two singles, each of which is the spouse of the other. The "two spouses" was emphasized with it lest it be understood that what is meant by that is the pairs, since *zawj* is applied to the collective. But the duality of that is a relative (iʿtibārīya) duality: that is, He made of every kind of fruits existing in this world two types and two categories, either in color, like white and black, or in taste, like sweet and sour, or in size, like small and large, or in quality, like hot and cold, and what is similar to that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 3 (part 5 of 5):

It has been said: the meaning is that He created in the earth, from all kinds of fruits, two pairs (zawjayn, zawjayn) when He spread it out. Then they multiplied and diversified after that. It has been objected that this is an assertion without evidence, and moreover the apparent sense is contrary to it, for the rational species, which needs a pair, was created first as a male, so how could that be the case with fruits? [Page 101] One (wahid) of each kind first is sufficient for generation (al-takawwun). The correct view is what was mentioned first.

It is also permissible for the prepositional phrase (al-jarr, the preposition with its object) to be connected to the first verb "ja'ala" (He made), and the second clause to be a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new independent sentence) explaining how the making occurred.

Some have claimed that, on the assumption that the prepositional phrase is connected to the earlier "ja'ala," the "two pairs" are the sun and the moon. It has also been said that they are the night and the day. Both opinions are worthless.

﴿He covers the night over the day﴾, i.e., He clothes it in its place, so that the atmosphere becomes dark after it had been bright. In this there is an attribution (isnad) to the place of something that belongs to the thing located there. In making the atmosphere a place for the day there is a figurative usage (tajawwuz), because time has no place, and place belongs only to the light which is its necessary accompaniment.

It is also permissible in the verse to take it as a metaphor (isti'arah), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He wraps the night over the day﴾, meaning He makes the night a covering for the day, folded over it like a garment over what it clothes. It has been said: the first (interpretation) is more apt and more eloquent.

He mentioned only the night covering the day, even though the reverse is also true, because it is known from it. Yet the wording allows both. However, covering (taghshiyah) means concealment, and this is more suitable to the night than to the day. This is counted among the lower signs (al-ayat al-sufliyyah), although its connection to the higher signs (al-ayat al-ulwiyyah) is evident in terms of its manifestation on the earth.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read ﴿yughashshi﴾ with the doubled letter (shaddah). The full discussion of this has already been given.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e., in what has been mentioned: the spreading of the earth, the placing of the firm mountains upon it, the flowing of the rivers in it, the creation of the fruits, and the covering of the night over the day. Pointing to these with "that" (dhalika) indicates the great importance of what is referred to within its category.

﴿are signs﴾ that are striking (bahirah). It has been said: they are the traces of the wondrous acts, the wisdom of their Maker being exalted. Thus the "fi" (in) is in its literal sense, because those traces are settled in those acts and dependent upon them. It is also permissible that "that" refers to those traces, which are indicated by those acts.

﴿for a people who reflect﴾. [(3)] For reflecting upon them leads to the judgment that each of these, in this fine pattern and fitting arrangement, must have a Creator who is All-Powerful and All-Wise, who does what He wills and decrees what He desires.

Al-Raghib said that thought (al-fikrah) is a power that directs knowledge to the known, and reflection (al-tafakkur) is the roaming of that power according to the examination of the intellect. This belongs to the human being and not to the animal. It is not used except for what can form an image in the heart. For this reason it was related: "Reflect upon the bounties of God, and do not reflect upon God," since God, glorified be He, is too exalted to be described by any form.

Some literary men said: "al-fikr" (thought) is metathesized from "al-fark" (examining), but "al-fikr" is used for meanings, and it is the examination and investigation of matters in pursuit of reaching their reality. The well-known definition is that it is the arrangement of known matters to arrive at an unknown. The reason for making this the concluding phrase of the verse has already been explained.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) mentioned that in most verses where the proofs existing in the lower world are mentioned, its concluding phrase is made to be ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ or something close to it. Its cause is that the philosophers attribute the events of the lower world to the variations occurring in the configurations of the stars. God, exalted is He, refuted this by His saying ﴿for a people who reflect﴾, because whoever reflects upon these will know that the occurrence of those events cannot be from celestial connections. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 4:

﴿And on the earth are tracts⁠﴾ is a resumed sentence (jumla musta'nafa) containing another group of signs, meaning: on the earth there are many plots differing in their qualities, some good and producing vegetation, some saline (sabakha) that produce nothing, some soft (rakhwa) and some hard (sulba), some suitable for crops but not for trees, and some suitable for trees but not for crops, and so on. ﴿Adjoining⁠﴾ means adjacent, and the intended meaning is to inform of the variation among adjacent parts of the earth in the manner you have learned. This is what is related from the majority. Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada that the meaning is: "And on the earth are villages near one another." He also related from al-Hasan that he interpreted it as al-Ahwaz, Fars, Kufa and Basra. From here it has been said that the verse is an instance of ellipsis (iktifa'), on the pattern of ﴿garments that protect you from the heat⁠﴾, and the meaning is: tracts that are adjoining and tracts that are not adjoining. In some copies of the Qur'an (wa-qita'an mutajawiratin), with the accusative, meaning: and He placed on the earth tracts... ﴿And gardens⁠﴾, meaning many orchards, ﴿of grapes⁠﴾, meaning vineyards, ﴿and crops⁠﴾ of every kind of grain. Its singular form is used in view of its verbal origin (asl), since it is a verbal noun (masdar). Perhaps the mention of the gardens is placed before it, though it is the main pillar of livelihood, because in the making of grapes there is something that dazzles the minds, and even if there were nothing in them but that they are liquids frozen in delicate vessels, to the point that some of them are so transparent that they do not block the sight from perceiving what is within, that would suffice. For this reason a sacred report (khabar qudsi) says: "Do you disbelieve in Me while I am the Creator of the grape?" In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim the reason for this is explained by the manifest state of the gardens in their difference from and distinction from the rest, and the firmness of this in them. The mention of His saying, ﴿and palm trees⁠﴾, is delayed so that it does not fall between them and their description, which is His saying, ﴿clustered and non-clustered⁠﴾, as an interruption, or so that the separation between the two conjoined items does not become long. Sinwan is the plural of sinw, which is a branch that joins with another from one root; its origin is "similar." From this it is said: "The paternal uncle is a sinw." Pronouncing the sad with a kasra in the plural, as in the singular, is the well-known dialect, and the majority read with it. The dialect of Tamim and Qays is (ṣunwān) with a damma, like dhi'b and dhu'bān, and Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, al-Sulami and Ibn Musarrif read with it, and al-Ja'bari in his commentary on al-Shatibiyya related it from Hafs.

Al-Hasan and Qatada read with a fatha, and in that case it is an collective noun (ism jam'), like al-si'dan, not a broken plural, because it is not of its patterns. Al-Hasan read (jannatin) with the accusative, being conjoined, according to some, to zawjayn, the object of ﴿ja'ala⁠﴾ (He made), and (min kulli al-thamarat) then is a preposed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddama), not a relative clause of ﴿ja'ala⁠﴾, because the meaning would be corrupted on that reading: He made in them two pairs, being of every kind of fruit, and gardens of grapes. Here it is not necessary to restrict the conjoined item.

Some have claimed that the conjunction is upon ﴿rawasi⁠﴾ (mountains). Abu Hayyan said: "It is better to supply a verb, because of the distance between the two conjoined items," or it is in the genitive, conjoined upon (kulli al-thamarat), with the latter being the object with the addition of min in affirmative speech, and (zawjayn ithnayn) as a circumstantial clause of it. The sense is: He made in them, of every kind of fruit, two kinds (sinfayn) as a state. Perhaps the arrangement of His saying, ﴿And on the earth are tracts, adjoining⁠﴾, was not placed in this series, although the specification of "every" of those tracts with their states and attributes is by the sheer creation of the Wise Creator, may His power be exalted, when He stretched out the earth and spread it, as has been said, is an indication that those states are firmly established attributes of those tracts. A group of the seven readers read ﴿and crops and palm trees⁠﴾ with the genitive, on the basis that the conjunction is upon "grapes." This, as in al-Kashf, is of the type of "girding on a sword and a spear." Or the meaning is that in the gardens there are cultivated open spaces between the trees, for otherwise a cultivated field alone is not called a garden, and this is more beautiful in appearance and more pleasant. Abu Hayyan claimed that in describing the garden as of grapes there is a figurative usage, because the garden in reality is the land in which the grapes are.

﴿And it is watered⁠﴾, meaning what has been mentioned of the tracts, gardens, crops and palm trees. Most of the seven read with the feminine, observing the wording, and this is the reading of al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far. It has been said: the first is more fitting to the context of explaining the uniformity of all in the state of irrigation with one water, with no difference in its nature, whether the irrigation is from rainwater or from river water. It has also been said: the second is more fitting to His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿and We favour⁠﴾, meaning, along with the existence of the causes of similarity, by the sheer power and kindness of Ours, ﴿some of it over some other⁠﴾ of it, ﴿in the fruit⁠﴾, because of the feminine. Hamza and al-Kisa'i incline the fatha of the qaf. Al-Ukul with a damma on the hamza and the kaf, and its sukun in place of it, means what is eaten, which here is fruit and grain. The saying of some: "meaning in the fruit, in shape, measure, scent and taste, by way of predominance (taghlib)." Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (yufaddilu) with the ya', in the active form, as a response to (yudabbiru), (yufassilu) and (yughshi). Yahya ibn Ya'mur, who was the first to dot the Mushaf, and Abu Haywa and al-Halabi from 'Abd al-Warith read with the ya' in the passive form, and raised some of it (ba'duha). In this there is what is not hidden of majesty and of indicating that the impossibility of the verb being attributed to another agent suffices in place of building the verb for the active.

﴿Indeed in that⁠﴾, which has been detailed of the states of the tracts and other things, ﴿are signs⁠﴾, many, great and striking, ﴿for a people who use reason⁠﴾. (4)

They act according to the dictates of their intellects, for whoever understands those strange states, and the emergence of different fruits in shapes, colours, tastes and scents from those differing and adjacent tracts, along with the taking of what they are watered with, and indeed all the causes of their growth, will not hesitate to affirm with certainty that for this there is a wise Maker, a capable Governor of them, whom nothing can defeat. It has also been said: the meaning is that whoever understands this does not hesitate to affirm that whoever is able to originate what has been mentioned is able to restore what He originated, indeed this is easier by analogy. What was mentioned first is perhaps more appropriate. Then, although the states are themselves the signs and not merely contain them, they have been stripped of their like, for emphasis on their being a sign. So it is with the stripping of its like in His saying, ﴿For them therein is the abode of eternity⁠﴾, according to the well-known view. It is also permitted that the thing pointed to is the general states, and the signs are their individual instances occurring gradually over times, and their single occurrences in regions and places witnessed by their people, so "in" retains its meaning. Some explained the signs as indications (dalalat) so that "in" remains in that sense, and this, as you see, is weak. Since the indication of these states upon what they signify is clearer than what preceded, He, glory be to Him, attached their being signs solely to intellection, as Abu Hayyan and others said. For this reason, it has been said, He, exalted is His majesty, did not address anything except the preference of some of them over others in the manifest eating, which is evident to every intelligent person, while the verification of that in properties and qualities is something whose discovery depends on a kind of reflection and contemplation, as if there were no need to reflect on that either. In this there is an implicit reproach that the polytheists are not people of reason.

And for one of the rajaz poets concerning what this verse points to:

The earth in it is a lesson for the one who takes heed,
it tells of the work of a King, Mighty in power.

Its trees are watered with one water,
and its place of settlement is one spot.

The sun and the air do not differ,
yet their fruits differ and do not agree.

If this one made the natures,
or it is the work of a non-maker,

it would not differ and would be one thing.
Do children resemble anything but their parent?

The sun and the air, O stubborn one,
and water and earth are one thing.

So what made this preference
except a Wise One who does not let it be vain?

Ibn Jarir related from al-Hasan concerning this verse that he said: "This is a parable which Allah, exalted is He, struck for the hearts of the children of Adam. The earth was in the hand of the Merciful one as one clay, then He spread it out and flattened it, and it became adjoining tracts. Water descends upon it, and this one brings forth its blossom, its fruit and its trees, and that one brings forth its herbage, and this one brings forth its salt, its brine and its filth, and both are watered with one water. Were the water salty, it would be said: this one has become brackish because of the water. Likewise, mankind was created from Adam, peace be upon him, and there descends upon them from heaven a reminder, so hearts soften and humble themselves and submit, and hearts harden and become heedless and forgetful." Then he said: "By Allah, no one sits with the Qur'an without rising from it with an increase or a decrease." Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss⁠﴾. End quote. Abu Hayyan said: "This resembles the discourse of the Sufis."

﴿And if you marvel﴾, i.e., if wonder occurs in you, O Muhammad, ﴿then wondrous is their saying﴾, after witnessing the signs that indicate the greatness of His power, exalted is He. That is, let your wonder be at their saying: ﴿When we are dust...﴾ to its end, for it is what ought to be marvelled at. ʿAjab (wonder) is read with a damma as a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam, a predicate preceding its subject), and ﴿qawluhum﴾ (their saying) is a subject placed last (mubtada' muakhkhar, a subject following its predicate). The predicate was placed first for restriction (al-qasr) and emphasis (al-tasjil) from the outset, indicating that their saying is a wondrous matter.

In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan) it is said that a qualifying attribute must be estimated for ʿajab, because the meaning is not complete with an unqualified noun. So it is estimated, and God knows best: "then wondrous is a wonder of some kind," or "then wondrous is a strange thing." When we estimate it as qualified, it is permissible to parse it as a subject (mubtada'), because of the justifying factor (mussawigh), which is the adjective. It does not matter that the predicate is definite. This is like what Sibawayh said regarding kam māluka ("how much is your property"): inna kam ("indeed how much") is a subject because of the justifying factor in it, which is interrogation. And in such as iqsud rajulan khayrun minhu abūhu ("aim at a man whose father is better than him"), inna khayrun ("indeed better") is also a subject, because of the justifying factor, which is the governing action (ʿamal).

Abu al-Baqa' transmitted the view that ʿajab means muʿjab (that which causes wonder). Then he said: on this basis, it is permissible for qawluhum to be raised by it.

This was objected to, saying that it is not permissible, because it does not follow that if something has the meaning of something else, its rule in governing is the same as its rule. Muʿjab governs, but ʿajab does not govern. Do you not see that the form faʿl, like dhabḥ (slaughter), the form faʿla, like qabḍ (seizing), and the form fuʿla, like ghurfa (a handful), are used with the meaning of maf'ūl (passive participle), yet do not govern its action? So one does not say: مَرَرْتُ بِرَجُلٍ ذَبَحَ كَبْشَهُ ("I passed by a man who slaughtered his ram"), or قَبَضَ مَالَهُ ("who seized his property"), or غُرْفَةٌ مَاؤُهُ ("a handful whose water..."), with the meaning of مَذْبُوحٍ كَبْشُهُ ("whose ram is slaughtered"), مَقْبُوضٍ مَالُهُ ("whose property is seized"), and مَغْرُوفٌ مَاؤُهُ ("whose water is scooped"). They have explicitly stated that these forms substitute for the passive participle in meaning, not in governing. The grammarians have restricted what raises the agent (fāʿil) to certain categories, and they did not count among them the verbal noun (maṣdar) when it has the meaning of the active participle.

Apparently, ﴿أإذا كُنّا﴾ to its end is in the accusative position, as a direct object of an implied verb of saying (maqūl). The interrogative is denunciatory (inkārī), indicating the utmost remoteness and rejection. It is also permissible for it to be in the nominative position, as an appositive (badal) of qawluhum, on the basis that qawluhum has the meaning of al-maqūl (what is said). According to Abu Hayyan, this is a strained parsing and a departure from the apparent sense. On this view, the wonder is their speaking of that, and on the first view, their saying is that.

The governing element of idhā (when) is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿أإنّا لَفي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ﴾ ("Are we indeed in a new creation?"), namely "we will be raised" or "we will be returned." Al-jadīd (new) is the opposite of al-khalq (old, worn) and al-bālī (decayed). One says thawbun jadīd ("a new garment"), meaning as it has just been finished being made. It is faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl (passive), as if it were cut from its weaving. Fronting the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) serves to strengthen the denial of resurrection, by directing it toward a state contrary to it. The repetition of the hamza in ﴿أإنّا﴾ is for emphasis of the denial. The basis of their denial is not that they would actually be established in a new creation while being dust, but that they are in a state of potential for it and readiness for it. This indicates their obstinacy and persistence in denial, which is not hidden.

Abu al-Baqa' said: it is not permissible for idhā to be governed by kunnā, because idhā is annexed to it (muḍāfa ilayhā); nor by jadīd, because what follows inna does not govern what precedes it, and likewise the interrogative. Ibn Hisham in al-Mughni rejected the first point: idhā, according to those who hold that its governing element is its condition, which is the well-known view, is not annexed. This is as all agree when it governs the jussive (jazm), as in the line: وَإِذا تُصِبْكَ خَصاصَةٌ فَتَحَمَّلِ ("And if poverty befalls you, then bear it"). It was said: the way to reject this is that its governing in it depends on determining its referent, and determining it is only through its condition, so it becomes circular. Al-Shihab considered this and said: they regard it as like matā ("when") and ayyāna ("when") which are not determined but indefinite, as its proponents stated, and Ibn Hisham also stated this explicitly in al-Mughni.

It was said: the meaning of the verse is: if you marvel, O Muhammad, at their saying in denying resurrection, then their saying is truly deserving of being marvelled at. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr criticized this, saying that it is not the literal meaning of the wording, because it makes the object of the Prophet's (ﷺ) wonder their saying in denying resurrection, while the answer to the condition is that same saying. Thus the condition and the consequence become identical, since its implied sense is: if you marvel at their denial of resurrection, then marvel at their saying in denying resurrection. This is not correct. It was answered: this is among the cases where the condition and the consequence are identical in form but differ in reality, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever's migration was to God and His Messenger, then his migration is to God and His Messenger." And there is the saying: "Whoever reaches Ṣumman has reached the pasture." This is more eloquent in speech, because its meaning is that it is a matter whose reality cannot be fully grasped and whose truth cannot be attained, and that it is a great matter.

Some held that the address in ﴿إنْ تَعْجَبْ﴾ is general, and the meaning is: if you marvel, O one who considers these signs and knows the power of the One whose works these are, then increase your wonder at the one who denies, despite this, that He is able to resurrect them, which is the easiest thing for Him. It was said: the meaning is: if wonder arises in you at their denial of resurrection, then persist in it, for their denial of it is among the wonders. It was said: what is intended is: if you are one who wishes to marvel, O seeker, then come, for among the greatest marvels is their denial of resurrection.

The readers differed regarding the two interrogatives when they occur together in eleven places: this place, and in al-Muʾminūn, al-ʿAnkabūt, al-Naml, al-Sajda, al-Wāqiʿa, al-Nāziʿāt, two places in Banū Isrāʾīl, and likewise in al-Ṣāffāt. Nāfiʿ and al-Kisāʾī read by making the first an interrogative and the second a statement, except in al-ʿAnkabūt and al-Naml, where Nāfiʿ reversed this. Al-Kisāʾī combined the two interrogatives in al-ʿAnkabūt, and in al-Naml he followed his own principle, except that he added a nūn.

Ibn ʿĀmir read by making the first a statement and the second an interrogative, except in al-Naml and al-Nāziʿāt, where he reversed this, and in al-Naml he added a nūn like al-Kisāʾī. He read with two interrogatives in al-Wāqiʿa. This is the reading of the rest of the seven in this chapter, except Ibn Kathīr and Ḥafṣ, who in al-ʿAnkabūt read the first as a statement and the second as an interrogative. They follow their own principles regarding the joining of two hamzas: easing (takhfīf), realizing (taḥqīq), and separating (faṣl) between the two hamzas.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ ("Those") is a subject (mubtada'), and the relative clause is its predicate, i.e., those who deny resurrection, even though they have witnessed the great signs of their Lord that would guide them to faith, if they had been seeing. ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بِرَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("who disbelieved in their Lord"), and persisted in that, because denying His power, exalted and majestic is He, is a denial of Him, glorified be He, since a god cannot be incapable, along with the denial of Him, exalted is His majesty, and the denial of His messengers, upon whom be peace, on which there is consensus.

﴿وأُولَئِكَ﴾ ("And those") is a second subject, whose predicate is the sentence of His saying: ﴿الأغْلالُ في أعْناقِهِمْ﴾ ("the shackles are around their necks"). Here there are two possibilities. The first is that the intended meaning is describing them by this in this world. It is then a simile and illustration of their state in refusing faith and not turning to the truth, by the state of a people who have shackles and fetters on their necks which prevent them from turning, as in the line: كَيْفَ الرَّشادُ وقَدْ خُلِّفَتْ في نَفَرٍ لَهم عَنِ الرُّشْدِ أغْلالٌ وأقْيادُ ("How can there be guidance, when among a group left behind there are shackles and fetters preventing them from righteousness?"). It is as if it were said: those are bound by the fetters of error, and their release is not hoped for.

The second possibility is that the intended meaning is describing them by this in the Hereafter. The speech then either remains on its literal meaning, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿إذِ الأغْلالُ في أعْناقِهِمْ والسَّلاسِلُ﴾ ("when the shackles are around their necks and the chains"). This is narrated from al-Ḥasan, who said: the shackles were not placed around the necks of the people of the Fire because they had made the Lord incapable, but they were placed on their necks so that when the blaze overpowers them, it casts them into the Fire. Or it is presented in the manner of a simile for their state, likened to the state of one who is brought forward for punishment. It was said: what is meant by the shackles is their corrupt deeds, which they have hung upon themselves like shackles. This is consistent with the possibility that it refers to this world or the Hereafter. The first view looks to what was said, and the second looks to His saying: ﴿وأُولَئِكَ﴾, i.e., those described by what was mentioned.

﴿أصْحابُ النّارِ هم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("are the companions of the Fire; they therein abide eternally") (5). They will not depart from it. It was said: the placing of the separating pronoun (ḍamīr faṣl) here is not to restrict eternal abiding to the deniers of resurrection alone, but to all, which is implied by His saying: ﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بِرَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("those who disbelieved in their Lord").

It was objected to this that hum ("they") is not a separating pronoun, because its condition is that it occur between a subject and a predicate that is a definite noun, or like the definite in that it does not accept the article, such as af'al (the comparative form), and this predicate is not like that. It was answered that the intended meaning of separation (faṣl) is the detached pronoun, and it was used, and the predicate was made a sentence, although the original form of the predicate is singular, for the purpose of restriction and specification mentioned, as in huwa ʿārifun ("he is knowing").

Some said: perhaps the one who said what was mentioned does not follow the grammarians in the stated condition, just as al-Jurjānī and al-Suhaylī permitted it when the predicate is a present-tense verb and an active participle like it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 6:

﴿They ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾ with the punishment with which they were threatened, out of persistence in disbelief, mockery and denial. ﴿Before the good﴾, that is, well-being and safety from it. The meaning of its being "before" it is either that their asking for it comes before asking for the good, or that their asking for it comes before the end of the time appointed for it. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Qatadah that he said regarding this verse: These are the polytheists of the Arabs. They hastened toward evil before good, and they said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment.﴾

﴿And the exemplary punishments have already passed away before them﴾. Al-mathulat is the plural of mathulah, like sumrah and sumurat. It means a disgraceful punishment. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, explained it as a punishment that uproots a limb, such as the cutting off of an ear and the like. It was so named because of the likeness between the punishment and the one punished by it. This is like His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. Or it is derived from al-mithal, meaning retaliation. It is said: amthaltu al-rajul min sahibihi and aqsastuhu, meaning the same thing. Or it is from the proverbial example (al-mathal) struck because of its greatness.

The sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), to show the feebleness of their opinion in hastening (the punishment), by way of mockery. That is, they ask you to hasten it while mocking your warning and denying that what you warned them of will come to pass, while the reality is that the disgraceful punishments that descended upon the like of them, among the deniers and mockers, have already passed.

Mujahid and al-A'mash read al-mathalat with a fatha on the mim and the tha. Isa ibn Amr, in a narration from al-A'mash, and Abu Bakr read them with a damma on both. This is an original dialectal form (lughah asliyyah), and it is possible that the vowel of the ʿayn was made to follow the vowel of the fa'. Ibn Wththab read it with a damma on the mim and a sukun on the tha, which is the dialect of Tamim. Ibn Musarrif read it with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the tha, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

﴿Indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness﴾, great, ﴿for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾, against themselves by sins and disobedience. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is in the position of a circumstantial clause from "mankind", and its governing element is the governing element of its referent, which is "forgiveness". That is, He, exalted is He, is indeed Forgiving toward mankind while they are wrongdoers.

It has been said: this verse is clear in support of the position of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni school), namely the permissibility of forgiving major and minor sins without repentance. This is because He, glorified is He, mentioned forgiveness along with wrongdoing, that is, sin, and this only occurs before repentance, since the one who repents from sin is like one who has no sin. The Mu'tazilah interpreted this by saying that what is meant is forgiveness of minor sins for one who avoids major sins, or forgiveness of them for one who repents, or that what is meant by forgiveness is its linguistic meaning, which is concealment, through postponement and the delay of punishment until the Hereafter. It is as if it were said: He, exalted is He, does not hasten punishment upon mankind even if they are wrongdoers, but rather He conceals them by delaying it. This interpretation was objected to on the ground that it is a restriction (takhsis) of a general term without evidence. It was answered that disbelief has been specified by consensus (ijma') (the agreement of the scholars), so the specification extends to this. The last view was criticised as being far-fetched, because, as the Imam said, such a thing is not called forgiveness, for otherwise it would be correct to say: "The disbelievers are forgiven." It was answered that the real meaning of forgiveness in the language is concealment, and that their being forgiven in the sense of having their punishment postponed until the Hereafter presents no problem, and that this fits their asking for punishment. It was answered also that what is meant is that this is contrary to the apparent meaning and to the Qur'anic usage. The Allamah al-Tibi mentioned that the verse must be interpreted in one of three ways, because in its apparent sense it is like an encouragement to wrongdoing, since He, glorified is He, promised complete forgiveness together with the existence of wrongdoing. Al-Kashshaf commented on this, saying: There is room for consideration, because the wording indicates that He, exalted is He, is abundantly forgiving toward them while they deserve the opposite, since they are involved in what makes punishment more fitting for them in His sight. The apparent point is that the interpretation is based on the Mu'tazili position. As for the position of Ahl al-Sunnah, it is only interpreted if wrongdoing is general and includes disbelief. Then he said: The interpretation by concealment and delay is better. Thus His saying, ﴿And indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾ (6), serves to confirm the threat against them, even if they are under His concealment and respite. In this there is an indication that this is respite and not neglect. The word "mankind" may refer either to those specifically known, namely the hastening ones mentioned earlier, or to the whole category, indicating the large number of those who perish, since it includes them and their likes. This applies according to both positions. Al-Tibi also chose this interpretation and said it is the preferable way. The verse is in the same pattern as His saying: ﴿Say: He has sent it down who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed He is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, according to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned in his tafsir. You have heard what is for it and what is against it, so reflect. Others than one chose to take "mankind" in the generic sense, and this is also intended in "severe in punishment".

Specifying it to the disbelievers is not the preferred view. This is supported by what Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And indeed your Lord...﴾ and so on, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Were it not for the pardon of Allah, the Exalted, and His overlooking, no one would enjoy life. And were it not for His threat and His punishment, everyone would rely upon it."

Page 107

﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾, and they are the ones who sought to hasten (the punishment), as was narrated from Qatada. It seems that he only referred to them in this way to censure their disbelief in the signs of Allah the Exalted, which mountains would crumble before, because they did not pay them any heed and did not count them among the kinds of signs. They said: ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down upon him from his Lord?﴾, like the signs of Musa and Isa, upon them both be peace, such as the turning of the staff into a serpent and the raising of the dead, out of obstinacy or arrogance. Otherwise, in the least of the signs sent down upon him (peace and blessings be upon him) there is sufficiency and a lesson for people of understanding. The use of the present tense (in "say") is to bring the past situation vividly to mind. It has also been permitted that it indicates that this saying was their habitual practice. The tanwin (nunation, the "-un" ending) on *āyatun* (آيَةٌ, "a sign") is for magnification, and it has also been permitted that it is for unity (indicating one sign).

﴿You are only a warner﴾, one sent to warn of the evil consequence of what Allah the Exalted has forbidden, as was the case with the messengers before you. It is not incumbent upon you except to bring that by which your prophethood is known, and this has been achieved with what admits of no addition, and there is no need to bind them and silence them by bringing what they have proposed. ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾. (7) That is, a prophet who calls to the truth and guides to it with a sign suited to him and to his time. The indefiniteness (of "guide") is for generality, and this was also narrated from Qatada and Mujahid. Based on this, the statement of the Exalted:

**[Page 107 continues]** ﴿Allah knows what every female bears﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question). The question is: why were they not granted the thing they proposed, so that their argument would be cut off and perhaps they would be guided? The answer is that this is a matter ordered by One of complete knowledge and irresistible power, not something done arbitrarily or in accordance with their flimsy opinions. It is also permissible that the guide (*al-Hadi*) be Allah, the Exalted. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jubayr, and in that case the tanwin (nunation) on *hadin* is for magnification and exaltation. The meaning of the verse on this reading is that when they denied the signs out of obstinacy, arising from their blind imitation (*taqlid*) of their forebears, and did not reflect upon the signs, it was said: "You are only a warner, and every people has a guide," and the guidance that establishes faith in their hearts and turns them away from their denial belongs to Allah alone, and He, glory be to Him, is able to do it. Based on this, it has been said that His words ﴿Allah﴾ may be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "He is Allah," and this would be an explanation of *hadin*, while ﴿Knows﴾ is a confirmatory clause

**[Page 108]** for the exclusive guidance of the Exalted, functioning like a reason for it. It is also permissible that the clause ﴿Allah knows﴾ be confirmatory, in which case it is an instance of placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, as if to say: He, the Exalted, knows, that is, that guide. The first (interpretation) is very far-fetched.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Jarir from Ikrimah and Abu al-Duha, that the warner and the guide is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The justification for this is that *hadin* is coordinated with *munthir* (warner), and "for every people" (*li-kulli qawmin*) is related to it, placed before it for the sake of the rhyme (*fasila*). This indicates the universality of his prophethood and the comprehensiveness of his call. It involves separating the conjoined word from the word it is conjoined to by a prepositional phrase, and the grammarians differ on its permissibility. It may also be that *hadin* is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "and he is a guide," or "and you are a guide." On the first reading there is an *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person). Abu al-Aliyah said: the guide is the deed. Ali ibn Isa said: he is the one who precedes to guidance, ﴿and for every people﴾ there is one who precedes them to guidance. Abu Hayyan said: this comes back to the view that the guide is the Prophet, because he is the one who precedes to that. It is narrated from Abu Salih that he is the leader towards good or towards evil. All of these, as you see, [are weak]. The Shia said that he is Ali, may Allah honour his face, and they related reports to that effect. al-Qushayri mentioned this from among us. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Daylami and Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When the verse ﴿You are only a warner﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed his hand on his chest and said: 'I am the warner,' and he pointed with his hand to the shoulder of Ali, may Allah honour his face, and said: 'You are the guide, O Ali. Through you the guided will be guided after me.'" Abdullah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id of the Musnad, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Hakim (who declared it sound), and Ibn Asakir also narrated from Ali, may Allah honour his face, that he said about the verse: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is the warner, and I am the guide." In another wording: "The guide is a man from the Banu Hashim," meaning himself.

The Shia used this to argue for the caliphate of Ali, may Allah honour his face, immediately after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is answered that we do not accept the soundness of the report, and al-Hakim's authentication is considered by the people of hadith to be unreliable. Nothing in the verse indicates what they claim, in any way whatsoever; at most it shows that through him, may Allah honour his face, the guided will be guided after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that requires only the establishment of the rank of guidance, which is a matter [distinct from]

**[Page 109]** the caliphate that we uphold, and there is no necessary connection between them in our view.

Some have said: if the report is sound, it necessitates affirming the validity of the caliphate of the three, may Allah be pleased with them, since it indicates that he, may Allah honour his face, is right in what he does and leaves, and that he is the one through whom guidance is sought. He had pledged allegiance to those caliphs willingly, praised them, spoke well of them, and did not criticise their caliphate. Therefore it is fitting to follow him and walk in his path in this matter, and not to establish the opposite of what he manifested, which is like pulling out thorns with a bare hand (*kharṭ al-qatad*). Abu Hayyan said: even if we accept the soundness of the narration, the Prophet (ﷺ) only made Ali, may Allah honour his face, an example from among the scholars of the Community and its guides to the religion. It is as if he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "O Ali, this is your description." Therefore the three caliphs and the rest of the scholars among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, enter into it, and indeed all the scholars of the Community. According to this, the meaning of the verse is: "You are only a warner, and for every people, in the past and in the present, until Allah wills, there are guides, callers to good." End of quote. Its apparent meaning is that the fronting of the complement in the report of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, was not taken as a true restriction (*hasr haqiqi*). In that case there is no obstacle to the view that many are guided by him. What supports the absence of restriction is what has come to us from his saying (ﷺ): "Follow the two after me, Abu Bakr and Umar," and other reports including the affirmation of others besides Ali, may Allah honour his face, through whom one is guided. I think you do not give attention to interpretation (*ta'wil*) nor care about what has been said, and are content with denying the soundness of the report, saying that there is nothing in the verse, neither explicitly nor by trace, that indicates this.

"Ma" (*ma*) may be a verbal-masdar (*masdariyya*), meaning: He knows the bearing of every female's womb, from whatever females they are; and in this case *al-haml* (the bearing) means *al-mahmul* (what is borne). It may also be a relative pronoun (*mawsula*) with an omitted returning pronoun, meaning:

**[Page 110]** "what she carries in her belly from the moment of conception until the time of birth, after the creation is complete," and nothing else. It is also permissible that it be an indefinite qualified noun. As for ﴿knows﴾, it has been said that it is transitive to one object, and so it is cognitive knowledge (*'irfani*). This was objected to on the grounds that the verb *ma'rifa* (to know by acquaintance) cannot properly be used of the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted. That objection arises from a lack of knowledge of the reality of this matter, and it has already been mentioned. It is also permissible that *ma* be an interrogative suspending the verb *ya'lamu* (knows), functioning as the subject or as a fronted object, and the clause takes the place of the two objects, meaning: He knows what you carry and in what state it is, from among the conditions that come upon it, from time to time. It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent and immediate meaning. Just as these possibilities were allowed for this *ma*, they are also allowed for what follows it. As for the connection of this verse to what precedes it, this is already known from what has passed. It has also been said that its connection is this: since their denial of resurrection was mentioned, and among their doubts was the scattering of parts and their mixing with one another such that their separation is not possible, He, glory be to Him, drew attention through this verse to the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, to remove their doubt. It has also been said that its connection is this: since they hastened the evil, the Mighty and Majestic drew attention to the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, to indicate that His wisdom, may it be exalted, only sends down punishment according to what He knows of benefit and wisdom. In the Mushaf of Ubayy there is the reading "What every female bears and what she bears" (*ma tahmilu kullu unthā wa-ma taḍa'*), and what has been said about its like has already passed.

﴿And what the wombs diminish and what they increase﴾: that is, what they reduce and what they increase in the body, such as the miscarried and the full-term child. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas. And in duration, such as the child born at the minimum period of pregnancy, the child born at its maximum, and what lies between them. This is another narration from the Rabbi (Ibn Abbas). It has been said: al-Dahhak was born after two years, and Harim ibn Hayyan after four, and for this reason he was named Harim (the aged). To the view that the maximum period of pregnancy is four years, al-Shafi'i went. According to Malik, its maximum is five years. According to the Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, its maximum is two years, and this is also narrated from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her. Ibn Jarir narrated from her: "Pregnancy does not last more than two years, the time it takes for the spindle whorl (*falaka mighzal*) to turn." And in number, such as one or more than one. It has been said: the highest number known is four, for it is narrated that Shurayk ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Numayr al-Qurashi was the fourth of four (quadruplets), and he is the one whom our great Imam (Abu Hanifa), may Allah be pleased with him, examined. al-Shafi'i, may mercy be upon him, said: a shaykh in Yemen told me that his wife gave birth to several litters, with five in each birth. This is one of the rare cases, and something like it has occurred, but whatever exceeds two, due to weakness, rarely survives.

As for what is related, that one of them gave birth to forty in a single womb, each of them the size of a finger, and that they all lived, the apparent view is that this is a lie. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the decrease and increase of menstrual blood. This was narrated from a group, and it involves likening the blood in the womb to water in the earth, which sometimes recedes and sometimes appears. *Ghāḍa* is used both transitively and intransitively, as *naqaṣa* is, and likewise *izdāda*. This is something on which the lexicographers agree. If you take both as intransitive, then *ma* cannot be a relative or qualified pronoun, for lack of a returning pronoun. The attribution of the two verbs, however they are taken, to the wombs is either in the intransitive sense, concerning what is in them, or in the transitive sense, to Allah, the Majestic, whose authority is great. ﴿And everything﴾ among things ﴿with Him﴾, glory be to Him, ﴿is by measure﴾ (8). That is, by a measure that it does not exceed nor fall short of, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, all things We created with measure﴾. For every created thing, whether accident or substance, has at every stage of the process of coming into being, and at its beginnings, a specific time and a particular state from which it hardly departs. Perhaps the state of the non-existent is known by inference, if we say that a thing is what exists. *ʿInda* (with) is an adverbial complement connected to an omitted element that functions as an attribute of "thing" or of "every," and ﴿by measure﴾ is the predicate of "every." It is also permissible that the adverbial be connected to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of "measure," which was originally its attribute, but when it was fronted it was parsed as a circumstantial qualifier in fulfilment of the rule. It is also permissible that it be an adverbial of what the prepositional phrase depends upon. By "being with Him" is meant presence in knowledge, or rather knowledge by presence (*ʿilm ḥuḍūrī*), as has been said, since the realisation of things in themselves, at whatever stage of existence and readiness for that, is knowledge in relation to Him, exalted is He. It has been said: the meaning of "with Him" in

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 9:

﴿ʿĀlim al-ghayb﴾ (Knower of the unseen), that is, what is absent from the senses, ﴿wa-l-shahāda﴾ (and the witnessed), that is, what is present to them. He expressed the two by these two for emphasis (mubālagha).

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that al-ghayb is the secret and al-shahāda is the public. It was also said: the first is the non-existent and the second is the existent. It is transmitted from some of them that he said: He, glory be to Him, does not know the unseen, in the sense that there is no unseen with respect to Him, exalted is His majesty, and non-existent things are witnessed by Him, the Exalted, on the basis of the view that the non-existent can be seen, as al-Kūrānī demonstrated in a treatise he composed for that purpose. But there is no concealing what this contains of excessive audacity toward God, the Exalted, and of contradiction to His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾. A Muslim should not utter such a phrase, which makes the skins of the believers shudder to hear. We ask God, the Exalted, to grant us success in keeping to our limits and to bestow upon us good manners toward Him, glory be to Him.

﴿ʿĀlim﴾ is read in the nominative (rufiʿa), either as the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ maḥdhūf) or as a predicate following a predicate. Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may God be pleased with them both, read ﴿ʿĀlima﴾ in the accusative, as a laudatory accusative (ʿalā al-madḥ). This statement serves as evidence for what precedes it, His saying, the Exalted: ﴿God knows﴾ ... etc.

﴿al-Kabīr﴾ (the Great): the one of great rank, before whom everything is small. ﴿al-Mutaʿāl﴾ (the Most High). (9) The one who is exalted above everything in His essence, His knowledge, and all His attributes, glory be to Him. It is also permitted that the meaning is: the Great who is too majestic to be described by the attributes of created beings, and who is exalted above them. On the first interpretation, the intent is to declare Him free of likeness in His essence and attributes from approaching anything of His kind; on this interpretation, the intent is to declare Him free of what the disbelievers ascribe to Him, so it is a refutation of them, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Glory be to God above what they describe﴾.

The scholar al-Ṭībī said: The meaning of ﴿al-Kabīr al-Mutaʿāl﴾ in relation to what precedes it, namely ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, is the one of great rank who is too great for the attributes of created beings, so as to join to knowledge greatness and power, in view of what preceded of His saying, the Exalted: (what every female bears) to the end of what conveys His transcendence above what the Christians and polytheists claim. ﴿al-Kabīr﴾ is in the nominative as a predicate following a predicate. It is also permitted that ﴿ʿĀlim﴾ is a subject (mubtadaʾ) and that the following is its predicate.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 10:**

﴿It is all the same to Him whether among you one conceals speech﴾, meaning he hides it within himself and does not utter it. It was also said: he utters it in such a way that he hears it himself but no one else does. ﴿And whoever speaks it aloud﴾ refers to the one who stands opposite to that in both senses. ﴿And whoever is hidden﴾ (*mustakhff*), one who is excessive in concealment, as though he were hiding himself, ﴿by night﴾, and seeking more of it, ﴿and goes forth freely by day﴾. (10) That is, one who is victorious in it, as was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, and this is what a group said. Originally it is an active participle from *sarab*, meaning he went along his *sirb*, i.e., his path, and it can have the sense of one who acts as he wishes. The poet said:

"Indeed I have roamed free, though I was not one who roams,
and dreams draw near, though they are not near."

And another said:

"Every people have kept their stallion tethered,
but we have loosed its tether, so it roams free."

That is, he acts as he wishes, and is not repelled from any direction. He takes pride in the might of his people. Thus what the scholar (*al-Ḥabr*, i.e., Ibn ʿAbbās) mentioned is a necessary implication of its meaning, and its indicator is its occurrence in contrast with *mustakhff*. The apparent sense from the words of some of them is that it is literal in its outward meaning.

*Sawāʾun* is in the nominative as a predicate (*khabar*) placed first, and *man* (whoever) is a postponed subject (*mubtadaʾ*). The predicate was not made dual because originally it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and it now carries the sense of *mustawin* (equal). Its dual did not occur in the most well-known dialects, though Abū Zayd related *humā sawāʾān* (both are equal). *Minkum* (of you) is a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of the pronoun concealed within it, not of *asarra* or *jahara*, because what falls within the relative clause (*ṣilah*) or the qualifier (*ṣifah*) cannot precede the relative pronoun or the described noun.

Abū Ḥayyān permitted *sawāʾun* to be a subject (*mubtadaʾ*) because it is described by *minkum*, and what follows it is the predicate. Likewise Sībawayh parsed the Arabs' saying *sawāʾun ʿalayhi al-khayru wa al-sharru* (it is all the same to him, good and evil) in this way. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah's statement that Sībawayh deemed this weak, on the grounds that it is beginning with an indefinite noun (*nakirah*) which is not valid,

[Page 111]

is refuted. *Sārib* is conjoined to *man*, as if it were said: "It is all the same among you whether one person is hidden and another goes forth freely." The purpose of adding *huwa* (he) in the first is that it indicates the completeness of knowledge, so it suits the addition of emphasis to confirm it. This is also the purpose of omitting the described noun in *sārib* as well. The reason for placing *asarra* first and making it operate on explicit speech, over *jahara*, and making it operate on his inner self, was also considered: it could be that it operates on *mustakhff*.

It was objected that *sawāʾ* requires mention of two things, so if *sārib* is conjoined to part of the relative clause or the qualifier, there would be only one thing, and this does not hold for the first case, because the meaning would be "what you know." It was answered that *man* is an expression for two persons, as in his saying:

"Come, if you pledge to me that you will not betray me,
we will be like those two, O wolf, who keep company."

So it is as if it were said: "It is all the same among you, two persons: one hidden by night and one going forth freely by day." Al-Kashshāf said: in both cases *man* is a qualifying (*mawṣūfah*) not a relative (*mawṣūlah*), and the first two are understood in this way too, so that the whole is consistent. Choosing it over the relative form indicates that the intended meaning is the description, for that is the object of knowledge. As for if it were said, "It is all the same to Him, the one who conceals speech and the one who speaks it aloud," then if the intended meaning is the category, as in the line "and indeed I pass by the base one who curses me," then he and the first are equal. But the first is explicit. If the intended meaning is a specific known individual, whether actual or assumed, it would necessarily imply the opposite of what is intended, for the reason already mentioned.

It was also said: there is an omitted relative pronoun in the speech, and the estimate is *wa man huwa sārib* (and whoever is one who goes forth freely), like the saying of Abū Firās:

"Would that the one between me and you were populated,
and between me and all the worlds there was ruin."

And the saying of Ḥassān:

"Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of God,
and praises him and supports him, is equal."

But this is extremely weak, because it involves omitting the relative pronoun together with the head of the relative clause. Al-Zamakhsharī claimed that one of the two omissions is permissible, but that their combination is one of the reprehensible things, unlike the two verses. Abū Ḥayyān said: the omission of *man* here, even though it is known, is not permissible according to the Basrans, and it is permissible according to the Kufans.

Some claimed that the intended meaning is the equality of the two states, whether they belong to one person or to two. The meaning is: it is all the same whether his concealment and his going forth freely are with respect to the knowledge of God, Exalted is He. Therefore there is no need to direct the verse by what has passed. Likewise the state of what preceded it: He expressed it in two styles while the intended meaning is one.

This was criticized: the Arabic language does not support it, because *man* is not a verbal (*maṣdariyyah*) particle, and there is no connecting element in the speech. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah supposed it permissible that the verse includes three categories: the one who conceals is one side, the one who speaks aloud is another side opposed to the first, and the third is one who changes colour, who disobeys by night while hidden and displays innocence by day. This, as you see, is [unsound]. Among the strange things is what is reported from al-Akhfash and Qutrub, interpreting *al-mustakhfī* as the manifest. Although it does occur in their speech with this meaning, what prevents it in the verse is what prevents it. Furthermore, in the explanation of His knowledge of what was mentioned after the explanation of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all things, there is an emphasis on this matter that is not hidden.

[Page 112]

﴿لَهُ﴾ (for him): the pronoun refers to those mentioned earlier, "whether he conceals his speech or openly declares it," through to the end of the verse. This is on the basis of interpreting it as referring to what was mentioned, and treating it as having the status of a demonstrative. The same applies to the one mentioned after it. ﴿مُعَقِّباتٌ﴾ (successive [angels]): angels who succeed one another in guarding him and watching over him. It is the plural of *mu'aqqibah*, from *'aqqaba*, an intensive form of *'aqaba*, meaning to come after someone, following on his heels. Its root is *al-'aqib*, the back part of the foot. It was then used figuratively for an action occurring without interval or delay,

[Page 113]

as if one person were treading in the heel-print of another. Thus the *tafʿīl* form (*'aqqaba*) indicates intensity, either in the agent or in the action. It is not for transitivity, because the triliteral *'aqaba* is already transitive. It is also possible that the designation of the angels as *al-mu'aqqibāt* is based on the fact that they follow the person's words and deeds, that is, they pursue them and record them in writing. Al-Zamakhshari said that the original form is *mu'taqibāt*, which is of the *ifti'āl* pattern, so the *tā'* was assimilated into the *qāf*, as in God's words ﴿وجاءَ المُعَذِّرُونَ﴾ (and those who make excuses came), meaning *al-mu'tadhirūn* (those who offer excuses). This was criticised as a gross error, since the *tā'* is not assimilated into the *qāf* in one word or in two words. The grammarians (*al-ṣarfiyyūn*) have explicitly stated that neither the *qāf* nor the *kāf* is assimilated into the other, nor are they assimilated into any other letter. The *tā'* in *mu'aqqibah* is for intensity, like the *tā'* in *nassābah* (a great genealogist), since the angels are not feminine. It was also said that it is for the feminine, in the sense that *mu'aqqibah* is an attribute of a group among them, so the meaning of *mu'aqqibāt* is groups, each group being a *mu'aqqibah*. *Mu'aqqibah* is not the plural of *mu'aqqib*. Al-Tabari mentioned that it is its plural and compared it to *rajul*, *rijāl* and *rijālāt*. This, as you see, is [unconvincing]. However, Abu Hayyan interpreted it by saying that what he meant by "the plural of *mu'aqqib*" is that it is used in practice as the plural of *mu'aqqib*, although its original usage is for the feminine of *mu'aqqib*. It thus becomes like *al-wāridah* used for a group of people who come to water, although its original usage is for a feminine *wārid* (one who comes to water). The comparison to what was mentioned is in terms of meaning, not in terms of grammatical technique (*ṣinā'at al-naḥw*). He thus explained that *mu'aqqibah*, insofar as it is intended as a plural, is like *rijāl*, insofar as it is constructed for the plural, and that *mu'aqqibāt*, insofar as it is used as a plural of *mu'aqqibah* used in the plural sense, is like *rijālāt*, which is the plural of *rijāl*.

Ubayy and Ibrahim read ( *ma'āqīb* ), which is a plural. As al-Zamakhshari said, it is the plural of *mu'aqqib* or *mu'aqqibah* with the *qāf* doubled in both. The *yā'* is a substitute for the deletion of one of the two *qāf*s in the broken plural. Ibn Jinni said that it is a broken plural of *mu'aqqib*, like *muṭa'im* and *maṭā'īm*, and *muqaddim* and *maqādīm*, as if it were pluralised as *ma'āqibah*, then the *hā'* was deleted from the plural and the *yā'* was substituted for it. This is perhaps the most apparent view. It is also read ( *mu'taqibāt* ), from *i'taqaba*.

﴿مِن بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ ومِن خَلْفِهِ﴾ (before him and behind him): this is attached to a deleted element that occurs as an attribute of *mu'aqqibāt*, or as a circumstantial element (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase which functions as the predicate of *lahu*. The meaning is that the successive [angels] surround him on all sides. Alternatively, it is attached to *mu'aqqibāt*, and *min* indicates the starting point, so the meaning is that the successive [angels] guard what he has put forward and what he has delayed of his deeds, that is, they guard all his deeds. It is also permitted that it be attached to God's words ﴿يَحْفَظُونَهُ﴾ (they guard him), and the sentence is then an attribute of *mu'aqqibāt*, or a circumstantial element from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase.

Ubayy read ( *min bayni yadayhi wa raqībun min khalfihi* ), and Ibn 'Abbas read ( *wa ruqabā'u min khalfihi* ). Mujahid transmitted from him that he read ( *lahu mu'aqqibātun min khalfihi wa raqībun min bayni yadayhi yaḥfaẓūnahu* ).

﴿مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ (by the command of God): attached to what is in his presence (*mā 'indahu*). *Min* indicates causation, meaning they guard him from harms by reason of God's command to them to do so. This is supported by the fact that 'Ali, may God honour his face, Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad and 'Ikrimah, may God be pleased with them, read ( *bi-amri Allāh* ) with a *bā'*, which is clearly causative.

It is also permitted that it be attached to that as well, but with the meaning that they guard him from God's punishment whenever he sins, by seeking respite for him or by seeking forgiveness for him. That is, they guard him by asking God to give him respite and delay His punishment so that he may repent, or they ask God to forgive him and not punish him at all. Abu Hayyan said in *al-Bahr* that on this view the meaning of the speech becomes one of implication (*tadmīn*), that is, they invoke for him protection from the vengeance of God.

Al-Farra' and a group said that there is inversion (*taqdīm wa ta'khīr*) in the speech, meaning: for him are successive [angels] by God's command, who guard him from before him and from behind him. This was also transmitted from Mujahid, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Jurayj. In this case ﴿مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ is attached to a deleted element occurring as an attribute of *mu'aqqibāt*, meaning: arising from His command. It was also said that this meaning does not require a claim of inversion. Rather, God described the successive [angels] with three attributes: first, that they are from before him and from behind him; second, that they guard him; third, that they are from His command, glory be to Him. If ﴿مِن بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ﴾ is attached to *yaḥfaẓūnahu*, then there are two attributes: the sentence and the prepositional phrase. Placing the attribute by way of a sentence before the attribute by way of a prepositional phrase is permissible and common in eloquent Arabic. It seems that the attribute by way of a sentence, which indicates continuity in guarding, was placed first because it is more emphatic, and so it was placed before the other attribute.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that by *al-mu'aqqibāt* is meant the guards whom rulers take to protect them from being killed and the like. Something similar was transmitted from 'Ikrimah. The meaning of ﴿يَحْفَظُونَهُ مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ (they guard him from God's command) is that they guard him from God's decree and His destiny, and they repel that from him, supposing it to be a thing he should fear, because of their ignorance of God, may He be exalted. It is also possible that it is of the kind of metaphor used ironically (*al-isti'āra al-tahakkumiyya*), in the manner well known in God's words ﴿فَبَشِّرْهم بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾ (so give them tidings of a painful punishment). So it is a metaphor for its opposite, and its literal meaning is that they do not guard him. On this basis is explained the view of some of them that the meaning is "they do not guard him," not on the basis that there is an implied negation, as is supposed. Most scholars hold that by *al-mu'aqqibāt* is meant the angels.

In the Sahih [of al-Bukhari and Muslim] it is stated: "Angels succeed one another among you by night and angels by day, and they assemble at the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer." They also mention that with the servant there are, besides the noble recording angels, guarding angels. Abu Dawud, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi al-Dunya and others transmitted from 'Ali, may God honour his face, that he said: "For every servant there are guardians who guard him, so that no wall falls upon him, nor does he fall into a well, nor does an animal strike him. But when the appointed destiny that was decreed for him comes, the guardians leave him, and what God wills to befall him befalls him."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, al-Tabarani and al-Sabuni transmitted from Abu Umama, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "There are entrusted to the believer three hundred and sixty angels who repel from him what has not been decreed against him. For his sight there are seven angels who drive away [harm] from him, as flies are driven away from a bowl of honey on a summer day. And [there are others] which, if they were to appear to you, you would see them on every plain and mountain, all with hands outstretched and mouths open. And if the servant were left to himself for the blink of an eye, the devils would snatch him away."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Kinana al-'Adawi, who said: "'Uthman, may God be pleased with him, entered upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of God, tell me about the servant: how many angels are with him?' He said: 'An angel on your right over your good deeds, and he is the commander over the one on the left. When you do a good deed, it is recorded as ten. When you do an evil deed, the one on the left says to the one on the right: "Shall I record it?" He says: "No, perhaps he will ask God's forgiveness and repent." When he says it three times, [the angel on the right] says: "Yes, record it. May God relieve us of him. How evil a companion he is, how little he watches over himself before God, and how little he is ashamed before Him." God, exalted and majestic, says: ﴿not a word does he utter but there is an observer ready beside him﴾. And two angels are before you and two angels are behind you. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿for him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who guard him by the command of God﴾. And an angel holds your forelock: when you humble yourself before God, He raises you, and when you exalt yourself against God, He breaks you. And an angel stands guard over your mouth, not letting a snake enter it. And two angels are over your eyes. These are ten angels who descend upon every son of Adam by day, and the same number descend by night.'"

The reports on this subject are numerous. The matter of guarding raised a difficulty: what is decreed must occur, and what is not decreed does not occur, so from what is the guarding? It was answered that among God's decree and destiny there is that which is conditional (*mu'allaq*), so guarding is from that. This is why the adoption of means is considered good. Otherwise, the same difficulty applies to means as well: the matter one wishes to pursue is either decreed to exist, so it must exist, or decreed not to exist, so it must not exist. What then is the point of pursuing it and clinging to its causes? This was challenged: what was mentioned is considered good by us only because of our ignorance of whether what we seek is conditional or otherwise, whereas the problematic matter is not like that. You know that God has placed in perceptible things perceptible causes and linked their effects to them, in accordance with His overwhelming wisdom. Had He willed, He could have produced the effects without causes, owing to His self-sufficiency, glory be to Him. There is no obstacle to His placing in non-perceptible matters causes by which He links effects. In that case it may be said: He, whose greatness is exalted, made those guardians causes for guarding, just as He placed in the perceptible realm, for example, the eyelid as a cause for the protection of the eye, even though it is a cause only for protection against what has not been decreed by His decree and destiny, glory be to Him. The knowledge of wisdoms in their particulars is not something we are charged with. Knowing in general that God's acts are not devoid of wisdoms and benefits is enough for the believer. The same applies to the noble recording angels: they exist by explicit text, and God made them guardians of the servant's deeds, recording them. We believe this, even if we do not know their pen, their ink, their paper, how they write, where they reside, or what the wisdom of this is. God's knowledge is sufficient for reward and punishment for them. Likewise, a person's remembering them and his knowledge of them on the Day of Resurrection suffices to dispel whatever doubt might arise in his heart when he witnesses what follows from them. Some people have engaged in explaining the wisdom, but that is easier than explaining what accompanies it.

Al-Imam al-Razi, in answering the question about the benefit of making angels entrusted over us, gave a lengthy discussion. He said: Know that this is not far-fetched, for the astrologers agree that the governance of each day belongs to a separate star, and likewise for each night. There is no doubt that these stars have spirits in their view. Those governances that differ are, in reality, for those spirits. The same applies to the governance of the *hīlāj* and the *kadkhudāh*, according to what they say. As for the practitioners of talismans (*aṣḥāb al-ṭalsamāt*), this discourse is well known on their tongues, for they say: "The perfect nature-worker informed us of such-and-such." What they mean is that each person has a stellar spirit that takes charge of the proper handling of his affairs and the repelling of his calamities and afflictions. If this is agreed upon among the early philosophers and the practitioners of judgments, then how can its occurrence in the Shari'ah be considered far-fetched?

Al-Alusi's commentary continues:

The full verification of this is that human souls differ in their essences and natures: some are good and some are wicked, some are noble and some are base, some are strong in subjugation and some are weak. Just as the matter is with human souls, so it is with the celestial souls. There is no doubt that the celestial souls are stronger than human souls in every respect and quality. Every group of human souls shares a particular nature and a specific attribute, and in the rank of a celestial soul there is one that resembles them in nature and property. Those human souls are then like children of that celestial soul. If this is so, that celestial soul will be a helper for them in their affairs, a guide to their interests, and a protector of them from various calamities. This is a statement mentioned by the verifying philosophers. From this it is known that what the Shari'ah has conveyed is something accepted by all, so it cannot be denied. End of quotation.

Perhaps his intention by this is to liken the matter of the guardians (al-hafazah) with the servant to the matter of the celestial souls with him, according to the claim of the philosophers in general. Otherwise, what the Muslims say about their matter and what the philosophers say about the matter of those souls are two different things, and far be it, far be it, that we should say what they said, for it is far removed from what came from the Lawgiver, upon him be prayers and peace.

Then the one whose mercy is upon him mentioned, among the benefits of the guardians for deeds, that when the servant knows that the angels, peace be upon them, attend him and record his deeds, and they are as they are, he is closer to caution against committing sins, like one who stands before a group of honourable people, servants of a king appointed over him, for he scarcely attempts a sin in their presence. Others have also mentioned this, and it is not devoid of good sense.

Then there was related from the theologians, concerning the benefit of the written records, that they are weighed on the Day of Resurrection: whoever's scales are heavy will be in a pleasing life, and as for whoever's scales are light, his mother is the Abyss. Each of the two matters will be manifest to the creatures.

Al-Qadi criticised this, saying that it is far-fetched, because the evidences indicate that each person, before his death, at the moment of witnessing, knows whether he is among the blessed or among the wretched, we seek refuge with God Most High. Therefore it is not permissible that the attainment of knowledge should depend on the scale. Then he answered that what we have mentioned is also not impossible, for a matter that returns to the servant's joy before the great multitude when it becomes manifest that he is among God's friends, and the opposite happening to whoever is among God's enemies. It is not hidden that this is built upon the view that what is weighed is the pages, which is one of the opinions on the question. Indeed, a group of great scholars held it, on account of the well-known hadith of the card and the registers, and likewise upon the view that the writing is in its apparent meaning, which is what the People of Hadith held, and others besides them as far as I know. And from the sages of Islam another meaning has been related: they said that writing is an expression for particular marks which were established by convention to designate certain specific meanings. So if we suppose that those marks signify those meanings in their very essences and realities, that writing would be stronger and more perfect. And then we say: when a person performs a deed many times in succession, a strong and firmly rooted disposition arises in his soul because of that. If that disposition is one in beneficial deeds concerning spiritual felicities, his joy after death will be greatly magnified; and if that disposition is a harmful one in spiritual states, his harm from it afterward will be greatly magnified.
