Then he said: when this is established, we say: if frequent repetition is the cause of the arising of that firmly rooted disposition, then each of those deeds has an effect in producing that disposition, and that effect, though not perceptible, is nonetheless actually present. When this is understood, it becomes clear that no glance, movement or stillness occurs to a human without there arising from him, in the essence of his soul, an effect of the effects of felicity or the effects of wretchedness, whether little or much. This is what is meant by the recording of deeds according to the sages of Islam. And God Most High knows the realities of matters. End of quotation. I have seen this attributed to some of the Sufis.

You know that this is contrary to what the verses and reports have declared, and in such matters we do not depart from the apparent meaning as far as possible, and the truth is clear, and what follows the truth is only error.

Furthermore, some people have made the pronoun in (lahu) refer to the last-mentioned party, but the first is preferable. Others have made it refer to God Most High, and what follows it refers to the people, but this involves dislocating the pronouns without need. Others have made it refer to the Prophet ﷺ, which is known from the context, and his being the subject of the earlier report was mentioned in the words of God Most High: ﴿And they say, "Why has not a sign been sent down upon him?"﴾ and so on. This is supported by what Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il transmitted through 'Ata' ibn Yasar from Ibn 'Abbas: that Arbad ibn Qays and 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl came to Medina to the Messenger of God ﷺ. They arrived at him while he was sitting, and they sat before him. 'Amir said: "What will you give me if I become Muslim?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "You will have what the Muslims have, and you will bear what they bear." He said: "Will you make the affair after you mine if I become Muslim?" He, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "That is not for you nor for your people, but you will have the reins of horses." He said: "Then make the wool (of the camels) mine, and the clay (of the land) yours." He ﷺ said: "No." When he departed from him he said: "I will fill it against you with horses and men." The Prophet ﷺ said: "God will protect you." In another narration: "and the sons of Qaylah," meaning the Aws and the Khazraj. When they went out, 'Amir said: "O Arbad, I will distract Muhammad from you with talk, then strike him with the sword, for if the people see you have killed him they will not go beyond accepting the blood-money and disliking war, and we will give them the blood-money." Arbad said: "I will do it." Then they returned, and 'Amir said: "O Muhammad, stand with me, I want to speak with you." So he, upon him be prayers and peace, stood with him, and they went aside to a wall. 'Amir stood speaking to him, and Arbad drew the sword, but when he placed his hand on it, it dried up on its hilt, so he could not draw it, and he delayed on 'Amir's account. The Messenger of God ﷺ turned and saw Arbad and what he was doing, so he left them. 'Amir said to Arbad: "What is wrong with you?" He said: "I placed my hand on the hilt of my sword and it dried up." When they went out, and when they were at al-Raqm, they dismounted, and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Usayd ibn Hudayr came out to them. Usayd rebuked them, saying: "Begone, O enemies of God, may God curse you!" 'Amir said: "Who is this, O Sa'd?" He said: "This is Usayd ibn Hudayr, the commander of the battalions." He said: "By God, Hudayr was a friend of mine." Then God, glorified be He, sent a thunderbolt upon Arbad and it killed him. 'Amir went out until, when he was at Wadi al-Jarid, God Most High sent upon him an ulcer, and death overtook him. In another narration, he was crying out: "O 'Amir! A swelling like the swelling of a camel, and death in the house of a woman of Salul!" So God Most High revealed concerning them both: ﴿God knows what every female bears﴾ up to His words: ﴿For him are successive guardians﴾ to the end." Then he said: "The successive guardians are from the command of God; they protect Muhammad ﷺ." It came in another report from him, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "This applies to the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, specifically." Most scholars, however, take the generality, and the occasion of revelation does not preclude that. And God knows best.

Then, after mentioning the comprehensiveness of His knowledge regarding the servants and that they have successive guardians who protect them by His command, glorified be His majesty, He drew attention to the obligation of obedience and the ruin of disobedience, saying, Mighty is the One who speaks: ﴿Indeed God does not change what is with a people﴾ of blessing and well-being ﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾: what their essences are characterised by of praiseworthy conditions, not merely what they conceal and intend. Changing that means replacing it with its opposite, not merely abandoning it. And there came from 'Ali, may God ennoble his face, a report traced to the Prophet: "God Most High says: By My might, My majesty and My exaltation above My Throne, there is no people of a town, nor people of a house, nor a man in the desert, who were upon what I disliked of disobedience to Me and then turned from it to what I love of obedience to Me, except that I will turn for them from what they dislike of My punishment to what they love of My mercy. And there is no people of a town, nor people of a house, nor a man in the desert, who were upon what I loved of obedience to Me and then turned from it to what I disliked of disobedience to Me, except that I will turn for them from what they love of My mercy to what they dislike of My punishment." Related by Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh.

The apparent meaning of the verse has been raised as a difficulty, since it indicates that the change of blessings does not befall a people until a change occurs among them through sins, whereas that contradicts what the Shari'ah established regarding the general body being taken for the sins of the elite. Among this is the words of God, glorified be He: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾, and His words, upon him be prayers and peace, when he was asked: "Shall we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases." And His words, may God Most High bless him and grant him peace: "If they see the wrongdoer and do not take him by the hands, it is near that God will overtake them all with punishment," along with many other things. Also, God Most High may send upon the servant calamities by which his reward increases, and the sinner may be led on gradually by the absence of such things.

Ibn 'Atiyyah answered this by saying that the meaning is: until a change occurs in what is among them, or in whoever is of them, just as He changed by the defeated ones on the day of Uhud because of the archers' change in what was in themselves. The truth is that the meaning is that this is God Most High's customary practice in most cases, not that He does not afflict a people except after a prior sin on their part, so there is no difficulty. It was said: and you may say that His words, glorified be He: ﴿And when God intends evil for a people, there is no turning it back﴾ are a completion to remedy what was mentioned, and there is room for reflection in this. Evil (su') encompasses everything that distresses, of sickness, poverty and other kinds of affliction. And (maradd) is a noun of place/time pattern (masdar mimi), meaning there is no turning back of it. The governing element of (idha) is what indicates

...the answer to it, because the object of the verbal noun, and likewise what follows the *fa'* (the conjunctive particle), may not precede it. The implied meaning, as Abu al-Baqa said, is: "it occurs, or it does not come," or something similar. The apparent view is that *idha* (when) is for generality, and it has come in this way in most verses.

﴿And they have no one besides Him﴾, glorified is He, ﴿who could be a protector (*wali*)﴾. (11)

[It means] one who takes charge of their affairs, whether of harm or of benefit. This includes, primarily and without dispute, warding off evil from them.

It has been said: the first (*dafa*, "repelled") alludes to negating the one who repels, with the letter *dal*, and this alludes to negating the one who lifts away, with the letter *ra*, so that there is no repetition. But there is no need for this, as is not hidden.

The verse has been cited as evidence that opposing the will of God, exalted is He, is impossible. It has been objected that it shows only that when God wills evil for a people, its occurrence is necessary; it does not show that every will of His is like this, nor that its opposite is impossible, but rather that it does not occur. It has been answered that there is no difference between willing evil and willing something else, but the verse is restricted to willing the first because the discourse concerns retribution against the disbelievers, and this is more forceful in frightening them. So when the averting of evil is impossible, whatever else is like it. What is meant by "impossibility" is the non-occurrence of possibility in fact, not in essence. It is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Among the most surprising things said: the majority of scholars argued from the verse that sins are among the things that evil includes, and that they are by God's creation. Some people made the verse connected to His words: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil﴾, to the end of the verse. Abu Hayyan explained this in a way no one would approve of.

It has also been said: in it is an announcement that they, by what they engaged in, namely denying the resurrection, hastening evil, and demanding a sign, had altered what was within themselves of the natural disposition (*fitra*), and therefore deserved the descent of God's wrath.

Ibn Kathir paused (*waqf*) on *hadin* (﴿guide﴾), and likewise on *waqin* wherever it occurs, and on *wali* here, and on *baqin* in *al-Nahl* with the *ya'* retained. The rest of the Seven paused by omitting it. In *al-Iqna'* by Abu Ja'far ibn al-Baadhish, citing Ibn Mujahid, the pausal reading for the whole category is for Ibn Kathir with the *ya'*, and this is not known to the Meccans. In the same work, citing Abu Ya'qub al-Azraq, from Warsh, it is stated that he gave him the choice in pausing throughout this category between pausing with the *ya'* and pausing without it. So said *al-Bahr*. In it also: Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr in one transmission retained the *ya'* of *al-Muta'al* (﴿the Most High﴾) both in pause and in continuation, and this is the common usage in the Arabic language, while the rest omitted it both in continuation and in pause, because it is written so in the *Imam* (the Uthmanic codex, *rasm*).

Sibawayh cited its omission in the rhyme endings of verses and in the rhyming words of rhymed prose (*fawasil* and *qawafi*), and others permitted omitting it absolutely. The reason for omitting it, although it is omitted with *tanwin* and *al-* (the definite article) as an alternative to them, is his treating the substitute as taking the place of...

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 12:

﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, [causing] fear﴾ of the thunderbolt, ﴿and aspiration﴾ for the rain. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hasan that he said: "[Fear] for the people of the sea and [aspiration] for the people of the land." And from Qatadah: "Fear for the traveler of the harm of rain, and aspiration for the resident of its benefit." And from al-Mawardi: "Fear of punishment and aspiration for reward." The intended meaning of "lightning" is its well-known sense. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that what is meant by it is the water, so it is a metaphor (majaz) by way of naming a thing after what usually accompanies it.

﴿Fear and aspiration﴾ are in the accusative (naṣb) on the basis that they are objects of purpose (maf'ul lahu, the object indicating the reason for the action) to ﴿yurikum﴾ (He shows you). The unity of the agent of the cause and the agent of the action being explained is not a condition for the accusative. In the commentary on al-Kafiyah by al-Radi and according to some grammarians, their sharing the same agent is not required, and this is what seems stronger to me, although the more common view is the first. The permissibility of non-sharing of the agent has been argued from what we mentioned in our glosses on the commentary of al-Qatr by its author.

In Hama' al-Hawami: al-A'lam and the later scholars made it a condition that the action shares the same time and agent, while Sibawayh and none of the earlier scholars required this. Those who make it a condition had to interpret this difference of agent, since the agent of the showing is Allah, the Exalted, and the agent of the aspiration and fear is other than Him, glory be to Him. It was said: there is an implied omitted noun, namely "irada" (intention), meaning: He shows you that out of the intention that you should fear and aspire. Thus the object of purpose is the omitted noun with its agent, and the agent of the action explained by it is one and the same. It was also said: "fear" and "aspiration" are placed in the position of "causing fear" and "causing aspiration," just as "plants" (nabat) is placed in the position of "causing to grow" (inbat) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾. Verbal nouns may stand in for one another, or both are verbal nouns with their augmenting letters removed, as in the commentary on al-Tashil. It was also said that they are objects of purpose with respect to the addressees being viewers, because their being shown includes their seeing, and fear and aspiration are among their actions. Thus they performed the action explained by that, which is seeing. This returns to the meaning of "I sat out of the war out of cowardice." This is according to the manner of the saying of al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani:

"My dwellings settled on a high, fortified ridge,
where the herder of the camel-caravan thinks it a bird.
Out of caution lest my herd be harmed,
nor my women, until they die free."

It was said that this means: "I settled my dwellings out of caution." Abu al-Su'ud, the scholar, rejected this, saying there is no way to it, because what occurs in the position of a final cause, especially fear, is not suitable as a cause for their seeing. 'Izmi-zadah and others criticized him, saying it is a feeble statement, because the speaker declared that it is of the kind of "I sat out of the war out of cowardice," and he means that the object of purpose is what drives the action and exists before it, and it is not among what is placed in the position of a final cause, as they say in "I struck him to discipline him." So there is no basis for the rebuttal with what was mentioned. It was also said: the causality here is like that of the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), not that this is of the kind of "I sat out of the war out of cowardice" as he supposed, because cowardice is a motive for sitting, not for the two (fear and aspiration) being the cause of seeing. This is not valid, because it is a motive without doubt. Al-'Izmi objected to it that the lam implied in the object of purpose was never said by anyone to be the lam of consequence, and usage does not support it. This is nothing. How so, when the grammarians have said, as in al-Durr al-Masun: it is like the saying of al-Nabigha mentioned above. He also said: there remains a question here, namely that the implication of making the verse like "I sat..." etc., according to what that speaker said, is that fear and aspiration precede the seeing in existence, and this is not so; rather they arise from it. It may be said that what is meant by each of fear and aspiration, according to what he said, is what is among the psychological dispositions, like cowardice in the example mentioned. And it is valid to explain the seeing, which comes from the showing, by these two; that is, the seeing that occurs by the showing of Allah, glory be to Him, occurred only because of what is in them of fear and aspiration, since if that were not in their nature, that seeing would have no benefit. End. There is no hiding what is in it of artificiality, and you have known that it is not valid.

It was also said: the accusative may be in the adverbial state (hal) from ﴿al-barq﴾ (the lightning), or from the addressees, with an implied noun, or by interpreting the verbal noun as a passive or active participle, or by keeping the verbal noun as it is for emphasis, as it is said in "Zayd is justice" (zayd 'adlun).

﴿And He produces the clouds﴾, meaning the cloud that is drawn out in the air, ﴿the heavy﴾ (al-thiqal). (12) With water. It is the plural of "thaqilah" (heavy), and "cloud" is described by it because it is a collective noun (ism jins) with the meaning of plurality. It may be masculine or feminine. So it is as if it were the plural of "heavy cloud" (sahabah thaqilah), not that it is a plural or a collective noun of plurality, because it is applied to a single one and to others.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 13 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And the thunder glorifies [Him] with His praise﴾. It has been said: it is the name of the known sound, and the speech is elliptical, meaning "those who hear the thunder." Or the ascription is figurative, of the type of ascribing an action to its bearer or its cause (*isnad majazi*, figurative ascription). The *ba'* in His words, "﴿with His praise﴾," expresses accompaniment, and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The meaning is: those who hear that sound glorify while accompanied by the praise of God, Exalted, so they cry out "Glory be to God" and "Praise be to God."

It has been said: there is no ellipsis and no figurative usage in the ascription. The figurative usage lies only in the glorifying and the praising, since the thunder's indication of His transcendence above a partner and above incapacity is likened to the verbal glorification and declaration of His transcendence, and its indication of His bounty and mercy, may He be exalted, is likened to the praise of one who praises, because both contain indications of the attributes of perfection. It has also been said: it is a metonymy (*majaz mursal*), used in its necessary consequence. And it has been said: "the thunder" is the name of an angel, so ascribing glorification and praise to it is literal.

[p. 119]

Al-Kashshaf says: "The more likely reading of the verse is to take it as figurative ascription, so that the speech coheres. The word 'thunder' in common usage refers to the particular sound, which is mentioned together with lightning and clouds, and the discourse is about showing the signs that indicate His overwhelming power and bringing them into being. The glorification of the angel of thunder does not fit that context. As for taking the particular sound as glorifying and praising to those who hear it, this is an extremely strong fit. If it is taken as literal ascription, the best view is that it is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraDan*) indicating the acknowledgment by the angel charged with the clouds, and the rest of the angels, of the perfection of His power, glory be to Him, and the denial of that by man. You know that the glorification of the angels, according to what he claimed is more likely, remains like a parenthetical clause in the middle." The view preferred by most of the scholars of hadith is that the ascription is literal, on the basis that "the thunder" is the name of the angel who drives the clouds. Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i and others transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that:

"The Jews asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: 'Tell us, what is this thunder?' He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'It is an angel among the angels of Allah, the Exalted, charged over the clouds. In his hands is a whip of fire, with which he drives the clouds, driving them wherever Allah, the Exalted, commands him.' They said: 'Then what is this sound that we hear?' He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'It is his voice.' They said: 'You have spoken the truth.'"

The reports on this are numerous. An objection is raised: if it were a proper name for the angel, it would not be permissible to make it indefinite (*tankir*), yet it appears indefinite in al-Baqarah. It is answered that it has two usages, the second being its application to the sound itself, and the indefinite form is used according to this usage. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It has been said that the thunder is a wind flapping between the clouds, and this was transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas." Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying: "In my view this is not sound, for it is one of the speculations of the naturalists and others."

Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: "The investigating philosophers mention that these upper phenomena are only accomplished through spiritual celestial powers, and the cloud has a specific spirit from among the celestial spirits that manages it. Likewise the case of the winds and of the other upper phenomena. This is the very thing we have said, that the thunder is the name of an angel among the angels who glorifies God, the Exalted. So this which the exegetes expressed in this phrasing is the very thing the investigating philosophers mentioned. How then is it fitting for a sensible person to deny it?" Abu Hayyan also criticized this, saying: "His aim is to make what the philosophers imagine run upon the paths of the Sharia, and that will never be. May God, the Exalted, have mercy on him, for he was right that the reconciliation between what the Sharia brought and what the cobwebs of philosophers' thoughts have woven is not valid. Yes, such a thing is possible in a very small matter of that and this." The well-known view of the philosophers is that the wind is confined within the body of the cloud, and cold dominates its outer surface, so the outer layer freezes. Then that wind tears it apart violently, and from this a violent motion arises, which necessarily produces friction. The lightning and the thunder are nothing but what results from that motion and its heating. As for the cloud, it is vapors rising, which have reached in their ascent the cold layer of the air. But since the cold was not strong enough, they condensed to that extent of cold, gathered, and dripped down, and what drips is called rain. Al-Razi's first view was refuted as contrary to reason in several respects:

First: if the matter were as stated, then whenever lightning occurred, thunder would occur, which is the sound produced by tearing the cloud. It is well known that a strong flash of lightning often occurs without thunder.

Second: the heat resulting from the strength of the motion is opposed by the watery nature which causes cold, and when this strong opposing factor is present, how could the fiery nature arise? Rather, it is said that great fires are extinguished by pouring water on them, and the cloud is entirely water. So how could a weak fiery flame arise within it?

Third: according to your own doctrine, pure fire has no color at all. Grant that the fiery nature arose from the force of the friction occurring among the parts of the cloud; yet from where did that red color come?

The second objection was answered by saying that rains vary: sometimes their drops are large, sometimes small, sometimes close together, sometimes far apart, and other such differences. Yet the nature of the earth is one, and the nature of the sun heating the vapors is one, which refuses that this is as they have determined. Also, experience shows that supplication and prayer have a great effect on the formation of clouds and the descent of rain, and this refuses that it be due to nature and inherent property. So all of that is nothing but the bringing into being of a wise, powerful Originator who creates what He wills however He wills. Some of the investigators said: "It is not far-fetched that in the formation of what has been mentioned there are customary causes, as in many of the acts of God, the Exalted. That does not contradict its attribution to the wise, powerful Originator, glory be to Him. Whoever is fair-minded will not be helped by denying causes entirely, for some of them are known by necessity. It is on this basis that I say, and some of this discussion has already been presented in this place."

[p. 120]

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to do, as Ibn Marduwayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah: "When the wind blew or the sound of thunder was heard, his color would change, so that it was recognized in his noble face. Then he would say to the thunder: 'Glory be to the One whom you glorify.' And to the wind: 'O Allah, make it a mercy and do not make it a punishment.'"

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others transmitted from Ibn 'Umar: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard the sound of thunder and the thunderbolts, he would say: 'O Allah, do not kill us by Your anger, do not destroy us by Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that.'"

Abu Dawud in his al-Marasil transmitted from 'Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far: "A people heard the thunder and exclaimed 'Allahu akbar,' so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'When you hear the thunder, glorify [God], and do not exclaim Allahu akbar.'" Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: "He, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say when he heard the thunder: 'Glory be to Allah and with His praise, glory be to Allah the Mighty.'" Ibn Marduwayh and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "He (ﷺ) would say, when he heard the thunder: 'Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise.'"

﴿And the angels out of fear of Him﴾: that is, the angels, peace be upon them, glorify out of awe of His majesty, may His majesty be exalted. It has been said: the pronoun refers to the thunder, and what is meant by the angels is its helpers, whom Allah, the Exalted, placed under its authority, fearful and submissive to it. This is a weak view.

﴿And He sends the thunderbolts﴾: the plural of *sa'iqah* (thunderbolt). It is originally, like *sa'iqah*, a great crash, except that *al-saq'* is used for earthly bodies and *al-sa'q* for heavenly bodies. What is meant here is the fire descending from the cloud together with a violent sound.

﴿So He strikes﴾ with them, glory be to Him, ﴿whom He wills﴾ to strike, so that He destroys him. It has been said: this fire is said to arise from the friction of the parts of the cloud. It is cited as evidence what Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Marduwayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The thunder is an angel named 'the Thunder,' and this sound is its glorification. When its driving becomes intense, the cloud rubs against itself and collides out of its fear, and the thunderbolts come out from between it."

The philosophers said: the smoke trapped in the interior of the cloud, when it descends and tears the cloud, may ignite through the force of heating produced by the intense motion and the violent collision. When it ignites, its subtle part is quickly extinguished, and this is the lightning. Its dense part does not go out until it reaches the earth, and this is the thunderbolt. When it reaches the earth, it may become subtle, penetrating into what is porous without burning it, leaving only a trace of blackness, and melting whatever solid dense bodies it strikes. Thus it melts gold and silver in a purse, for example, without burning them, except what is burned of the melting agent. It has been reported by a reliable, mass-transmitted account that a thunderbolt struck, some time ago, in Shiraz, upon the dome of the great shaykh Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Khafif, may his secret be sanctified. It melted a lamp that was in it, without burning anything of it. Sometimes it is very dense and thick, and then it burns everything it strikes. Often it falls on a mountain and crushes it to dust. Sometimes it falls on the sea and plunges into it, burning the animals within it. Sometimes the body of the thunderbolt is very fine, like a sword, and when it reaches something it cuts it in two, with the separation being only slight.

It is recounted that a boy was sleeping in a desert when a thunderbolt struck his two legs, and his legs fell off, and no blood came out, because of the cauterization by its heat.

What they have said about the cause of its formation is not far from what has been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, on this matter. Its material, according to what some have reported from Ibn Sina, is fiery bodies from which heat has departed, and which have become, because cold has overcome their essence, equal in their composition. Al-Imam said in his commentary on al-Isharat: "Thunderbolts, according to what has been reported from the Shaykh (Ibn Sina), resemble iron at times, copper at times, and stone at times, and this is clear evidence that their material is not one thing, unless it differs." From here it has been said that their material is vapors and smokes resembling the materials of these bodies. It has also been said that it is fire that comes out of the mouth of the angel charged with the cloud when his driving becomes intense.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, who said: "There are seas of fire beneath the Throne, from which the thunderbolts come." If what has been transmitted from the rabbi (Ibn 'Abbas) is sound, there is no departing from it.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Whoever hears the sound of thunder and says: 'Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise, and the angels out of His fear, and He is powerful over all things,' and then a thunderbolt strikes him, then I am liable for his blood-money (*diyah*)." Ibn Abi Hatim and others transmitted from Abu Ja'far, who said: "The thunderbolt strikes the believer and the disbeliever, but it does not strike one who remembers Allah." There is a raised report (*marfu'*) that supports this.

It has destroyed Arbad, as you know. His maternal brother Labid al-Amiri alluded to this in his elegy for him, saying:

*I fear for Arbad the calamities, and I do not dread the star of rain of al-Simak or of al-Asad,*

*The lightning and the thunderbolts have bereaved me of the horseman, on the day of the dread battle, the valiant.*

According to what Ibn Jurayj and others said, this verse was revealed concerning that incident. It is also related from Mujahid that a Jew disputed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and while he was thus, a thunderbolt descended and seized the top of his skull, and so this verse was revealed. It has also been said: "He (ﷺ) sent to a tyrant among the Arabs, inviting him to Islam. He said: 'Tell me about the God of Muhammad: is He made of pearl, or of gold, or of copper?' So a thunderbolt descended upon him and destroyed him, and this verse was revealed."

[Page 121]

The word (man) is the object of ﴿yuṣību﴾ (He strikes). The construction regarding what is in the sea is an instance of *al-i'māl* (the grammatical principle in which one of two competing verbs governs a shared noun, here the second verb governing it). Both (yursilu, "He sends") and ﴿yuṣību﴾ require (man) as their object. Had the first verb been made to govern it, the construction would have been: "He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills." However, the second verb governing the noun is the more common and preferred usage in the speech of the Arabs according to the *al-Baṣriyyūn* (the grammarians of Basra).

Then, after He mentioned His all-pervading knowledge of everything, and the equality of the apparent and the hidden before Him, and what indicates His overwhelming power and oneness, He, exalted is His majesty, said: ﴿wa-hum﴾ (yet they), that is, those who disbelieved, denied the Messenger (ﷺ), and rejected His signs, ﴿yujādilūna fī Allāh﴾ (dispute concerning God), by denying what the Truthful One (ﷺ) describes Him with, of perfection of knowledge and power, sole divinity, the resurrection of people, and their recompense. So the meaning of "disputing concerning Him" (exalted is He) is disputing about His affairs and what He, exalted is His majesty, has informed about Him. The word *jidāl* (disputation, from the root j-d-l) with a fatha on both letters means the most intense enmity. Its root is *al-jadl* with a sukūn (the root sense), which is the twisting of a rope or similar, because it becomes strong and its strands are tightened.

Al-Rāghib (al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī) said: The origin of this is from *jadaltu al-ḥabl*, meaning I twisted the rope firmly, as if each of the two disputants twists the other away from his opinion. It has also been said that the origin of *jidāl* is conflict and one person throwing his companion onto the *jadāla*, which is hard ground. The interpretation of the verse in the manner mentioned was adopted by al-Zamakhsharī. In *al-Kashf* he said: In his words there is an indication that the speech contains an *iltifāt* (shift in grammatical person), since His words ﴿sawā'un minkum﴾ (alike among you)…

﴿huwa alladhī yurīkum﴾ (It is He who shows you): In this there is an *iltifāt* from the third person to the second person. If you wish, reflect on His words: ﴿ulā'ika alladhīna kafarū bi-rabbihim﴾ (Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord) up to His words, exalted is He: ﴿al-kabīr al-mutaʿāl﴾ (the Great, the Most High). Then turn from the second person to the third person, and consider the excellence of its placement. As for the first, there is what it contains of specifying the threat embedded in ﴿sawā'un minkum﴾, and for this reason it is concluded with His words, exalted is He: ﴿inna Allāha lā yughayyiru mā bi-qawmin﴾ (Indeed, God does not change what is with a people) up to ﴿min wālin﴾ (any protector). And in it is a degree of threat that is not hidden from one who has insight, and an urging to seek deliverance. The increase in reproach is in His words, exalted is He: ﴿huwa alladhī yurīkum﴾, and in the coming of ﴿sawā'un minkum﴾.

﴿huwa alladhī yurīkum﴾ comes after His words, exalted is He: ﴿Allāhu yaʿlamu﴾ (God knows), in this way without a conjunction, because the first (statement) confirms His words, exalted is He: ﴿Allāhu yaʿlamu﴾, together with the added embedding (*idmāj*) mentioned, establishing knowledge; and the second confirms what was implied of the indication of power in His words, exalted is He: ﴿wa-kullu shay'in ʿindahu bi-miqdār﴾ (and everything with Him is in measure), together with observing the pattern of enumeration in the manner of ﴿al-Raḥmān ʿallama al-Qur'ān﴾ (The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an), which reveals to the contemplative, regarding the aspect of the inimitability of the revelation, what is astonishing to the minds and wondrous.

As for the second, there is in it an indication that they, despite the clarity of the signs, their recitation to them, and the far-reaching warning both by way of encouragement and deterrence, did not care for them at all. So it is as if He complains of their offence to one who deserves to be addressed, or as one who murmurs within himself: "How I shall deal with them and do such-and-such," as a recompense for what they committed, so that He may see what He wants to bring upon them. On this basis, His words, exalted is He: (hum) to its end are conjoined to His words, exalted is He: ﴿wa-yaqūlu alladhīna kafarū law-lā unzila﴾ (And those who disbelieved say, "Why was it not sent down…"), which is conjoined to ﴿wa-yastaʿjilūnaka﴾ (and they urge you to hasten). The shift from the verbal sentence to the nominal sentence, and the abandonment of observing correspondence, indicate that they did not increase after the signs except in obstinacy: ﴿wa-ammā alladhīna kafarū fa-zādat-hum rijsan ilā rijsihim﴾ (As for those who disbelieved, it adds to them filth upon their filth).

It is also permissible to say that it is conjoined to ﴿huwa alladhī yurīkum﴾, with the meaning: "It is He who shows you these perfect signs that indicate His power and mercy, while you dispute concerning Him, exalted is He." This is closer in its derivation, while the first is more hopeful regarding benefit. End of quotation. The signs of verification are evident in it.

Al-Ṭībī claimed that the most fitting for the composition of the structure is that this be a consolation to His beloved (ﷺ). For when He censured the disbelievers of Quraysh for their obstinacy in demanding signs like the signs of Moses and Jesus (peace be upon them both), and their denial that the one who came with them (peace and blessings be upon him) was a sign, He consoled him, exalted is His majesty, with what has been mentioned, as if He said: "Do not grieve; you are not singled out in this. For despite the manifest signs and the proofs of monotheism, they dispute concerning God by taking partners and ascribing children to Him; and despite the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the perfection of His power, exalted is His majesty, they deny the gathering and the resurrection; and despite the overwhelming force of His authority and the severity of His might, they proceed to scheming and obstinacy. So let not your soul go out after them in regret." Let this be contemplated. The conjunction to (yursilu al-ṣawāʿiq) (He sends the thunderbolts) is not considered good, because of lack of coherence. It is permitted that the clause be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the object of ﴿yuṣību﴾, meaning: "He strikes with them whom He wills while they are disputing," or from the object of ﴿yashā'u﴾ (He wills), according to what has been said, and this is, as you see, weak. The circumstance of revelation does not specify the circumstantial sense, as is not hidden.

﴿wa-huwa shadīd al-miḥāl﴾ (And He is Mighty in strength/severe in planning). (13)

Al-*miḥāl* means *al-mumāḥala*, which is scheming, from *maḥala bi-fulān* (with a light vowel) when he schemed against him and exposed him to destruction. From it comes *tamaḥḥala li-kadhā* when one exerts effort to use a stratagem and strives in it. It is therefore a verbal noun like *al-qitāl* (fighting). It has also been said that it is a noun rather than a verbal noun, from *al-maḥl*, meaning power. This meaning is applied to the verse of al-A'shā:

"A scion of arrows swaying on the branch of glory,
Great in generosity, severe in power (*miḥāl*)."

And to the words of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib:

"Let not their cross overcome, nor their scheming,
O enemy, overcome Your scheming."

It seems its origin is from *al-maḥl*, meaning drought. Both interpretations are narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās. It has also been said that it is *mif'al*, not *fiʿāl*, from *al-ḥawl*, meaning power. Ibn Qutayba said it is likewise, from the well-known *ḥīla* (stratagem), and its *mīm* is an augmentation like the *mīm* of *makān* (place). Al-Azharī criticized this, saying that if it were *mif'al* it would be like *mirwad* and *miḥwar*. He excused this by saying it was irregularly altered. He supported the claim of augmentation by the reading of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-A'raj, *al-maḥāl* with a fatḥa on the *mīm*, [Page 122]

considering it *mafʿal* from *ḥāla yaḥūlu* when he deployed a stratagem, since the origin is the agreement of the two readings. *Al-maḥāla* is also said for stratagem, and from it the proverb: "The man is helpless, not the stratagem." Abū Zayd said it means vengeance, apparently taken from *al-maḥl* meaning drought also. Ibn ʿArafa said it means disputation; it is said: *māḥala ʿan amrihi*, meaning he disputed about his matter. It has also been said that it means rancour, narrated from ʿIkrima, and they took it as metaphorical.

It is also permissible that *al-maḥāl* with a fatḥa means the spine, which is the backbone and its support. Al-Zamakhsharī said in *al-Asās*: A horse is said to be *qawiyy al-maḥāl*, meaning strong in spine. Its singular is *maḥāla*, and the *mīm* is original. In that case it becomes an image of strength and power, as in the authentic hadith: "The forearm of God, exalted is He, is firmer, and His razor sharper" (*fa-sāʿid Allāh taʿālā asaddu wa-mūsāhu aḥadd*), because when a person's spine is strong, he is described as having great strength and as capable of what others cannot accomplish. Do you not see the saying: "The calamities broke his spine" (*faqarathu al-fawāqir*), which is an image for weakening the powers. By this interpretation, it does not entail attributing corporeality to Him, exalted is He. The sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the sublime Name.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 14:**

﴿To Him﴾, that is, to Allah, the Exalted, belongs ﴿the call of truth﴾. That is, the supplication and entreaty that is established and rightly placed, which is answered when it is made. The idafah (genitive construction) here serves to indicate the connection of the call with truth, its exclusivity to it, and its being far from any taint of falsehood, error, or loss, as one says "the word of truth." The meaning is that the answering of such a call belongs to Him, the Exalted, and not to anyone else. This is supported by what follows, as is not hidden. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "the call of truth" is supplication at the time of fear, for in that situation none is called upon except Allah, the Exalted, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Those whom you call upon besides Him have strayed away﴾. Al-Mawardi claimed that this is closer to the context of the verse. It has also been said that the "call" means supplication, that is, the seeking of attention, and what is intended is worship, by way of inclusion, and the idafah is in the manner of what preceded. Some say that this idafah is from the construction of the qualified noun to its attribute, and the discussion of it is well known. The essential meaning is that the one who truly deserves to be worshipped is Allah, the Exalted, and none other.

It is understood from the words of some, as it has been said, that the "call" means supplication and its object is omitted, that is, [supplication] for worship. The meaning is that He is the one who truly deserves to be called upon to worship Him, and none other. There is no hiding the mutual implication between the two meanings: when the call to worship Him, glorified is He, is true, then His worship is true, and vice versa. It is related from al-Hasan that the intended meaning of "the truth" is Allah, the Exalted. This, as in al-Bahr, is the second of the two views mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, and the meaning according to it is, as he said: "To Him is the call of the one called upon, the Truth, who hears and responds." The first is what we pointed to at the outset, and "the truth" in it is set in contrast to falsehood.

The author of al-Kashf has clarified the essence of the two views by saying that the discourse is directed to establish His exclusivity, glorified is He, in being called upon and worshipped, as a refutation of those who dispute concerning Allah, the Exalted, and associate rivals with Him, glorified is He. There must be in the idafah an indication of this exclusivity. As for making "the truth" the opposite of falsehood, this is clear. If it is taken as one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, then the original form would be "To Allah is His call," emphasizing exclusivity through the lam and the idafah. Then this was intensified by placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, and by restating it with a description that indicates its exclusivity to Him in the strongest way. Thus it was said: "To Him is the call of the one called upon, the Truth." "The Truth" is among His names, glorified is He, and it indicates that He alone is truly established, and that anything else is false in itself, though it is true by the act of His making it so. It is restricted according to each context, to indicate that its opposite has no reality. When the one called upon besides Him is shown to be false because it does not respond, then He is "the Truth who hears and responds." End of quotation. With this, what Abu Hayyan objected to regarding the second view is refuted, namely that its outcome would be "the call of Allah to Allah," which is like saying "to Zayd is the call of Zayd," and that this is not valid. And one can dispense with what the scholar al-Tibi said in his interpretation, that the meaning is: "And to Allah, the Exalted, belongs the call that is fitting to be attributed to and linked with His presence, the Exalted, because He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing, Generous, whose petitioner is never disappointed, so He answers the supplication." For this, as you see, is of little benefit. From what is in al-Kashf, the connection of this sentence with what came before is known.

Some have said: the connection of this sentence, and of the sentence before it, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is severe in might﴾, is as follows. If the occasion of revelation is the story of Arbad and Amir, then their destruction in a way they did not perceive is a judgment from Allah, the Exalted, and a response to the supplication of His Messenger ﷺ. It is related that he, peace be upon him, said: "O Allah, restrain them from me by whatever means You wish." Or it is an indication of the Messenger ﷺ being upon the truth. If the occasion of revelation is not that, then the meaning is that this is a warning to the disbelievers for their disputing with the Messenger, may Allah, the Exalted, send blessings and peace upon him, that His might will descend upon them, and a threat that His answering of his supplication will come upon them if he prays against them, peace be upon him. Or it is a statement of their misguidance and the corruption of their opinion in worshipping other than Allah, the Exalted. From what has been mentioned, the connection according to some interpretations is also known, if we say that the occasion of revelation is the story of the Jew or of the tyrant. So reflect.

﴿And those who call upon﴾, that is, the idols whom they call upon, that is, the polytheists. The omission of the returning pronoun of the relative clause in such a construction is common. It has also been permitted that the relative pronoun refers to the polytheists, with the plural pronoun in the verb referring back to it, and the object of ﴿call upon﴾ being omitted, that is, [they call upon] the idols. It is omitted because the phrase ﴿besides Him﴾ indicates it, for its meaning is "transgressing beyond Him," and their transgression is only by worshipping them. The first view is supported by the reading of al-Bazdawi on the authority of Abu 'Amr: "tad'una" (you call upon) with the second person, and the pronoun in ﴿do not respond﴾ refers to "those" (alladhina). According to the second view it refers to the object of "yad'una." In either case, the meaning is that the idols do not respond to them, that is, to the polytheists, with anything of their requests, ﴿except like one who stretches out his palms toward water﴾. That is, they respond with nothing of the response, nor with any part of it, except a response like the response of water to one who stretches out his palms toward it from afar, seeking it and calling it, ﴿that it may reach his mouth﴾, that is, that the water may reach it of its own accord without being taken up in a vessel or anything similar, ﴿but it does not reach it﴾, that is, the water does not reach his mouth at all, because it is an inanimate thing that does not perceive his thirst or the stretching of his hands toward it. Abu Hayyan permitted that "huwa" (it/he) refers to the mouth, and the "ha'" in "bali'ihi" refers to the water, meaning: nor is his mouth one that reaches the water, since each of them does not reach the other in this state.

Some have permitted that the first pronoun refers to "the one who stretches" (basit) and the second refers to ﴿the water﴾. Abu al-Baqa' said: It is not permissible for the first to refer to "basit" and the second to refer to the mouth, because when the active participle applies to other than the one who possesses it, the agent must be made explicit. Thus it would have been necessary to say: "wa ma huwa bi-balighihi al-ma'" (and he is not one who reaches it, the water). But the majority hold what you have heard first. The purpose, as one of the careful scholars said, is that the response is categorically negated, by depicting them as being in the greatest need of it, yet least able to attain their goals; and in this case one is most disappointed in his effort concerning what he most needs. The summary is that He likened their idols, when they seek their help for what concerns them, in the language of necessity, to the lack of perception, let alone the ability to respond, and their remaining in that loss to the state of water seen by a thirsty man who stretches his palms toward it, calling to it by word and by gesture. So it increases his burning thirst and ruin. The comparison according to this is in the original sense a compound allegorical simile (al-murakkab al-tamthili), presented in the manner of mockery, in which it affirms that they are two responses, as an increase in their loss and ruin. Thus the exception is a "mufarragh" (open) exception from the most general class of the verbal noun, as we pointed out. It is apparent that the response there is a verbal noun from the active form, which is what the apparent verb requires. It has also been permitted that it is a verbal noun from the passive form, and it is attributed to the one who stretches out, on the basis that a verbal noun from the active form implies a verbal noun from the passive form, both in existence and non-existence. So it is as if it were said: "They do not respond to them with anything, so no response is granted to them like the response to one who stretches out his palms to the water," as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"And the biting of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth only the one who is stripped bare, or the one who is cleaned out."

That is, time has left nothing, so there remains only one who is stripped bare or one who is cleaned out. Abu al-Baqa' takes "al-istijabah" as the verbal noun of the passive form, and its idafah to "basit" as an idafah of the verbal noun to its object, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Man does not tire of supplicating for good﴾. The agent is the pronoun of "the water" according to the second view of the relative clause. It may also be intended by the spreading of the two palms toward the water: the spreading of them, that is, the extending of their fingers and stretching them out for drinking, not for supplication or pointing to it, as we have pointed out before. On this basis it has been said: those who call upon other than Allah, the Exalted, are likened to one who wants to scoop up water with his two hands, so he spreads them out, extending his fingers, in that neither of them will obtain any benefit. Some have made the point of comparison to be the scarcity of benefit, and perhaps he meant its absence, but he exaggerated by mentioning scarcity while intending absence, to indicate the crushing of the truth and the preference for sincerity, and to convey a touch of mockery. The comparison according to this is of the simple comparison of a restricted single item, like your saying to one whose effort yields nothing: "He is like one who writes on water." For the one compared is the striver restricted by his effort being such, and the one compared to is the writer restricted by his writing being on water in such a way. In what we are dealing with it is not at all a compound intellectual comparison, contrary to what has been supposed. Yes, the point of comparison is intellectual and conventional. The exception is "mufarragh" from the most general class of states, meaning: the gods do not respond to these disbelievers who call upon them, except as those who resemble the one who stretched out his palms and did not close them, and brought them out in that manner, so he obtains nothing, because water is obtained by closing the hand, not by spreading it. It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that this is a comparison to a thirsty man at the edge of a well, without a rope, who cannot reach the bottom of the well, nor does the water rise up to him. This returns to the first view and is not different from it, as has been said. And it is narrated from Abu 'Ubayda that this is a comparison to one who grasps water, in that he obtains nothing from it. Then he said: "The Arabs strike the proverb concerning one who strives for something he cannot attain by that means." And he recited the verse of the poet:

"So I became, in what was between me and her, of affection, like the one who grasps water in his hand."

And his saying:

"And I, and you, and longing for you, am like one who grasps water which his fingertips could not hold."

This returns to the second view, except that from "basit" the meaning of "qabid" (one who grasps) does not clearly appear, for the spreading of the palm is apparent in the extending of the fingers stretched out, as in his saying:

"He became accustomed to spreading the palm, such that if he wanted to close it, his fingertips would not obey him."

Whatever the case, the intended meaning of "basit" is a person who stretches out, whoever he may be. What the apparent sense of what is narrated from Bukayr ibn Ma'ruf requires, namely that he is Qabil, since when he killed his brother, Allah, the Exalted, made his punishment that He seized him by the forelock in the sea, with nothing between him and the water but a finger, and he wants it, is something one should not rely upon.

It was also read ﴿like one who stretches out his palms﴾ with tanwin, meaning: like a person who stretches out his palms. ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾, that is, in loss, ruin, and falsehood. If the supplication here means their supplication to their gods, then it is evident that it is so, but it is understood from what precedes, and in that case it is a repetition for emphasis. If it means their supplication to Allah, the Exalted, then they have raised a difficulty concerning this, namely that the supplication of a disbeliever may be answered, which is explicitly stated in the fatwas, and that the answering of the supplication of Iblis, who is the head of the disbelievers, is a clear text on that. It has been answered that what is intended is their supplication to Allah, the Exalted, concerning matters of the Hereafter. On this basis is to be understood what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the voices of the disbelievers are veiled from Allah, the Exalted, so their supplication is not heard. It has also been said that it is permissible for the intended meaning to be their supplication in general, without restricting it to what they were answered with.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 15:

﴿And to God﴾ alone ﴿prostrates﴾, that is, submits and yields, to no other, glory be to Him, either independently or in partnership. Thus the restriction (qasr) encompasses both the heart and the singling out (ifrad). ﴿Whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, of the angels and the two weighty ones (humans and jinn), as the apparent expression "man" (man) requires. The singling out of the rational beings for submission, although the rest are likewise, is because they are the main part (al-umda), and their submission is evidence of the submission of others. In what follows, God willing, there is an explanation of this. It has also been said: the meaning includes those and others, and the use of "man" is by way of predominance (taghlib). ﴿Willingly and unwillingly﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). If we say that the verbal noun (masdar) occurs as a state without interpretation, then it is clear; otherwise it is by interpretation as "obeying and unwilling," meaning: they are humbled before His greatness, may He be exalted, and yield to the bringing into being and the annihilation that He wills for them, whether they wish or refuse, without the intervention of the judgment of any other, may He be majestic and exalted; rather, no other judgment than His, may He be exalted, has any part in any of that.

It is permissible that the accusative be a causal accusative (ʿilla), so that "unwillingly" (al-kurh) means "compulsion" (al-ikrah), which is the verbal noun of the passive form, so that the agent is one (li-yattahid al-fa'il), based on the condition of that in the accusative of the object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) according to those who stipulate it. As for what has been objected to this, that regarding unwillingness as a cause is not apparent, because it is what is opposed to willingness and is refusal, and it cannot be conceived as a cause for prostration, it is rebutted by saying that the cause is what moves one to an act, or what results from it, not what is not an aim for it. This has passed shortly before, so recall it. It has also been said: the accusative is absolute (mutlaq) object, meaning the prostration of willingness and unwillingness. ﴿And their shadows﴾, that is, the shadows of those among them who have that quality also submit to Him, may He be exalted, and these are humans only, or what includes them and everything dense.

In the Shihabi marginalia (al-Hawashi al-Shihabiyya) it is said: the pronoun should refer to "whoever is on the earth," because whoever is in the heavens has no shadow, unless it is taken as predominance or metaphor. The meaning of the submission of shadows to Him, may He be exalted, is that they follow His disposal and His will in lengthening and shortening, in the shade and the decline. The origin of "shadow" (zill), as al-Farra' said, is a verbal noun, then it was applied to the image that appears for a body, which is either reversed or upright, and rulings are built on each of these, which they mentioned in their proper place. ﴿In the mornings and the evenings﴾. (15) The phrase is an adverbial complement (zarf) for the implied prostration, and the preposition "bi" means "fi" (in), which is common. The intended meaning of both is permanence, because the like of this is mentioned for the sake of perpetuity. It has been said: so it is not asked why this was singled out for mention. Likewise it is said: when both are in the position of a state for the shadows. Some explain this by saying that their lengthening and shortening are more apparent at those two times.

Al-ghuduww is the plural of ghada (morning), like qunniy and qanah, and al-asal is the plural of asil, which is what lies between the afternoon prayer (al-asr) and sunset (al-maghrib). It has been said that it is the plural of uşul, the plural of asil, and its original form is a'sal with two hamzas, then the second was changed to an alif. It has also been said: al-ghuduww is a verbal noun, and this is supported by the reading of Ibn Mijlaz (al-iyṣal), with a kasra on the hamza, as the verbal noun of "aṣalna," meaning we entered the asil, as Ibn Jinni said. Furthermore, it has been said that the intended meaning is the literal prostration, for the unbelievers in a state of necessity single out prostration to Him alone, and this is the meaning of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and unwillingly﴾. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion﴾. It is not far-fetched that God, may He be exalted, creates in the shadows perceptions and minds by which they prostrate to God, exalted is His majesty, as He, may His majesty be great, created this for the mountains until they became occupied with glorification, and the traces of manifestation appeared in them, as Ibn al-Anbari said. It has also been permitted that by their prostration is meant what is observed in them of the form of prostration, following their owners. This, as has been said, is based on resorting to the general metaphor (umum al-majaz) in the prostration mentioned in the verse, by intending by it falling upon the ground, so that it includes the prostration of the shadows in this sense; or by supposing a verb that conveys that, removing the shadows, or a predicate for it in the same way; or by adopting that the intention of what was mentioned does not harm the literal sense, because it is incidental and accidental; or that combining the literal and the metaphorical is permissible. What is in some of these divisions of consideration is not hidden. It is reported from Qatada that prostration is an expression for the specific posture, and "willingly" has been used to refer to the prostration of the angels, peace be upon them, and the believers, and "unwillingly" to refer to the prostration of one whom the sword has brought into Islam, so he prostrates unwillingly, either out of hypocrisy, or the unwillingness is at the beginning of his state, so the attribute continues upon him even if his faith is sound afterward. It has also been said: the one who prostrates willingly is one for whom prostration is not burdensome, and the one who prostrates unwillingly is one for whom it is burdensome. It is reported from Ibn al-Anbari that the first is one whose period of Islam has been long, so he has grown accustomed to prostration, and the second is one who has just begun Islam until he becomes accustomed. In any case, it is a general expression by which a particular is intended, since whoever does not prostrate is excluded from it. It has also been said: it is general for all kinds of rational beings, and by "prostrates" is meant "must prostrate," but the obligation is expressed by the occurrence for emphasis.

Many have chosen, in interpreting the verse, what we mentioned first. In al-Bahr it is said: what appears is that the context of the verse is only that the whole world is subdued to God, may He be exalted, submitting to what He wills of it, restricted to His will, so that nothing comes from it except what He, may He be majestic and exalted, has decreed. Thus those you worship, whatever they are, are included under the subjection, unable to bring benefit or harm. This meaning is indicated by the association of the shadows in the prostration, and they are not persons of whom prostration in the specific posture can be conceived, but they fall under His will, may He be exalted, who turns them as He wills, since they are part of the world, and the world, its substances and accidents, falls under the subjugation of His will, may He be exalted, as He, may He be glorified, said: ﴿Have they not seen what God has created, of a thing whose shadow turns from the right and the left, prostrating to God?﴾. That the intended meaning of "shadows" is the persons, as some said, is weak, and weaker than it is what Ibn al-Anbari said. Their analogy to the mountains is nothing, because a mountain may have intellect on condition of supposing life, but the shadow is an accident, and it is not conceivable that life subsists in it. Rather, the meaning of its prostration is its inclining from side to side and the variation of its states, as He, may He be glorified and exalted, willed. In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim, after quoting what was said first, it says: you know well that restricting the prostration of the unbeliever in a state of necessity and hardship to God, may He be exalted, is not beneficial, for his prostration to an idol in a state of choice and ease undermines the restriction derived from the fronting of the prepositional phrase. Therefore the proper course is to take prostration as submission, and because the realization of the submission of all in origination and annihilation to Him, may He be exalted, is more fitting for the rebuke of taking allies apart from Him, may He be exalted and majestic, than the realization of their prostration to Him, may He be exalted. End of quotation. In those sayings there is a distance that is not hidden from the discerning critic.

[Page 128]

﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?"﴾ This is a verification (tahqiq), as some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said, because the Creator of both and the One who manages their affairs, together with everything in them, absolutely, is God Most High. It was also said: after He mentioned that what is contained (al-mazrufu) submits to His will, Glorified is He, He mentioned what serves as a proof for that, namely that He, Majestic and Exalted, is the Creator of this great container, which dazzles the minds, and its Manager. That is, say, O Muhammad, to these disbelievers who have taken protectors (awliya') besides Him: Who is the Lord of these great celestial and terrestrial bodies?

﴿Say: "God."﴾ The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was commanded to give the answer, to indicate that he is the one specified for answering. So he, may the prayers and peace be upon him, and his opponent are equal in establishing this. It is permissible that this is a prompting of the answer, so as to make clear to them what they are in, namely their opposition to what they know. It was also said that it is a report of their acknowledgment, but the context rejects this.

Makki said: they did not know the answer, so they asked it from him, peace be upon him, and so he was commanded to inform them of it. But this is far-fetched, because God Most High has already reported their knowledge in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "God."﴾ And in that case, how can it be said that they did not know the answer and asked for it? Indeed, al-Baghawi said: it is narrated that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, said that to the polytheists, they turned on him and said: "You answer." So God commanded him to give the answer. Even if this is accepted as sound, it does not indicate their ignorance, as is not hidden.

﴿Say﴾ as a rebuke to them and a reproach: ﴿Have you then taken﴾ for yourselves ﴿besides Him, protectors﴾ who are powerless and do not possess for themselves ﴿benefit﴾ they could seek, and they are more precious to them than you are, ﴿nor harm﴾ they could repel from themselves, let alone having power to bring benefit to others or repel harm from them.

[Page 128 continues]

The interrogative hamza (alif al-istifham) here is for denial (al-inkar). The meaning is: after you have known Him as the Lord of the heavens and the earth, you have taken besides Him protectors who are utterly incapable of benefiting you. Thus you have made what should have been the cause of monotheism, namely your knowledge, into the cause of polytheism. So the fa' is a conjunction of causation and sequence (li-l-tasabbub wa-l-tafri'), and the hamza entered upon it, because what is denied is the taking after knowledge, not the knowledge itself, nor both together. The protectors are described with what was mentioned, which strengthens the denial and emphasises it. It is understood, as some have said, that this is a second proof of their error and the corruption of their opinion in taking protectors in hope that they would benefit them. There is disagreement about the first proof. It was said: it is what is understood from His saying: ﴿Say: "Have you taken besides Him protectors?"﴾. It was also said: it is what is understood from His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And those who call upon others besides Him...﴾ etc. So reflect.

﴿Say﴾ depicting their feeble opinions in the form of the perceptible: ﴿Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ The blind is the polytheist who is ignorant of worship and of who deserves it, and the seeing is the monotheist who knows this. This is the view of Mujahid, and in this speech there is an explicit metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya). Likewise, according to what has been said, that the first refers to one ignorant of this kind of proof and the second to one who knows it. It was also said that the speech is by way of simile (tashbih), and the meaning is: the believer and the disbeliever are not equal, just as the blind and the seeing are not equal. So there is no metaphor. Some have explained the first as the heedless deity and the second as the deity knowing everything, but this is far-fetched.

﴿Or are the darknesses﴾, which are an expression for disbelief and misguidance, ﴿equal to the light﴾, which is an expression for faith and monotheism? This was also narrated from Mujahid. The word "darknesses" is in the plural because of the multiplicity of kinds of disbelief, such as the disbelief of the Christians, the disbelief of the Magians, and the disbelief of others. That all disbelief is one religion (millah wahidah) is a separate matter.

And "am" (or, rather), as in al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit), is disjunctive (munqati'a) and is to be estimated as "bal" (rather). The hamza is, according to the preferred view, [also present], and the estimate is: "Rather, are [they] equal?" And "hal" (is/are), although it substitutes for the hamza in many places, has also been combined with it, as in the verse:

*"Did they see us in the valley of al-Quff, the one with hillocks?"*

And when it is combined with it with explicit mention, that combination is more appropriate with "am", which implicitly contains it. After this "am" it is permissible to bring it (the hamza), because of its resemblance to the nominal interrogative particles, which in the matter of non-originality in interrogation are like it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or who controls hearing and sight?﴾. And it is permissible not to bring it, because "am" implicitly contains interrogation. Both cases have come in His saying:

*"Is what you knew and what you entrusted hidden? Or is her camel-halter cut off today, as she has departed from you?"*

*"Or is it that an old man wept, not having relieved his tears, after the beloved ones, on the day of parting, one who is thanked?"*

And Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read ﴿"Or does [it] equal"﴾ with the yā' (third person masculine, i.e., "yastawi" rather than "tastawi").

Then God, Exalted is He, emphasised what the preceding speech required, namely the refutation of the polytheists. So He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿Or have they set up for God partners﴾, that is, rather, have they set up ﴿for God﴾, Majestic and Exalted, ﴿partners who created as He creates﴾, Glorified and Exalted is He? The hamza is for denying occurrence, and what is denied is not the setting up, since that occurs from them; rather, what is denied is creating as His creating. The meaning is: they have not set up for God, Exalted is He, partners who created as He creates. ﴿So creation became confused to them﴾ because of that, and they said: "These have created as God's creation is created, and so they deserve worship as He, Glorified is He, deserves it." Thus this would be the source of their error. Rather, they have only set up for Him partners who are powerless and cannot do what creation can do, let alone what the Creator can do. The purpose of the denial and negation [is] the restriction and the restricted (al-qayd wa-l-muqayyad), as several verifiers have stated explicitly.

In al-Intisaf (by Ibn al-Munayyir) it is said that ﴿who created as He creates﴾ in the context of denial was brought for mockery (tahakkum), for a being other than God Most High does not create anything equal or inferior. And had it not been for this, the denial would have sufficed, because the gods they took do not create.

[Page 129]

al-Tibi objected to this, saying: asserting mockery is forced, for it is mentioning a thing while intending its opposite in order to belittle the addressee, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾. And here, ﴿as He creates﴾ was brought for emphasis in establishing the powerlessness of their gods, by way of gradual progression and giving rein. For when God first denied their taking partners besides Him, and described them as not possessing for themselves any benefit or harm, then how could they possess that for others? Then, secondly, by way of gradation, He denied them the attribute of creating as well. That is: suppose those partners were able to benefit themselves and benefit their worshippers, would they then be able to create anything? And suppose they were able to create some things, would they be able to do what the Creator does, namely create the heavens and the earth? End quote. But the truth is that the verse rebukes them and mocks them, for whoever does not possess for himself anything of benefit or harm is further still from giving that to them. How could it be imagined that he is a creator, and how could it be confused for one of sound mind, so that he is alerted to its negation? This degree is sufficient for the purpose, so understand.

﴿Say﴾, establishing the truth and guiding them: ﴿God is the Creator of everything﴾, of substances and accidents. This necessarily entails that there is no creator besides Him, so that there is no sharing (tawarud), and this is the intended meaning, to indicate what is meant, namely the negation of the entitlement of anyone other than God Most High to worship and divinity. That is: there is no creator besides Him, and so no one shares with Him in that entitlement.

By the generality of this verse, the People of the Sunnah have argued that the actions of the servants are created by Him, Exalted is He. The Mu'tazilah claim that it is restricted to other than their actions. Some people also argue for what the People of the Truth hold by the first verse, and it is, as you see, [weak]. ﴿And He is the One﴾, who is singular in divinity and alone in lordship, ﴿the Subduer﴾ (al-Qahhar), (16) who prevails over everything other than Him. Among all that are their gods. So how can the subdued be a partner to Him, Exalted is He? This, as has been said, is like a conclusion to what precedes it, and it may be either part of the speech that is said, or a new independent sentence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 17 (part 1 of 2):

﴿He sent down from the sky﴾ i.e., from its direction, according to what is observed. It is also said: from the sky itself, and there is no figurative usage in the speech. This view has been supported by reports, the soundness of which God Most High knows best. It is also said: He sent down from it, i.e., from the sky itself, ﴿water﴾, i.e., abundant water, or a kind of it, which is rain water, on the basis that its origins are from it. That is due to the influence of the celestial bodies on the rising of vapour, so "from" (min) is used figuratively.

﴿So the valleys flowed﴾ with it ﴿valleys﴾, meaning those which hold it in their places, not all valleys, since rains do not cover all regions. It is the plural of wadi (wād).

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: It is not known that fā'il is pluralized as af'ila, and it seems that this is due to the interchange of fā'il and fa'īl for the same thing, such as ʿālim and ʿalīm, shāhid and shahīd, nāṣir and naṣīr. Then, the pattern fā'il is pluralized as af'āl, like ṣāḥib and aṣḥāb, ṭā'ir and aṭyār, and the pattern fa'īl is pluralized as af'ila, like jarīb and ajriba. Then, since the aforementioned correspondence arose between fā'il and fa'īl, it is inevitable that fā'il takes the plural of fa'īl, so one says wādin and awdiya, and fa'īl takes the plural of fā'il, as in yatīm and aytām, and sharīf and ashrāf. End. The like of this is nādin and andiya, and nājin and anjiya. It has been said: there is no fourth for these. In the Sharh al-Tashil there is something that contradicts this.

The wadi is the place where water flows abundantly, and by it the gap between two mountains is named. It is also applied to the flowing water in it, and it is an active participle from wada, meaning "to flow." If the first meaning is intended, the attribution is figurative, or the speech is on the assumption of an elided genitive, as al-Imam said, i.e., the waters of valleys. If the second meaning is intended, which is a figurative meaning by way of applying the name of the place to what is in it, then the attribution is literal. The choice of illustrating with valleys rather than the perpetually flowing rivers is due to the clear resemblance between their state and what is illustrated by them, as we will indicate, God willing.

﴿according to their measure﴾ i.e., according to their quantity which God Most High determined and which His wisdom, glory be to Him, required for the benefit of people; or according to their measure which varies in scarcity and abundance according to the variation of their receptacles in smallness and largeness, not by their being filled and covering them, but merely by their scarcity in smallness, which entails the scarcity of water sources, and their abundance in largeness, which calls for many sources, for the sources of a flood flowing in a small valley are fewer than the sources of a flood flowing in a large valley. This is when by the valleys is meant what flows in them. As for if by them is meant the literal sense, then the meaning is: their waters flowed according to the measure of those valleys, in the manner you have just understood. Or by its pronoun is meant its waters, by way of istikhdam, and by its measure is meant what was mentioned first of the two meanings. This was said by Shaykh al-Islam. The prepositional phrase, as reported from al-Hawfi, is connected to "flowed." Abu al-Baqa' said: it is in the position of an adjective to "valleys." It is also permissible that it be connected to "sent down." Zayd ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli and Abu 'Amr in one narration read "biqadrihā" with a sukun on the dal, and this is a dialect for that.

﴿Then the flood carried﴾ i.e., bore. The form ifta'ala comes with the meaning of the base form, like iqtadara and qadara. ﴿the flood﴾, i.e., the water flowing in those valleys. The definite article is because it is known and mentioned by His words: ﴿valleys﴾. It is not pluralized because, as al-Raghib said, it is originally a verbal noun. In al-Bahr it is said that it was made definite because it means what is understood from the verb, and what contains the verb from the verbal noun, even if indefinite, when it recurs explicitly becomes definite, as it would have been if it had been stated indefinitely. Likewise it is pronominalized when it refers back to what the verb indicates from the verbal noun, as in "whoever lies, it is worse for him," i.e., the lying. Had it come here as a pronoun, it would have been permissible, referring back to the verbal noun understood from "flowed." End.

It was objected to this: how can it be permissible to mean by it what is understood from the verb, which is an event, while the mentioned definite is an entity, as you know? It was answered that it is by way of istikhdam. It was rejected: istikhdam is that a word is mentioned in one meaning and a pronoun referring to it is used with another meaning, whether literal or figurative, and this is not so, because the first is a verbal noun, i.e., an event within the verb, while this is a manifest entity noun which is characterized by that; how then can istikhdam be conceived in it?
