Indeed, what they mentioned is a general rule, not restricted to what was mentioned, for the like of the pronoun is the demonstrative, and likewise the explicit noun. End.

Consider whether it is permissible to intend by "the flood" the verbal meaning, so that there is no need for the istikhdam discussion, or not. And on the permissibility, the meaning would be: the water sent down from the sky carried, by means of the flood, ﴿foam﴾. It is the scum that the valley casts up when its water seethes and its waves surge, according to what Abu al-Hajjaj al-A'lam said, and it is the meaning of Ibn 'Isa's words: it is the filth of boiling and its dross. The poet said:

"And what is the Euphrates when its billows surge, its shallows throw up foam onto the two banks."

﴿rising﴾, i.e., high, swelling above the water. The foam was described with this. It is said: as an explanation of what is intended by the carrying which is carried, since the carried is not floating like heavy trees. It was not averted by saying "the flood carried foam above it" in order to indicate that that height is required by the nature of foam and not from the side of what is carried, to establish the resemblance between it and what was illustrated by it, the hidden thing whose nature is to appear at first sight without intrusion into the truth. ﴿And of what they kindle﴾ is the beginning of a sentence, as reported from Mujahid, coordinated with the first sentence for striking another parable, i.e., and from that which they kindle fire upon. The plural pronoun refers to people, omitted without prior mention because it is evident. Most of the Seven, and Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj and Shayba read "tūqidūna" with the taa of address. The prepositional phrase is connected to what is before it, and likewise His words ﴿in the fire﴾, according to Abu al-Baqa' and al-Hawfi. Abu 'Ali said: one may kindle upon a thing without it being in the fire, like His words: ﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, upon the clay﴾, for the clay upon which he was commanded to kindle is not in the fire, but its flame reaches it. Makki and others said: "in the fire" is connected to an elided word that is in the position of a circumstantial to the relative pronoun, i.e., existing or established in it. They denied its connection to "tūqidūna," saying: because one does not kindle upon a thing except that it is in the fire, and connecting it to that would entail restricting one circumstance by another. Abu Hayyan said: if we say that one does not kindle upon a thing except that it is in the fire, it would also be permissible to connect it for emphasis, as they said in His words: ﴿nor a bird flying on its wings﴾. It was said: the addition of that is to indicate exaggeration in the effort of melting and the emergence of foam. The relative refers to things like gold, silver, iron, copper, and lead. In not naming them by their names, and turning to describe them by kindling upon them, which indicates striking them with hammers, since that is for its sake, and by their being like low wood, He belittled them to show His greatness, glory be to Him, as it has been said. This does not contradict that this is a parable for the truth, because the station of greatness requires belittling them, together with an indication that they are desired by His words: ﴿seeking an ornament or a commodity﴾. Thus each of the two stations received its due. So what was said: that taking it as belittling is not suited to the context, because the intent is to illustrate the truth by them and disparaging them is not suited to it, is void. So reflect.

﴿seeking﴾ is in the accusative, and it is the apparent reading as an object. Al-Hawfi said it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial, i.e., seeking and desiring to make an ornament, which is what one adorns and beautifies oneself with, like ornaments made of gold and silver, and to make a commodity, which is what one enjoys of vessels and tools made of iron, lead, and other metals. ﴿scum﴾ is dross. ﴿like it﴾, i.e., like what was mentioned of the foam of the water in being high above it. ﴿Foam﴾ is raised as the subject, its predicate being "of what you kindle," and "of" is for the beginning of the source, indicating merely that it is a subject and originates from it. Abu Hayyan preferred that it is partitive, because that foam is part of what is kindled upon from those minerals. Some verifiers did not accept this, because according to him it disturbs the parable. The reason it did not address the removal of that from the earth, as it addressed the heading of sending water down from the sky, is that this heading has no bearing on the parable, as you will know, God willing, just as the previous heading has a bearing on it. Rather, it disturbs that.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that wondrous striking containing delicate subtleties: ﴿God strikes the truth and the falsehood﴾, i.e., like the truth and like the falsehood. The omission is to indicate complete resemblance between the illustrated and that by which it is illustrated, as if the parable struck were the very truth and falsehood. ﴿As for the foam﴾ of each of the flood and what they kindle upon, it is singular and not dual, though two foams preceded, because they share the general notion of foam, so they are one by the common measure. ﴿goes away as scum﴾, cast out. It is said: the water cast out the foam when it threw it away. It is also said: ajfa with the same meaning. Ibn al-Anbari said: jufa'an means scattered, from "jafa'at al-rih al-ghayma" when the wind cut and scattered the clouds, and "jafa'tu al-rajul" I threw him down. It is also said: "jafa al-wadi" and "ajfa" when it dried up. It was read "jufalan" with lam instead of hamza, and it means scattered too, derived from "jafalat al-rih al-ghayma," like "jafa'at." This reading is attributed to Ru'ba. Ibn Abi Hatim said: it is not read with his reading, because he used to eat mice, meaning that he was a rude Bedouin. And from him: the readings of Bedouins are not to be taken into account in the Qur'an. The accusative is as a circumstantial.

﴿As for what benefits people﴾, i.e., of pure water free from foam and of pure metallic essence free from dross, ﴿remains﴾, stays, ﴿in the earth﴾. As for the water, part of it remains in its pools, and part of it runs through the veins of the earth to springs and the like. As for the metallic essence, some of it is fashioned into various kinds of ornaments, and some of it is made into kinds of tools and implements, and by each of these various uses are gained for a long period. So "remaining in the earth" is meant more generally, both as remaining in itself and as remaining in the hands of those who move about in it. The change in the order of the wrapping, which occurs in the conclusion, to match the order in the parable, is said to be for the sake of harmony between the two states of going away and remaining, and their mention, since what is considered is only the remaining of what remains after the going away of what goes, not before it. It is also said: the reason for placing foam before what benefits is that foam is what is seen first and foremost, while the other remains and is later in existence because of its persistence. The verse is of the type of comprehensive and divided expression, as is not hidden.

The summary of the discussion of the two verses is that God Most High has illustrated the Truth, which is the Mighty Qur'an, according to the majority, in its outpouring from the sacred presence upon hearts empty of it, varying in readiness, and in its flowing over them through attention and preservation, and upon the tongues through study and recitation, while it sustains their spiritual life and the noble qualities and pleasing deeds that follow it, by the water sent down from the sky, flowing in dry valleys whose custom was not to flow, in a measure determined by the wisdom for the revival of the earth and what is upon it, remaining in them as the benefit of people revolves around it. And in its being an ornament with which souls are adorned and reach eternal joy, and a commodity enjoyed in this life and the hereafter, through gold, silver, and the other metals from which various kinds of tools and implements are made, which remain benefited from for a long period. And it has illustrated the falsehood with which the disbelievers were tested, because of the shortcoming of their vision, by what appears in these two without any intrusion of it into them, and without any disturbance to their purity, from the foam rising above them, which quickly vanishes.

Sahih (authentic) from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The likeness of the guidance and knowledge with which Allah the Exalted has sent me is like rain that fell upon a land. A part of it was good ground that absorbed the water and produced abundant grass and herbage. Another part of it was hard ground (ajadib) that held water, so Allah benefited people through it: they drank from it, gave others to drink, and grazed their animals. And the rain fell upon another part of it, which was flat barren plains (qi'an) that hold no water and produce no grass. That is the likeness of one who gains understanding (faqiha) of the religion of Allah the Exalted and is benefited by what Allah the Exalted has sent me with, so he learns and teaches. And the likeness of one who does not lift his head toward it and does not accept the guidance of Allah the Exalted with which I have been sent."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The beginning of the verse is an admonition about the power of Allah the Exalted and the establishment of proof against the disbelievers. When he finished with that, he made it an example of truth and falsehood, faith and disbelief, and certainty in the Shari'ah (sharia, the revealed law) and doubt concerning it. It seems that by coordinating faith and what follows it, he intended to explain what is meant by truth and falsehood. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he took the foam (zabad) as a sign of doubt and its pure part as a sign of certainty.

﴿Thus﴾, that is, like that wondrous manner, ﴿Allah strikes the parables﴾. (17)

In every matter, this shows the perfection of Allah's gentleness and care in guidance. It also magnifies the status of this illustration and emphasizes His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Allah strikes truth and falsehood﴾, either because this is built upon the first illustration, or by making the demonstrative refer to both of them together.

After Allah, exalted is He, had made clear the condition of each of the truth and falsehood, in both their present state and their outcome, with the most complete clarity, He began to explain the condition of the people of each of them in their outcome, to complete the call through both encouragement and warning. So He, glorified is He, said: ﴿For those who respond to their Lord﴾, since He called them to the truth through the various methods of da'wah (calling to the faith), among which is the striking of parables (ḍarb al-amthāl). This is because it has a powerful effect in winning over souls, by depicting the intelligible in the form of the sensible.

[Page 133]

The prepositional phrase (al-jār wa'l-majrūr) is a predicate placed before its subject (khabar muqaddam). His, glorified is He, saying ﴿al-ḥusnā﴾ means: the reward that is good (al-mathūba al-ḥusnā), which is Paradise, as Qatādah and others said. From Mujāhid: "the good life" (al-ḥayāt al-ḥusnā), meaning the pure life that is not mixed with any turbidity at all. From Ibn 'Abbās: the intended meaning is the reward of "the good word", which is lā ilāha illā Allāh. In this there is a remoteness that is not hidden. (It is) a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). ﴿And those who did not respond to Him﴾, glorified is He, and opposed the manifest truth, ﴿even if they had whatever is on the earth﴾ of kinds of wealth, ﴿all of it﴾, in such a way that no part of it was missing in any of its regions, or gathered together and not dispersed according to the times, ﴿and the like of it with it, they would ransom themselves thereby﴾, meaning: with what has been mentioned of what is on the earth and the like of it along with it, all of it, in order to free themselves from what they are in. In this there is a terrifying depiction of what will befall them that no explanation can encompass. The relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) is the subject, and the conditional sentence is its predicate. It is said that this conditional sentence stands in the place of "the evil" (al-sū'ā), which is the counterpart of "the good" (al-ḥusnā) that occurs in the first clause. So it is as if it were said: "And for those who did not respond to Him is the evil." It has been objected that although the conditional sentence indicates the wretchedness of their state, it is far from standing in the place of the word al-sū'ā accompanied by the prepositional lām that enters upon the relative pronoun or its pronoun, and upon this the achievement of the aim depends. So what should be relied upon is that what occurs in that counterpart is "the evil of the reckoning", in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿For them is the evil of the reckoning﴾. Since the demonstrative pronoun that occurs as subject in this sentence refers to the relative pronoun that occurs as subject in the preceding sentence, its predicate, namely the adverbial sentence (al-jumla al-ẓarfiyya), is in reality a predicate concerning the relative pronoun, and an explanation of the vagueness of the content of the conditional sentence that occurred earlier as its predicate. For this reason the conjunction was omitted. So it is as if it were said: "And those who did not respond to Him, for them is the evil of the reckoning." This is equivalent to saying: "And for those who did not respond to Him is the evil of the reckoning," with added emphasis. Thus the excellence of the counterpart is complete in the most eloquent and most emphatic manner.

It has been offered as an excuse that it is possible the intended meaning is that ﴿if they had whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾ up to the end of the verse stands in the place of that, on the basis that observing the excellence of the counterpart to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿For those who responded to their Lord is the good﴾ requires that it be said: "And for those who did not respond to Him is the evil," and nothing more would be added to that. But instead, His, glorified is He, saying ﴿if they had...﴾ etc. was brought in place of what was mentioned. Perhaps in the words of al-Ṭībī there is something that can be taken as support for this. And to the consideration of "the evil" as the counterpart went also the author of al-Kashf, who said: His, exalted is He, saying ﴿if they had﴾ is in counterpart to "the good" in place of "the evil", with added depiction and regret. The general statement was preferred in the first (clause) to indicate that the reward of those who respond does not fall under the description. So reflect. The meaning of "the evil of the reckoning" is: the bad reckoning, according to what was transmitted from Ibrāhīm al-Nakha'ī and al-Ḥasan, that they will be reckoned for all their sins, and none of them will be forgiven for them, and this is what is meant by scrupulous reckoning (al-munāqasha). From Ibn 'Abbās: it is that they will be reckoned, so their good deeds will not be accepted and their bad deeds will not be forgiven. ﴿And their refuge﴾, meaning their place of return, ﴿is Hell﴾. This is an explanation of the outcome of what preceded, and in it there is a kind of support for interpreting "the good" as Paradise. ﴿And wretched is the resting place﴾. (18). Meaning: the resting place. The thing to which the dispraise applies is omitted, meaning: "their resting place" or "Hell."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: The lām in His saying ﴿For those who responded﴾ is connected to ﴿Allah strikes the parables﴾. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿al-ḥusnā﴾ is an attribute of the verbal noun (ṣifa li'l-maṣdar), meaning: they responded with a good response (al-istijāba al-ḥusnā). His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿and those who did not respond﴾ is conjoined to the first relative pronoun. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿if they had...﴾ etc. is a resumed sentence (kalām mustaʾnaf), brought to explain what was prepared for those who did not respond, of punishment. The meaning is: Thus Allah, exalted is He, strikes the parables for the believers who respond and for the disbelievers who oppose, i.e., these two are the two parables of the two groups. End of quotation. Abū Ḥayyān said: The first interpretation is preferable, because in it the striking of parables is not restricted to such as these two, and Allah has struck many parables in these two and in other than them. And because in it is mention of the reward of those who respond, unlike this. And because the supposition of "a good response" implies a restriction of the response, while its counterpart is not the negation of response absolutely but rather the negation of the good response, whereas Allah has negated response absolutely. And because in that case ﴿if they had...﴾ etc. becomes a detached statement, or like a detached one, since the meaning becomes: Thus Allah strikes the parables for the believers and the disbelievers, if they had... etc. And if there were a particle connecting "if" to what precedes it, the detachment would disappear. Also, it gives the impression of a shared pronoun, although restricting that to the disbelievers is known.

It was objected that there is no dispute about the preferability of the first interpretation, but that what was mentioned is a basis for it is open to discussion, since there is no requirement in the second interpretation to restrict the parables in general to such as these two. Do you not see His saying, "Thus (kadhālika)"? Furthermore, in it there is an indication of the reward of those who respond as well; do you not see the restriction derived from the fronting of the adverbial phrase? Also, His saying, exalted is He, ﴿al-ḥusnā﴾ is an explanatory attribute (ṣifa kāshifa) with no implied restriction, since response to Allah, exalted is He, is only ever good. How can His saying, glorified is He, ﴿if they had...﴾ etc. be detached when they have said that it is an independent statement to explain the condition of those who respond? They mean that it is an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), an answer to the question about the outcome of their condition. Then how can a shared reference be imagined when the restriction of it to the disbelievers is known? End of quotation.

Some of the verifiers said: What has been mentioned is valid according to first consideration and initial glance. But if it is looked at with an eye of fairness, after conceding that that (the first interpretation) is preferable and stronger, it becomes known that what Abū Ḥayyān said applies. For His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Thus﴾ requires that this is His, exalted is His, habit and custom in striking parables, and so it requires that what the Qur'anic custom has followed is restricted to these people. That is not the case. What the objector mentioned, even if it were conceded, is contrary to the apparent meaning. As for his saying that those who respond are known from what was mentioned, there is a difference between knowledge implicitly and knowledge explicitly. As for whether the attribute is emphatic or has no implied restriction, that too is contrary to the default. That the sentence is not connected to what precedes it is clear, and the question about the condition of one of the two groups, together with mention of both after conveying the last interpretation and taking the parables in it to refer to the earlier parables, is also clear. But you know well that the heading of response and its absence has no relevance to what the matter of the parable revolves around. The commonly used usage is that the lām enters upon the one whom the parable is intended to remind. Yes, it may also be used in this sense, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah has struck a parable for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh﴾, and its like. Furthermore, some of the parables struck, especially the last parable attached to the discourse, is not the parable of the two groups, but rather a parable of truth and falsehood. And there is no room for making the two groups also struck for, by putting it in the position of saying: "Thus Allah strikes the parables for people," since in that case there would be no basis for classifying them into those who respond and those who do not respond. This is supported by what is in al-Kashf, where it says: Making ﴿for those who responded﴾ part of the parables, rather than connected to "strikes", is forced, because they are the parables of truth and falsehood primarily, and connecting it to "strikes" is even more remote, since parables are only struck for one who understands.

Moreover, that the intended meaning of "the parables" is the earlier parables is based on the premise that what preceded was parables, whereas the well-known view is that there are two parables. Yes, Ibn Jarīr and others transmitted from Qatādah that he said about the verse: "These are three parables that Allah struck in one parable." After all of this, there is no doubt that the first interpretation is free of contention and debate, and that it is what the sublime composition requires, since the perfection of the closing rhyme (fāṣila) is that it be like its name. For this reason the verse of Imru' al-Qays has declined from the saying of al-Mutanabbī:

"O night, so long! Will you not part with a dawn? And the morning is not better than you."

[compared with]

"If it is praise, then the prelude of love comes first; is every eloquent person who composes poetry a lovesick one?"

This is what the early generation (al-salaf) understood from the verse. For this reason most of the shaykhs stopped at "the parables" and began with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for those who responded﴾. The author of al-Murshid said: It is a complete pause (waqf tāmm), and pausing at ﴿al-ḥusnā﴾ is good, and likewise at ﴿they would ransom themselves thereby﴾. It is strange that al-Zamakhsharī chose the opposite of this despite its clarity. And Allah knows best.

* * *

(From the Gate of Allusion, ishāra)

﴿Alif, Lām, Mīm, Rā'﴾: meaning the Essential Unity (al-dhāt al-aḥadiyya), its name is the All-Knowing (al-'Alīm), its greatest name, and its manifestation is the Mercy. ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾: the signs (ʿalāmāt) of the Book, the comprehensive Book, which is the Absolute Existence. ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾: that is, without visible pillars, but with invisible pillars. Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, made their pillar the Perfect Human Being. It has also been said: the disembodied soul which moves them through the soul that is conformed (al-nafs al-munṭabiqa), which is a corporeal power pervading all parts of the sphere, not particular to one part over another, due to its simplicity; and it is like the imagination within us. There is much to say about this. It has also been said: He raised the heavens of the spirits without a material supporting them, but rather disembodied and self-subsisting. ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ by influence and ordering. It has been said: the Throne of the heart by manifestation. ﴿And He subjected the sun﴾: the sun of the spirit, by perceiving universal knowledge and aspiring to lofty lights. ﴿And the moon﴾: the moon of the heart, by perceiving what is in both worlds, and drawing support from above and below, then receiving the manifestations of the attributes. ﴿Each runs for a term specified﴾, which is its perfection according to its natural disposition. ﴿He arranges the affair﴾ at the beginning, by preparing readiness and arranging the principles. ﴿He details the signs﴾ at the end, by arranging the perfections and stations. ﴿So that you may, in meeting your Lord﴾ at the witnessing of the signs of the manifestations, ﴿be certain﴾ with the certainty of certainty ('ayn al-yaqīn).

[p. 136]

Ibn ʿAtaʾ said: ﴿He arranges the affair﴾ by the preordained decree, ﴿and details the signs﴾ by the rulings of the outward law, ﴿that you may be certain﴾ that God, Exalted is He, who causes those states to pass, is the One to whom you must necessarily return, glory be to Him. ﴿And it is He who spread out the earth﴾, that is, the earth of the hearts of His friends (awliyaʾ), by spreading the lights of love. ﴿And placed therein firm mountains﴾ of gnosis (maʿrifa), so that they would not be shaken by the overwhelming surge of ecstatic states (mawajid). ﴿And placed therein﴾ rivers (anhaaran) of the sciences of realities (ʿulum al-haqaʾiq). ﴿And of all the fruits He placed therein two kinds, two﴾, and these are the fruits of the trees of the varied wisdoms. ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾: the manifestation of majesty (tajalli al-jalal) and the manifestation of beauty (tajalli al-jamal). ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ upon the signs of God, Exalted is He.

Abu ʿUthman said: reflection (fikr) is the relieving of the heart from the whisperings of managing and planning. It was also said: it is the clearing of the heart so that it receives the arriving benefits. It was also said: the allusion in this is to the spreading of the earth of the body, the placing in it of the firm mountains of the bones, the rivers of the veins, and the fruits of the characters: generosity and miserliness, depravity and chastity, cowardice and courage, injustice and justice, and the like; and blackness and whiteness, heat and cold, smoothness and roughness, and the like; and the covering of the night of the darkness of corporeal things over the day of spiritual things. In that are signs for a people who reflect upon the craft of God, Exalted is He, and the correspondence of His two worlds, the minor and the major.

﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts﴾: the hearts of the lovers are adjacent to the hearts of the longing ones, and these are to the hearts of the passionate lovers (ʿashiqin), these are to the hearts of the utterly bewildered (walihin), these are to the hearts of the wandering ones (hai­min), these are to the hearts of the gnostics (ʿarifin), and these are to the hearts of the monotheists (muwahhidin). It was also said: in the earth of the hearts there are neighbouring tracts: the tracts of the souls (nufus), the tracts of the spirits (arwah), the tracts of the secrets (asrar), and the tracts of the intellects (ʿuqul). The first produces the thorns of desires, the second the blossoms of gnosis, the third the plants of the unveiling lights, and the fourth the trees of the light of knowledge. ﴿And in it are gardens of grapes﴾, that is, the grapes of passionate love (ʿishq). ﴿And crops﴾, that is, the crops of subtle gnosis. ﴿And palms﴾, that is, the palms of faith. ﴿Some in pairs﴾ in the station of distinction (farq), ﴿and some single﴾ in the station of union (jamʿ). It was also said: the paired ones are faith accompanied by witnessing (shuhud), and the single ones are faith without it. ﴿Watered with one water﴾, which is the manifestation required by absolute generosity (al-jud al-mutlaq). ﴿And We favour some of them over others in fruit﴾: in the spiritual taste. It was also said: it is also indicated that in the earth of the body there are neighbouring tracts of bone, flesh, fat and sinew, and gardens of trees of the natural, animal and human powers; from the grapes of the appetitive powers, from which the desire of the soul is pressed; and of the intellectual powers, from which the wine of love and passion is pressed; and crops of the human powers; and palms of all the outward and inward senses, some in pairs like the two eyes and the two ears, and some single like the tongue and the instrument of thought and imagination. ﴿Watered with one water﴾, which is the water of life. ﴿And We favour some over others in the fruit of perceptions﴾ and faculties, as the objects perceived by the intellect are favoured over those of the senses, and sight over touch, and the faculty of wisdom over chastity, and so on.

﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying﴾, after the signs have appeared: ﴿"When we have become dust, shall we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ And they did not know that the One who is capable of that is capable of bringing the dead to life.

It was also said: the source of the amazement is that they denied the new creation on the Day of Resurrection, although a human being is in a new creation every hour, and indeed the whole world is renewed at every instant through the change of forms, states, conditions and shapes. The Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, held that the world is in a new creation at every instant. For him, substance and accident do not endure for two moments, just as, according to al-Ashʿari, accident does not. For the Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, this is based on the premise that all substances and accidents are His affairs, exalted is He far above what the wrongdoers say. He, glory be to Him, is each day, that is each moment, in a state. Most people object to al-Ashʿari's statement about the renewal of accidents. The Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, added sections to the chessboard, and what he says cannot easily be grasped by proof; rather it depends upon unveiling (kashf) and witnessing. Many people have been deceived by the apparent sense of his words and believed them without reflection; they have gone astray and led others astray.

﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord﴾, for they did not recognize His greatness, glory be to Him. ﴿And those, the shackles are upon their necks﴾, so that they cannot lift their downcast heads to look at the signs. ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾, because of the enormity of what they committed.

﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good﴾, in keeping with their readiness for evil. ﴿And there have already passed before them examples (mathulat)﴾, the punishments of those like them. ﴿And indeed your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing﴾ against themselves by acquiring the matters that veil them from the light, which have not yet taken root in them. ﴿And indeed your Lord is severe in punishment﴾ for those in whom these matters have taken root.

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why has a sign not been sent down to him?"﴾, because their insight is blind to witnessing the signs that testify to prophethood. ﴿You are only a warner﴾: your duty is only to warn them, not to guide them. ﴿And for every people there is a guide﴾. It is God, Exalted is He. It was also said: for every group there is a shaykh who makes known to them the path of the truth.

﴿God knows what every female bears﴾, so He knows what the female of the soul bears of the offspring of perfection, that is, what is in the potential of every readiness (istiʿdad). ﴿And what the wombs diminish﴾, that is, the wombs of readiness diminish through the abandoning of the soul and its desire. ﴿And what they increase﴾ through purification and the blessing of companionship. ﴿And everything with Him is in a measure﴾ of perfections, a specific measure according to receptivity. ﴿Equal is whoever among you conceals speech﴾ in the place of his readiness, ﴿and whoever speaks it aloud﴾ by bringing it out into action, ﴿and whoever hides by night﴾, in the darkness of his self-wronging, ﴿and goes about by day﴾, by coming out from the station of the soul and proceeding into the daylight of the spirit. ﴿For him are successive guardians before him and behind him, who guard him by the command of God﴾. This is an allusion to the prior mercies that protect him from the snatching flashes of wrath, or to the angelic supports that protect him from the jinn of the imaginative, the illusory, the predatory and the bestial powers, and from their destruction of him.

﴿Indeed God does not change what is with a people﴾ of outward or inward blessings, ﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾ of readiness and the power of acceptance.

Al-Nasrabadi said: this ruling is general, but the scrutiny of the elite is more severe than the scrutiny of the common people. It is reported from one of the early pious (salaf) that he said: "A mouse tore my shoe, and I know that this is only because of a sin I have committed; otherwise He would not have given it power over me." And he quoted the line of the poet:

"Had I been of Mazin, the sons of Laqita of Dhuhl ibn Shayban would not have plundered my camels."

﴿And when God intends evil for a people, there is no turning it back, and they have no protector besides Him﴾, since all are under His dominion, glory be to Him. Al-Qasim said: when God, Exalted is He, intends the destruction of a people, He makes their destinations appear good in their eyes, until they walk towards them with their own plans and feet. And how well one has said, for God is the Exalted:

"If there is no help from God for the youth, the first thing his striving will inflict upon him is harm."

[p. 137]

﴿He it is who shows you the lightning﴾, that is, the lightning of the flashes of holy lights, ﴿as a fear﴾, fearing its swift passing or its slow return, ﴿and as a hope﴾, hoping for its endurance or its quick return. ﴿And He produces the heavy clouds﴾ with the water of knowledge and gnosis. It was also said: He shows the lovers the lightning of unveiling, and He produces for the gnostics the heavy clouds of majesty with the water of awe, so that He rains upon them what gives them life, a life unlike any other life. They recited for al-Shibli:

"A cloud has shaded us from you one day; it lit for us a lightning, but its drizzle was slow.
So its cloud does not clear, and the hopeful despairs; nor does its rain come, so that its thirsty ones are quenched."

It is also reported from some that the lightning is an allusion to the lightning-like manifestations that occur to the people of states (ahl al-ahwal). The most famous manifestation, in likening it to lightning, is the essential manifestation (tajalli al-dhati). They recited:

"What you bestowed upon us of our union was nothing but a lamp that flashed and then went out."

The Imam al-Rabbani, may his secret be sanctified, mentioned in the Maktubat that the essential manifestation is permanent for the perfected among the people of the Naqshbandi path, not flashing like lightning. He spoke at length on this, differing from the great Sufi masters such as Shaykh Muhyi al-Din, may his secret be sanctified, and others. The truth is that what he mentioned of the essential manifestation is not what they described as lightning-like, as will be clear to anyone who examines his words and theirs.

﴿And the thunder glorifies﴾, that is, the thunder of the force of the majestic manifestations, ﴿praising Him﴾, exalting God, Exalted is He, above what the intellect may imagine, ﴿with His praise﴾ and affirming what befits Him, mighty is His affair. ﴿And the angels﴾ glorify, the spiritual powers, ﴿out of awe of Him﴾, out of the awe of His majesty, majestic is His majesty. ﴿And He sends the thunderbolts﴾, which are the thunderbolts of the divine veils (subuhat ilahiyya) at the manifestation of true severity that contains universal gentleness, ﴿and strikes with them whom He wills﴾, so that He burns him away from the remnant of his self. In a report: God, Exalted is He, has seventy thousand veils of light and darkness; if He were to uncover them, the veils of the splendour of His face would burn away whatever of His creation His sight reaches. Ibn al-Zanjani said: the thunder is the swooning of the angels, the lightning is the sighs of their hearts, and the rain is their weeping. Al-Zamakhshari regarded this as one of the innovations of the Sufis. It seems to you that you would say: most of what is mentioned under the heading of allusion (ishara) in this book is of this kind. The answer is that we claim only allusion; as for whether this is the meaning of the words or what God intends, God forbid that such a thought should pass through my mind. Believing it is manifest error and ignorance beyond which there is no further ignorance. The verifying Sufi scholars have explicitly stated that one who believes this is an unbeliever, and we seek refuge in God, Exalted is He. Perhaps you would say: with this, it would have been better to leave it out. We reply: someone better than us has mentioned something similar, and the purpose of mentioning it is not hidden from you if you are fair.

﴿And they dispute about God﴾, by reflecting upon His essence and by inquiring to stand upon the reality of His attributes. ﴿And He is mighty in strength﴾, glory be to Him, in repelling thoughts and glances from the sanctuary of His essence and the sacred enclosure of His attributes, majestic is His majesty:

"Far is it that the cobwebs of thought should catch the phoenix of permanence with their spittle."

﴿To Him is the true call﴾, that is, the call deserving of response, belonging to none other than Him, glory be to Him. ﴿And those they call upon besides Him﴾, the idols, ﴿do not respond to them with anything, except as one who stretches his hands toward water so that it reaches his mouth﴾; that is, they respond only with a response like that of the one described, for what they call upon has no power at all. ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers﴾, those veiled, ﴿is only in error﴾, that is, in loss, for they call upon none but the true One; they call upon a god they have imagined and carved out in their imagination.

﴿And to God prostrate﴾, submit, ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, of the realities and spiritual beings, ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾, whether they wish or refuse, ﴿and their shadows﴾, their forms, ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾, that is, constantly. It was also said: whoever is in the heavens prostrates, namely the spirit, the intellect and the heart, and their prostration is willing; and whoever is on the earth is the soul and its powers, and their prostration is unwilling.

[p. 138]

And it has been said: "Those who prostrate willingly" are the people of unveiling (ahl al-kashf) and direct witnessing (al-shuhud), and "those who prostrate unwillingly" are the people of reflection and inference (ahl al-nazar wa-al-istidlal). ﴿He sends down from the sky﴾ from the sky of the Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus) ﴿water﴾, meaning the water of knowledge, ﴿so valleys flow﴾, meaning the valleys of hearts, ﴿each according to its measure﴾ according to its capacity to receive (isti'dad). ﴿The torrent carries a foam﴾ from the impurity of the qualities of the soil of the self (ard al-nafs), ﴿rising﴾ and floating over that. ﴿And from that which they heat in the fire﴾, the fire of love ('ishq), from the gnosis, unveilings, realities and meanings that stir up love, ﴿seeking an ornament﴾, seeking the adornment of the self because they are perfections for it, ﴿or a utensil﴾, from the moral virtues that are obtained through them, for they are among the things the self enjoys, ﴿there is a foam like it﴾, namely impurity, such as looking at them, seeing them, being pleased with them, and all that is counted among the afflictions of the self. ﴿As for the foam, it passes away as scum﴾, rejected by knowledge. ﴿And as for what benefits people﴾, from the true meanings and pure virtues, ﴿it remains in the earth﴾, the earth of the self.

Some have said: He, exalted is He, likened what descends from the waters of the seas of His essence, attributes, names and acts to the hearts of the monotheists (al-muwahhidin), the gnostics (al-'arifin), the unveilers (al-mukashifin) and the seekers (al-muridin), with what descends from the sky to the valleys. Just as the valleys, according to their differences, carry rainwater, those hearts carry the waters of those seas according to the differences in their capacities (hawasil) and the measures of their preparedness in love, knowledge and monotheism. Just as the drops of rain become a torrent in the valleys, and the torrent carries foam and dross, and whatever obstructs flowing, so the continuous lights of the Truth, glory be to Him, become a torrent of knowledge and unveilings, which flows in the valleys of hearts. So it carries from the human attributes and whatever is below the Truth, which prevents hearts from seeing the unseen, what it can carry, and it passes away as scum. Then the heart becomes sanctified from the foam of ostentation (riya'), reputation-seeking (sum'ah), hypocrisy (nifaq) and blameworthy thoughts, and remains roaming in the lights of pre-eternity and post-eternity, without any barrier from the Throne to the earth (al-thara). He, glory be to Him, likened the works of the outward and inward and what opens with their keys from the unseen to the essences of the earth, gold and silver and others, when they are melted for benefit from them. He, exalted is He, explained that they have a foam like the foam of the torrent, which passes away, while their pure essence remains. So likewise, the works of the outward and inward enter the crucible of sincerity (ikhlas), and the fires of trial are kindled upon them, so what contains the share of the self passes away, and what is purely for Allah, exalted is He, remains. Likewise with thoughts: of them, the thought of the Truth remains, and the thought of falsehood quickly fades. And it is related from some of them: hearts are vessels, and in them are valleys. One heart flows with the water of repentance, another flows with the water of mercy, another flows with the water of fear, another flows with the water of hope, another flows with the water of gnosis, and another flows with the water of intimacy. Each of these waters grows in the heart a kind of nearness, and nearness to Allah, mighty and majestic, and some hearts are deprived of that, and we seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said, concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He sends down from the sky water﴾ ... etc., he meant by the water the Law (al-shar') and the religion (al-din), and by the valleys the hearts, and the meaning of their flowing according to their measure is the noble taking his share and the dull taking his share. Then he said: "This statement does not hold, and Allah knows best, to be from Ibn 'Abbas, because it tends toward the view of the people of symbols (ashab al-rumuz), which al-Ghazali and the people of that path adopted, and it involves taking the word out of the understanding of the speech of the Arabs without any reason requiring that." And if it is established from Ibn 'Abbas, then it may be said: Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) only intended that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus Allah strikes the truth and falsehood﴾ means the truth that becomes firm in the hearts and the falsehood that afflicts them. End of quotation. We say: If that is established, then the scholar's intent in it is an allusion, though he did not mean what is evident in it. And the Proof of Islam, al-Ghazali (may Allah have mercy on him), was the most severe of people against the people of symbols, who say that the apparent meaning is not what Allah intends, as is not hidden from those who follow his words. I heard from some people that the people of alchemy (kimiya') spoke about this verse in a way that suits their aim, but I have not come upon that.

﴿For those who responded to their Lord﴾ by purifying their readiness from the turbidities of the qualities of the self, ﴿is the best reward (al-husna)﴾, the goodly recompense, which is the perfection that overflows upon them when purified. ﴿And those who did not respond to Him﴾, exalted is He, and remained in human vices and natural turbidities, ﴿even if they had everything that is in the earth﴾, the lower realm, of wealth and means to which they were drawn by love, so they destroyed themselves by them, ﴿and the like of it with it, they would ransom themselves with it﴾ from the veil and deprivation that befall them. ﴿For them is the evil of reckoning﴾ because they stopped with the acts at the station of the self. ﴿Their abode is Hell﴾, which is deprivation, ﴿and wretched is the resting place﴾, Hell, and we seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He, and we ask Him for pardon and well-being.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 19:

﴿Is he, then, who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ is of the Qur'an, which is likened to water sent down from the sky and to pure gold (ibriz) in benefit and usefulness, is ﴿the truth﴾, the truth beyond which there is no truth, or the truth to which the parables that have been coined point? So he responds to it, ﴿like one who is blind﴾, blind of heart, who does not perceive it and does not appreciate its worth, and yet it is the very same; so he remains bewildered in the darkness of ignorance and the深 gloom of misguidance, and does not take heed by the parables that have been coined. The intended meaning is: like one who does not know this. But it is intended to increase the censure of his condition, so he is described as blind. The hamza is for denial, and the placing of the fa' after it is to direct the denial toward the consequence of the supposed equivalence, given the clarity of the state of each of the two through the parables that have been coined and the outcome and final destination that have been explained. It is as if it were said: After making clear the state of each of the two groups, and what belongs to each, could an equivalence between them be imagined?

Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read (Awa man ya'lamu) with a waw in place of the fa'. ﴿Only those who remember﴾ by what has been mentioned of reminders, so they reflect upon the disparity and distance between them, ﴿people of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾. (19) That is, pure intellects, freed from following habit and from opposing illusion. Thus lubb is more specific than 'aql, and this is the view taken by al-Raghib. It has been said that the two are synonymous. The purpose of what has been mentioned is to repel the supposition that the disbelievers are intelligent while they do not remember; and even if they were placed in the position of madmen, that would be fitting.

The verse, according to what has been related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, concerns Hamza, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Jahl. It has also been said: it concerns Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Jahl. And it has been said: it concerns Ammar ibn Yasir, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Jahl. We have already pointed to the manner of its connection with what precedes it. Al-Allama al-Tibi, after establishing the manner of connection, said that (Afa man ya'lamu) is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon the clause ﴿for those who responded﴾ ... etc., and the hamza is inserted between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. He mentioned the meaning of the verse on that basis, saying: Then, if you look closely, you will find it connected to the opening of the surah, meaning by His saying, ﴿And that which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, but most people do not believe﴾. And that is, as you see, far-fetched.

﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of God﴾: the covenant they made with themselves by acknowledging His lordship (rububiyyah), exalted is He, when they said, "Yes" (Qur'an 7:172). Or it means the covenant God, exalted is He, laid upon them in His books, that is, the rulings. In this case the intended people include all nations. The attribution of "covenant" (ahd) to the Name of Majesty is an attribution of the verbal noun to its object according to the first interpretation, and an attribution of the verbal noun to its agent according to the second. If "covenant" is taken to mean what God made binding upon them on the day when He, glorified is He, said, "Am I not your Lord?" (Qur'an 7:172), then the attribution is in every respect an attribution of the verbal noun to its agent. This is the apparent meaning, as in al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit). It is also reported that the covenant refers to the "Am I not" covenant, from Qatada. It is reported that it refers to what was enjoined upon them in the books, from some of them. It is reported from al-Suddi that it refers to what was enjoined upon them in the Qur'an. It is reported from al-Qaffal that it refers to what is in their innate nature and their statements, among the proofs of divine unity (tawhid) and prophethood (nubuwwat), and other things. It has been deduced that it should be understood in its general sense.

﴿and do not break the solemn pact﴾ (20). That is, the binding agreements (mawathiq) they confirmed between God, exalted is He, and themselves, concerning faith in Him, exalted is He, the rulings, and vows, and what is between them and His servants, such as contracts and the like. This is a generalisation after a specification, and it contains an emphasis on the continuity implied by the imperfect form of the verb.

Abu Hayyan said: The apparent meaning is that this sentence is an emphasis of the preceding one, because the covenant (ahd) is the solemn pact (mithaq), and fulfilling the covenant necessarily entails not breaking it.

Ibn Atiyya said: The intended meaning of the first sentence is that they fulfil all the covenants of God, exalted is He, which are His commands and prohibitions that God enjoined upon His servants. This includes adhering to all obligations and avoiding all sins. The intended meaning of the second sentence is that when they make a covenant in obedience to God, exalted is He, they do not break it. End quote. In light of this, the notion of generalisation after specification does not hold, as is not hidden.

God, glorified is He, has already warned His servants against breaking the covenant and forbade it in some twenty verses of His Book, as is reported from Qatada. Among the greatest covenants, according to what Ibn al-Arabi said, is that the servant should not ask anyone other than his Master, exalted is His majesty.

In the story of Abu Hamza al-Khurasani there is evidence for the greatness of this matter. He had made a covenant with his Lord not to ask anyone but Him. It so happened that he fell into a well, and he did not ask any of the people passing by to rescue him from it, until someone came and brought him out without being asked, and he did not see who had brought him out. Then a voice called out to him, "How did you find the fruit of trust in God (tawakkul)?" Therefore, it is fitting to follow his example in fulfilling the covenant, according to what he also said.

Ibn al-Jawzi has, however, criticised the action of this man, explained his error, and stated that trust in God does not contradict seeking aid (istighathah) in such a situation. He mentioned that Sufyan al-Thawri and others said: If a person became hungry and did not ask until he died, he would enter the Fire. He does not deny that God, exalted is He, may have shown kindness to Abu Hamza, the ignorant one. Yes, it is not fitting to seek aid from other than God, exalted is He, in the manner that people do today with the people of graves, imagining in them what they imagine. So, woe, then woe, because of what they do.

[Page 140]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 21:

﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾. The apparent meaning is generality, covering everything that Allah the Exalted has commanded in His Book and on the tongue of His Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Hasan said: the intended meaning is joining the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through faith in him. A similar report is narrated from Ibn Jubayr. Qatadah said: the intended meaning is maintaining the ties of kinship (silat al-arham). It has also been said: joining faith with action. And it has been said: joining the bond of Islamic brotherhood by spreading the greeting of peace, visiting the sick, attending funerals, and observing the rights of neighbours, companions and servants. Those who hold the view of generality include among it the Prophets, peace be upon them, that one believe in all of them and not make any distinction between any of them; and people in their various classes, joining them by observing their rights; indeed, all animals, joining them by observing what is required regarding their rights, whether obligatory or recommended. It is narrated from al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad that a group entered upon him in Makkah, and he said: "Where are you from?" They said: "From the people of Khurasan." He said: "Fear Allah the Exalted, and be wherever you wish. Know that if a servant performed all of goodness, but had a hen to which he did harm, he would not be a doer of good."

The object of ﴿amara﴾ (commanded) is omitted, and the estimated meaning is: "what Allah commanded them with." ﴿An yuwassala﴾ (that it be joined) is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in the genitive position, i.e., what Allah commanded to be joined to.

﴿And they fear their Lord﴾, i.e., His threat, glory be to Him. The apparent meaning is that it is meant absolutely. It has been said: the intended meaning is His threat, exalted be He, for severing what they were commanded to join.

﴿And they dread the evil of reckoning﴾ (21). That is, they take account of themselves before they are taken to account. This is from the category of mentioning the particular after the general, for emphasis.

Khashyah (fear with reverence) and khawf (fear) — it has been said that they have the same meaning. In al-Askari's Furuq (Distinctions) it is stated that khawf relates to the disliked thing and its cause: one says "I feared Zayd" and "I feared illness." Khashyah relates to the cause, not to the disliked thing itself. Therefore He, glory be to Him, said: "yakhshawna" first and "yakhafuna" second. Based on this, the consideration of threat would not be in its proper place. But this is not accepted, because of His saying: ﴿fear of poverty﴾ (khashyata imlaq) and ﴿for whoever of you fears hardship﴾ (liman khashiya al-'anat minkum). Al-Raghib distinguished between them, saying: khashyah is fear mixed with veneration, and it is mostly not without knowledge; for this reason the scholars were singled out for it in His saying: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ (innama yakhsha Allaha min 'ibadihi al-'ulama').

Some have said: khashyah is the intensest fear, because it is derived from their saying: "shajarah khashiyyah," i.e., a dry tree. For this reason it is restricted to the Lord in this verse. They also distinguished between them by saying that khashyah arises from the greatness of the one feared, even if the one who fears is strong, while khawf arises from the weakness of the one who fears, even if what is feared is a minor matter. What indicates this is that the permutations of the letters kha', shin and ya' indicate heedlessness, and in tadabbur (reflection). But the truth is that such distinctions are mostly general and conventional, and for this reason many did not distinguish between them. Indeed, the Imam chose that the meaning of "they fear their Lord" is that they fear Him with the fear of awe and majesty, claiming that without this it would entail repetition. But in this there is what there is.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 22:

﴿And those who are patient﴾ over everything the soul dislikes of calamities, whether of wealth or of body, and whatever goes against the desire of the soul, such as taking revenge and the like. What is mentioned includes the religious obligations (al-taklif). ﴿Seeking the countenance of their Lord﴾, meaning seeking His good pleasure, the Exalted, without looking to the side of the creation (for show, riya', or reputation, sum'ah), nor to the side of their own selves (for adornment and self-admiration, 'ujb). It was also said: the meaning is "seeking that," and so ﴿ibtigha'﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). According to the first view, it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). The discussion of the expression "wajh" being attributed to Him, the Exalted, is well known.

In al-Bahr: the apparent meaning here is "direction" (jihah) of God, the Exalted, i.e., the direction that is intended with good deeds before Him, the Glorified, so that reward falls upon them, as one says: "Zayd went out for the sake of such-and-such." In it also: the relative clause here came with the past tense, whereas in what preceded it came with the present tense, as a variation in eloquence, because the subject (mubtada') has the sense of the conditional noun (ism al-shart), and the past tense is like the present tense in the conditional noun; so likewise in what resembles it. Therefore the grammarians said: when the past tense occurs as a relative clause or as an adjective to an indefinite general noun, it may be intended to refer to the past, and it may be intended to refer to the future. From the first is ﴿those to whom the people said﴾, and from the second ﴿except those who repent before you gain power over them﴾. It also appears that the restriction of this relative clause to the past tense, and of what preceded it to the present tense, is because what preceded was intended to indicate continuation and ongoing state, whereas this one was intended to indicate that they preceded that; for the attainment of those relative clauses is only consequent upon the attainment of patience and its precedence over them. Therefore no relative clause in the Qur'an came except in the form of the past tense, since it is a condition for the attainment and enactment of the obligations. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim: since patience is the foundation of the matter in everything mentioned among the preceding and following relative clauses, it is expressed in the past tense, out of concern for its importance and to indicate the necessity of its realization, for that is something indispensable, either in the relative clauses themselves, as in what is other than the first, fourth and fifth, or in the manifestation of their rulings, as in the three mentioned relative clauses. For although they are independent of patience in themselves, since there is no hardship upon the soul in acknowledging the Lordship, fearing and dreading, nevertheless manifesting their rulings and acting in accordance with their requirements is not free of need for it, and it is not free of some difficulty. The better view, as has been said, is to limit the reason to concern for its importance. And His, the Glorified's, saying is conjoined: ﴿and they establish the prayer﴾, and likewise what follows it, upon that, as several have stated, by way of conjoining the specific to the general. By "the prayer" it is said: the obligatory prayer; and it is said: prayer in general, and this is better. Establishing it means completing its pillars and its forms. ﴿And spend of what We have provided them﴾, some of what We have given them, namely that which it is obligatory for them to spend, such as zakat and what is spent on dependents and slaves, or what includes that; and what is recommended secretly, where secrecy is fitting, as in the giving of one who is not known for wealth when he fears suspicion if he publicizes it, or one who is known for it but whose public giving might lead to showing off and vanity; and as in giving to one whom dignity prevents from taking openly, where openness is fitting, as when the matter is contrary to what has been mentioned. Some have said: the first is specific to voluntary charity and the second to the performance of obligatory charity. It is reported from al-Hasan that both matters apply to obligatory zakat: if he is not suspected of neglecting zakat, then the better course is to pay it secretly; otherwise, the better course is to pay it openly. It was said: "secret" means that one does not pay it himself, and "open" means that one does not pay it to the imam. The first is to take it in its generality. Perhaps the mention of the secret first is to indicate the excellence of his charity. And it has come in the authentic report: "One who gives charity in secret" is among those whom God, the Exalted, will shade in His shade on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And they repel evil with good﴾, i.e., they repel harm with good and repay wrongdoing with kindness, according to what Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd; and from Ibn Jubayr: they return kindness to one who wrongs them. This is like His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾. Al-Hasan said: when they are deprived, they give; when they are wronged, they forgive; and when they are cut off, they connect. It was said: they follow an evil deed with a good deed, so that it erases it. And in a hadith: "Mu'adh said: 'Advise me, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'When you do an evil deed, follow it with a good deed that will erase it: secret with secret, and open with open.'" And from Ibn Kaysan: they repel by repentance the harm of sin. It was said: by "there is no god but God," their polytheism; it was said: by charity, the punishment; it was said: when they see an evil, they command its change. And it was said, and it was said. The practice of some of the scholars indicates a preference for the first view, so they are as it has been said:

They repay the wrong of the wrongdoers with forgiveness, and the evil of the evildoers with goodness.

This is in contrast to the conduct of some of the ignorant:

Bold, whenever he is wronged, he punishes with his wrong, swiftly; and if he is not wronged first, he wrongs.

And in al-Kashf: the more apparent view is generality, i.e., they repel the evil with the beautiful, whether it was harm to them or not, whether specific to them or not, whether obedience or disobedience, honor or disgrace. Perhaps the matter is as he said. And the placing of the prepositional phrase before the accusative object is to show full concern for the good deed. ﴿Those﴾, i.e., those described with the sublime qualities and the beautiful dispositions; and the intended ones are not particular individuals, although the verse is said to have been revealed concerning the Ansar. The demonstrative is the subject, and its predicate is the adverbial clause, namely His, the Glorified, saying: ﴿For them is the good outcome of the abode﴾. (22). That is, the outcome of the world, and what the end of the affairs of its people should be, which is Paradise; so the definiteness of "the abode" is for a known reference, and the absolute "outcome" is explained by that. It is explained by it in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the outcome is for the God-fearing﴾. Al-Zamakhshari also explained it as Paradise, except that he said: because it is the one God, the Exalted, intended to be the outcome of the world and the return of its people. In it, according to some, there is a trace of Mu'tazilism.

It is permitted that "the abode" means the Hereafter, i.e., for them is the good outcome in the Hereafter. It was also said: the prepositional phrase is the predicate of the demonstrative, and "outcome" is the subject of the verb of settledness. In any case, there is no restriction in it, so that it could be objected that some of what is within the relative clause is not among the resolute obligations whose neglect would hinder reaching a good outcome.

Some have said: the intended meaning is that the destiny of those is Paradise without any interruption by entering the Fire; so there is no harm if it is said with restriction, and it does not follow that the sinful one who is punished does not enter Paradise. The claim that he is described with those qualities in a general sense is, as you see, not valid. The sentence is a predicate for the conjoined relative clauses if they are put in the nominative as subjects, or a resumptive grammatical or explanatory continuation, in answer to the question: what about those described with these qualities, if the conjoined relative clauses are made attributes of "those of understanding," in the manner of praise, without intending that the mentioned relative clauses have any role in reflection. The first is more appropriate, due to what is in al-Kashf concerning maintaining the contrast between the two groups. And the conjunction in His, the Exalted, saying ﴿and those who break﴾ is fine, and their being left as a resumed description of "the one who knows" and "him who is like the blind" is also fine.

[Page 143]

Allah's words: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ are a *badal* (substitute, or apposition) for ﴿the final abode﴾, as al-Zajjaj said: it is a *badal kull min kull* (an apposition in which the substitute is the whole of what it replaces). Abu al-Baqa' and others allowed that it could be a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is His words, ﴿they will enter it﴾. This was criticised as far from the context. The better view is that it is an omitted subject, as mentioned in *al-Bahr* (al-Bahr al-Muhit). This was rejected on the grounds that it has no basis, because the sentence is an explanation (*bayan*) of ﴿the final abode﴾, so it fits the context. ʿAdn means settling and remaining: one says ʿadana bi-makan kadha (he settled in such a place) when he has become established there, and from this comes *al-maʿdin* (the mine), the place where jewels settle. So the meaning is: gardens in which they will dwell permanently. Many transmitters report from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is the *butnan al-jannah*, meaning its middle. Something similar is reported from al-Dahhak, except that he said: it is a city in the middle of Paradise, in which are the prophets, the martyrs and the leaders of guidance. Other reports have also come concerning it. If by it is meant a specific place within Paradise, then the substitute is a *badal baʿd min kull* (a substitute of part from a whole). Al-Nakha'i read *jannat* (in the singular). It is reported from Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr that they read *yudkhalunaha* (in the passive voice).

﴿And whoever is righteous among their fathers﴾: this is the plural of the two parents of each one of them, so it is as if it were said: among their fathers and their mothers. ﴿And their spouses and their offspring﴾. This, as Abu al-Baqa' said, is conjoined (*ʿutifa*) to the subject in ﴿they will enter﴾. That this is permissible despite the absence of emphasis is due to the separation by the other pronoun. It was also permitted that it be an object of accompaniment (*maf'ul maʿahu*). It was objected that the particle of accompaniment (*waw al-maʿiyya*) only governs what is followed. This was answered by saying that this applies to *maʿa* and not to the *waw*, though there is room for debate. The meaning is that there will join them whoever among their family was righteous, even if he did not reach their level of excellence, following them out of honour for their rank. Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Jubayr that he said: a man enters Paradise and says: "Where is my mother? Where is my son? Where is my wife?" It is said to him: "They did not do deeds like yours." He says: "I used to work for myself and for them." Then he recited the verse. He explained ﴿who was righteous﴾ as ﴿who believed﴾; this is what is reported from Mujahid, and something similar is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Al-Zajjaj explained it as ﴿who believed and did righteous deeds﴾, and mentioned that by this Allah clarified that lineage does not benefit unless it is accompanied by righteous deeds; rather, the fathers, spouses and offspring do not enter Paradise except through righteous deeds. Al-Wahidi rejected this, saying: the correct view is what is reported from Ibn Abbas, because Allah made it part of the reward of the obedient that he is delighted by the presence of his family with him in Paradise. This indicates that they enter it as an honour for the obedient one who performs righteous deeds. If they entered it by their own deeds, there would be no honour in that for the obedient one, nor any benefit in the promise of it, since everyone who is upright in his deeds enters Paradise. The Imam (al-Razi) weakened this, saying: the intended purpose is the good news to the obedient of everything that increases his delight and joy. So when Allah gives the accountable person the good news that when he enters Paradise his family will be present with him, his delight grows greatly and his joy increases. It is said that among the greatest of their delights is that they gather together and remember their states in the world, then thank Allah for being saved from it. For this reason, He, glory be to Him, related of one of the people of Paradise that he says: ﴿Would that my people knew of what my Lord has forgiven me, and made me among the honoured.﴾ In light of this, the verse is not evidence that rank rises through intercession. Some who held that interpretation cited it as evidence for it, according to the first meaning of it.

It was objected that it is also not evidence for what was mentioned. It was answered that if it is permissible for one to be raised merely by following the perfect in faith, out of honour for their rank, then the elevation through their intercession is known all the more by the stronger reasoning (*al-tariq al-awla*). Some said: since they were, by their righteousness, deserving of entering Paradise, placing them at their rank is a consequence of their request and their intercession for them, by the implication of the attribution (*idafa*). The truth is that the verse is not fit to be evidence for that, especially if the *waw* is in the sense of *maʿa* (with), so reflect. It is apparent that there is no distinction between one wife and another wife, and the Imam declared this explicitly. Then he said: perhaps the most fitting is the one whose spouse has died, or who has died leaving a spouse, and what is reported from Sawda: that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intended to divorce her, she said: "Do not, O Messenger of Allah, let me be raised among your wives," serves as a kind of evidence for what was mentioned.

[Page 144]

Concerning a woman who has had more than one husband, if they have all died leaving her, it is said that she is in Paradise with her last husband. This is supported by the fact that the Mothers of the Believers, the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), are in it, although most of them had been married before to others, peace be upon him. It is also said that she belongs to her first husband, like a woman who was informed by a trustworthy person that her husband had died, and it settled in her heart that this was true, so she married after the end of her waiting period, and then his life became apparent; she is then his. This was criticised: this is not of this kind at all, rather it resembles the case where a man dies and an infallible person such as the Prophet announces his death, so his wife marries after the waiting period ends, and then Allah brings him back to life. Concerning that, they said: his wife belongs to her second husband. It is also said that the wife will be given a choice on the Day of Resurrection among her husbands, and whichever of them was best in character toward her, she will belong to him. A group has favoured this view. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read *ṣaluḥa* (with a *ḍamma* on the lam), though the *fatḥa* is more eloquent. ʿIsa al-Thaqafi read *dhurriyyatahum* (in the singular).

﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ (13:23): from the gates of the dwellings.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Anas ibn Malik that he recited the verse until he finished it, then said: indeed the believer is in a tent of hollow pearl, with no pillar or joint; its length in the air is sixty miles; in each corner of it there is a family and property for them; it has four thousand doors of gold, and at each door stand seventy thousand angels, and with each angel is a gift from the Most Merciful that his companion does not have the like of; they cannot reach him except with permission, and between him and them there is a veil. It is reported from Ibn Abbas something even greater than that.

Abu al-Asamm said: what is meant is from every gate of the gates of righteousness, such as the gate of prayer, the gate of charity, and the gate of patience. It was also said: from the gates of conquests and gifts. It was said: according to this, the meaning of *bab* (gate) is *naw* (type), and *min* (from) is for causation, and the meaning is that they enter because of their being presented with various kinds of gifts. This was criticised: there is a question about whether *bab* can mean *naw* in the sense of *babah*; the apparent wording of *al-Asas* and others requires that it be a metaphor or a metonymy for what was mentioned, because a house which has doors, when a great multitude comes to it, they enter it from every door. So what is meant is the entry of abundant provisions upon them, and that these come to them from every direction, and the multiplicity of directions indicates the multiplicity of things that come, for every direction has its own gift.

[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 13, verse 24]

﴿Peace be upon you﴾, meaning, saying this. It is good news of the continuance of safety. Thus the clause is a statement (maqul) belonging to an omitted saying, and it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal, a noun in the accusative describing the state of the subject) referring to the subject of ﴿enter﴾. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause without any implied saying, meaning "greeting [one another]." Originally it is a verbal clause, meaning "they greet with a greeting."

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿for what you endured﴾ is connected (muta'allliq, governed by a phrase) as Abu al-Baqa' said, to what is connected to ﴿upon you﴾, or to itself, since it substitutes for its own governing element. Al-Suyuti al-Saffaqisi rejected this, and said: "It has no basis. The correct view is that it is connected to what is connected to ﴿upon you﴾." Al-Zamakhshari permitted its being connected to ﴿peace﴾, with the meaning "we greet you and honour you for your endurance." Abu al-Baqa' prohibited this, because it would involve separating the verbal noun (masdar) from its complement (ma'mul) by a foreign element, namely the predicate (khabar). This was justified in *al-Durr al-Masun* on the ground that the prohibition applies only to a verbal noun interpreted with a verbal particle (harf masdari, a particle such as "an" that turns a verb and its subject into a verbal noun), and this case is not of that kind. Moreover, al-Radi permitted this even with such interpretation, and said: "I do not see it as preventing it, because everything interpreted as something does not possess all its rulings." On this same reasoning, al-ʿAllamah al-Thani permitted placing the complement of a verbal noun formed with "an" and the verb before it, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and let not compassion for them take hold of you﴾. He said in *al-Kashf*: "﴿upon you﴾, considered in its original form, is not foreign, and therefore it is permissible to separate by it." Yet al-Zamakhshari did not explicitly say that it is a complement; rather it is implied by it, and for this reason he said: "That is, we greet...," which shows that the connection is one of meaning, and what suits it is supplied. If it were made a complement of the stable adverbial phrase, namely ﴿upon you﴾, then it would be connected in meaning to ﴿peace﴾ necessarily, and this would be a view free of artificiality. Abu Hayyan made it the predicate of an omitted subject, with ﴿ma﴾ being a verbal particle and the "ba'" being causal or substitutive, meaning: "this great reward is because of your endurance in this world of hardships," or "in its place." From Abu 'Imran: "for what you endured in your religion." From al-Hasan: "for [abstaining from] the superfluities of this world." From Muhammad ibn al-Nasr: "for poverty." The generalization is better. The singling out of endurance for mention among the preceding qualities is because it is the foundation of the matter, and the matter is one of importance, as you have come to know.

﴿So excellent is the final abode﴾ (24). That is, so excellent is the outcome of this world: Paradise. It was said that the intended "abode" is the Hereafter. Some said: the meaning is that they were brought from Hell to Paradise. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "This is based on what has been transmitted, that every man of the people of Paradise had a place in the Fire, and Allah, exalted is He, turned him away from it to bliss. He is shown it and it is said to him: 'This is your place in the Fire; Allah, exalted is He, has replaced it for you with Paradise because of your faith and your endurance.'" Ibn Yu'mur read ﴿fa-ni'ma﴾ with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ʿayn, and that is the original form. Ibn Thabit read ﴿fa-na'ma﴾ with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the ʿayn, with the verb lightened (ni'ma being treated as na'ma), the dialect of Tamim. It also came in it, as in *al-Sihah* (of al-Jawhari), as ﴿ni'ma﴾ with a kasra on the nun and the ʿayn following it. The most common usage of these forms is that which the majority hold.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim who said: "The Prophet ﷺ used to visit the graves of the martyrs at the beginning of every year, and he would say: '﴿Peace be upon you, for what you endured; so excellent is the final abode﴾.'" And Abu Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with them, used to do likewise.

Some of them used the verse as evidence that the angel is better than the human. They said: "Allah, exalted is He, concluded the ranks of human happiness with the entry of the angels upon them, by way of greeting, honour, veneration and peace. Thus they were of the highest rank among humans, since their entry upon them for the sake of peace and greeting necessitated the elevation of their ranks and the nobility of their stations." Without doubt, whoever returns from his journey to his house, and it is said, in the context of the perfection of his rank, that he is visited by the emir, the vizier, the judge and the mufti, this indicates that the rank of the one visited is lower and inferior to the ranks of the visitors. So it is here as well. And this is of great feebleness.

Why could it not be that what is here is like the case where a sultan brings one of his distinguished agents, who has obeyed him in his commands and prohibitions, to the place of his honour, and then, after lodging him in the fitting station, sends his servants to him with gifts, tokens and good news that gladdens him? If it were said: "So-and-so, the sultan has lodged him in the place of his honour and the seat of his governance, lodged him in the fitting station, and sent his servants to him with what pleases him," would that be evidence that those servants are of a higher rank than him? I do not think you would say so.

Yes, some reports have come that support, in their apparent meaning, what preceded. Ahmad, al-Bazzar, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and a group, transmitted from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The first of Allah's creation to enter Paradise are the poor emigrants, by whom the frontiers are guarded and through whom adversities are averted, and one of them dies with his need in his chest, unable to fulfil it. Allah, exalted is He, says to whichever of His angels He wills: 'Go to them and greet them.'
