The angels say: 'Our Lord, we are the dwellers of Your heaven and the choicest of Your creation; do You command us to go to these and greet them?' Allah, exalted is He, says: 'These are servants of Mine who used to worship Me and did not associate anything with Me. The frontiers are guarded by them, and adversities are averted through them, and one of them dies with his need in his chest, unable to fulfil it.' Then the angels come to them at that moment, and they enter upon them from every gate: ﴿Peace be upon you, for what you endured; so excellent is the final abode﴾."

Whoever is just will see that this does not indicate that the angels are, absolutely, better than humans, absolutely, as is not hidden.

Al-Imam al-Razi, in his exegesis of the verse, mentioned in the manner transmitted from al-Asamm, regarding the entry of the angels from every gate, that the angels are groups: among them are spiritual beings (ruhaniyyun) and among them are cherubic beings (karrubiyyun). When the servant trains his soul with kinds of discipline, such as endurance, gratitude, watchfulness (muraqabah) and self-examination (muhasabah), each of these stations has a holy essence and a lofty spirit specially connected with that quality in an exceptional way. At death, when those holy essences shine, there are manifested in them, from every spirit of the heavenly spirits, what suits them of the specific qualities. Thus there is poured upon them, from the angels of endurance, specific perfections of the soul which appear only in the station of endurance; and from the angels of gratitude, spiritual perfections which are manifested only in the station of gratitude; and so it is for all the stations. End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan criticised it, saying: "This is a corrupt speech which the Arabs would not understand, and which the prophets, peace be upon them, did not bring. It is rejected and the Muslims do not give it any attention." And you know that much of this kind of speech is found among the Sufis.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 25:

﴿And those who break the covenant of Allah﴾ is meant to refer to those who confront the earlier ones and oppose them by adopting the opposites of their attributes, ﴿after its binding﴾, i.e., the acknowledgment of it. It has been said: the "covenant" (al-'ahd) here refers to His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ and the "binding" (al-mithaq) is an instrument noun, meaning that by which a thing is bound, and it is meant here as the acknowledgment expressed in the words: ﴿Yes indeed﴾. A covenant from both sides may also be called a mithaq because it binds the two parties to the agreement. The Imam (al-Razi) explained the covenant of Allah, exalted is He, as that which He obligated His servants to by means of rational proofs, because that is the strongest of every covenant and every oath, since oaths only produce confirmation through the proofs that indicate they necessitate fulfilling what they require. Then he said: The meaning of breaking it is that a person does not reflect upon it, so that he is then unable to act according to its requirement; or that he reflects and knows its soundness, then obstinately does not act on his knowledge; or that he reflects upon doubts and so does not believe the truth. The meaning of His, glorified is He, saying ﴿after its binding﴾ is after He bound them to those proofs and their rulings, because nothing is stronger than what Allah, exalted is He, has shown to be obligatory, in that its performance benefits and its abandonment harms.

It was raised as an objection: if the covenant cannot occur except through binding, what is the benefit of ﴿after its binding﴾? He answered: it is not impossible that the meaning is separation from one who was able to know it by oath, for one who was not able at first; it is not impossible that the meaning is the emphasized proofs, because it is said: "You have been emphatically addressed with other proofs, whether rational or traditional." End. It is not hidden that if by the covenant is meant that saying and by the binding the acknowledgment of it, there is no need for this discussion. Some have taken the covenant here to mean all that Allah, exalted is He, enjoined upon His servants, like the covenant mentioned earlier, and the binding to mean acceptance and assent. The verse, as reported from Muqatil, was revealed concerning the People of the Book. ﴿And they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾ refers to belief in all the prophets, peace be upon them, who agree on the truth, since they believe in some and disbelieve in others; and it includes the rights of kinship, allegiance to the believers, and other things. As some of the verifiers have said, He did not explicitly deny fear and dread of them, because breaking and severing indicate that. As for the non-mention of negating the aforementioned patience, it is because it was only considered to be realized within the enumerated good deeds, so that they would count; therefore there is no basis for negating it from one who stands far from those good deeds, especially after restricting it to seeking His face, exalted is He. Likewise there is no basis for negating prayer and spending, on the basis that what is meant by it is giving zakat from one who does not come near belief in Allah, exalted is He, let alone the branches of the sacred laws. If by spending is meant what includes that and other things, then its negation falls under severing what Allah, exalted is He, has commanded to be joined. Indeed, it may be said that the negation of prayer also falls under that. As for warding off evil with good, its absence from them is clear from what preceded and followed, for one who repays the kindness of Allah, exalted and majestic is He, with breaking His covenant, glorified is He, and opposing the command, and engages in corruption as His saying, exalted and majestic is He, indicates: ﴿and they cause corruption on the earth﴾ through wronging themselves and others, stirring up strife by opposing the call to truth, and provoking war against the Muslims, how could that warding off be conceived of him? Furthermore, it has been said that this indicates that it has some role in leading to the punishment which His saying, glorified is He, announces: ﴿Those﴾ ... etc., i.e., those described by those vices, for them, because of that, ﴿is the curse﴾, i.e., distance from the mercy of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿and theirs is the evil abode﴾ (25). I.e., the evil outcome of the abode, and by the abode is meant this world, and its evil outcome is the punishment of Hell, or Hell itself. He did not say "the evil outcome of the abode" out of concern to make it the outcome, since He made the absolute outcome to be Paradise. It is permitted that by the abode is meant Hell and by its evil its punishment; but the first is more apt for observing the antithesis, and because what comes first to understanding from "the abode" is this world, by the context of what preceded, and because it is what is present in their minds, and for the subtle point mentioned. That is because the placing of the judgment upon the relative pronoun indicates the causality of the relative clause for it. It is not hidden that this has no bearing on it according to most exegeses, for repaying an evil deed with its like is permitted, repelling bad speech with what is better, likewise giving when denied, pardoning when wronged, and joining when severed, is not something whose abandonment entails consequence. As for what is considered to fall under the second relative clause, namely neglecting some recommended rights, there is no harm in that, because its consideration is from the standpoint that it is among the consequences of neglecting the obligatory duties, like disbelief in some prophets, peace be upon them, disobedience to parents, and abandoning all the obligatory rights. It was qualified by "most" because on the many things we mentioned in its explanation the relevance is evident. It has been said: He adopted in describing the disbelievers and blaming them, and mentioning what awaits them and where their affair ends, a method other than that which He adopted in describing the believers and praising them and explaining what is prepared for them and where their affair ends. So in the first He used multiple relative pronouns and varied relative clauses, and so on, while He did not use the like in the second, to draw attention to the greater concern for the affair of the believers in word and deed and the lack of concern for the affair of their opposites, for they are impure, and one rinses one's mouth after mentioning them. This is with certainty that the requirement of the situation is precisely this. It has also been said: both methods are effects of the vast mercy. So reflect. The repetition of ﴿for them﴾ is for emphasis and to indicate the difference between the two and the independence of each in establishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 26:

﴿Allah extends provision﴾, that is, He widens it for whomever of His servants He wills, ﴿and straitens﴾, that is, He restricts it. It was also said: He gives in measure sufficient for need. The provision meant here is worldly provision, not what includes the provision of the Hereafter, because that, as it has been said, does not fit the context. The author of al-Kashf (al-Kashshaf) said that it includes both kinds of provision, the sensory and the spiritual, worldly and otherworldly. He mentioned, in explaining how the verse connects to what precedes it on this reading, what has been mentioned. It is as narrated from Ibn Abbas: it was revealed concerning the people of Makkah. Then, although it is so in a general sense, it seems to serve as a rebuttal to the assumption that they could be in ease of provision while being in the state of error they were in. So Allah, exalted is He, made clear that the abundance of their provision is not an honouring of them, just as the restriction of the provision of some believers is not a humiliation of them. Rather, each of these two matters proceeds from Him, exalted is He, for divine wisdoms that He alone knows. Sometimes He widens provision for the disbeliever as a respite and a gradual leading on, and He restricts it for the believer to increase his reward.

The fronting of the subject (al-musnad ilayhi) in a verse like this, according to al-Sakkaki and al-Zamakhshari, is for exclusivity (al-taqwa) alone. Another view holds that there is no obstacle to its being for both exclusivity and specification (al-takhsis). For this reason he said: that is, Allah alone is the One who extends and restricts, not other than Him, exalted is He. Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read ﴿yaqdur﴾ with a damma on the dal wherever it occurs. ﴿And they rejoice﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) that censures the ugliness of their deeds alongside what He has widened for them.

The pronoun is said to refer to the people of Makkah even though they were not previously mentioned, and a group chose this view. Abu Hayyan said it refers to ﴿those who break﴾. Some claimed that the clause is coordinated with the relative clause of ﴿alladhina﴾, and that the verse has inversion (taqdim and ta'khir), and that its place is after ﴿they cause corruption on the earth﴾. The distance of this is not hidden, because of the difference in general and specific reference, and in the future and past tenses. That is, they rejoiced with the joy of insolence and arrogance, not the joy of gladness at the grace of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿In the worldly life﴾, that is, in what has been spread out for them there of blessings, because their rejoicing is not in the worldly life itself, so attributing the rejoicing to it is figurative (majaz). Or there is an ellipsis, meaning: He extends life, or "the worldly life" is a metonymy for what is in it. ﴿And the worldly life, in the Hereafter, is nothing﴾, that is, it exists alongside its bliss. So the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (haal), and it is not attached to "life" or to "worldly," as Abu al-Baqa said, because they are not in it.

This "in" (fi) has the meaning of comparison (al-muqayasa). It is very common in speech, as one says: the sins of a servant within the mercy of Allah, exalted is He, are like a drop in a sea. This is the particle that comes between a lesser earlier thing and a greater later thing, and it is the figurative sense of "in" as a container, because what is compared is placed alongside something.

[p. 148]

The attribution of ﴿enjoyment﴾ in His words, exalted is He: ﴿except enjoyment﴾ (26) to the worldly life may be figurative and may be literal. What is meant is that it is nothing but a meagre thing enjoyed, like the provision of a rider on a journey, or a shepherd's provision that his family supplies him: a handful of dates, or some flour, or something similar. The meaning is that they were content with a portion of the worldly life, turning away from the bliss of the Hereafter, while what they took pleasure in, compared with what they turned away from, is of meagre benefit and quick to run out. Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and graded it sound, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) slept on a mat, and when he got up it had left a mark on his side. We said: O Messenger of Allah, if only we had made you a bed. He said: What have I to do with the worldly life? I am in the world only like a rider who took shade under a tree, then went on and left it." It was also said: the meaning of the verse is like the saying: "The world is the field of the Hereafter." That is, what was spread out for them in the world should have been a means to the Hereafter, like a merchant's goods that he sells in order to gain what concerns and benefits him in his aims, not that they should rejoice in them and regard them as ends in themselves. The first view is more preferable and more fitting.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 27:

﴿And those who disbelieved say﴾: that is, the people of Mecca, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Umayya and his companions. The choice of this manner of expression (the explicit noun) rather than a pronoun, although their intent is evident right after the mention of their joy, is based on the view that the pronoun in "faraḥū" (they rejoiced) refers to them, in order to censure them and to record their disbelief against them, in respect of what is related of their saying: ﴿Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾ For that is at the furthest extreme of obstinacy and stubborn denial, as if the great and dazzling signs that were sent down to him, peace and blessings be upon him, were not a sign in their view, so they proposed what the wisdom does not require of signs, such as the sky falling upon them in pieces, the moving of the two mountains (al-Akhshabayn), the making of the valleys (al-Biṭāḥ) into plowed fields, the making of the land into a desert like Jordan, the reviving of Quṣayy for them, and other such things. ﴿Say: Indeed Allah leads astray whom He wills﴾: His leading astray is a will that follows the wisdom that calls for it. This is a statement in the manner of a wonder at their saying. That is because the dazzling and abundant signs that were given to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, were not given to any prophet before him, and the Qur'an alone suffices as a sign. So when they deny them and do not regard them, this becomes an occasion for wonder and denunciation, and the apparent thing would have been to say in reply: "How great is your obstinacy, and how firm is your resolve upon disbelief," or the like. However, He placed this in its position to indicate that the one who is wondered at says: ﴿Indeed Allah leads astray﴾ ... etc., meaning that He, exalted is He, creates straying in whomever He wills, by turning their choice toward acquiring it, and leaves him immersed in it, because He knows that kindness does not succeed with him and guidance does not benefit him, due to the badness of his readiness, like one who is in your state of obstinacy, stubbornness, intractability and extremism in corruption, so there is no way for him to be guided even if every sign came to him.

﴿And guides to Himself﴾: that is, to His lofty and great side.

Abu Hayyan said: that is, to His religion and His law, exalted is He, with a guidance that conveys to Him, not merely an absolute indication toward what conveys; for that is not restricted to the guided, and in it is an honor for them that cannot be described. It was said: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an or to the Messenger, peace be upon him, but this is very much contrary to the apparent meaning. ﴿Whoever turns back (in repentance)﴾. (27) That is, whoever turns toward the truth and reflects upon the contents of the clear proofs that were sent down. The reality of inabah is returning to the state of goodness and preferring it. In the relative clause, the preference for it over mention of the will is as in the first relative clause, according to what our master Shaykh al-Islam said, to draw attention to what calls to guidance, indeed to its will, and to point to what prompted the first will, namely the stubbornness. In it is an exhortation to the disbelievers to desist from what they are upon of insolence and obstinacy. The choice of the past tense form is to hint at seeking the earlier guidance, just as the choice of the present tense form in the first relative clause indicates the continuity of the will in line with the continuity of their stubbornness. The verse is explicit in the doctrine of the People of the Sunna regarding the attribution of good and evil to Him, glorified and exalted is He. The Mu'tazila interpreted it, and Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i said: the meaning is "He leads astray whom He wills from His reward and mercy, as a punishment for his disbelief; so you are not among those whom Allah answers in what they ask, because you deserve punishment, and straying from reward; and He guides to His Paradise whoever repents and believes." Then he said: By this it becomes clear that guidance is the reward, inasmuch as it is attached to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿whoever turns back﴾; and the guidance that He, glorified is He, performs for the believer is the reward, because he deserves it for his faith; and that indicates that He, exalted is He, leads astray from the reward, not from the religion through disbelief, according to what he who opposes us has held. End quote. And what is in it is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 28:**

﴿Those who believe﴾ is a *badal* (substitution, i.e. a *badal kull min kull*, where the second term fully replaces the first) for ﴿whoever turns back in repentance﴾. If by guidance is meant the continuous guidance, the matter is clear, since it is evident that faith leads to it. If by guidance is meant its initial bestowal, then by ﴿those who believe﴾ is meant those whose affair has come to faith, as they said regarding ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾, meaning those who arrive at God-fearing. Otherwise, faith does not lead to guidance itself. It is also permissible that it be an *'atf bayan* (explicative apposition, i.e. an appositive clarifying what precedes) to that, or be in the accusative by way of praise, or be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are those who believe.

﴿And their hearts find rest﴾, i.e. become settled and tranquil, ﴿in the remembrance of God﴾, i.e. in His inimitable speech, to which falsehood does not come from before it or from behind it. This is what is related from Muqatil. The application of the term "remembrance" to this is common in the Qur'an, and from it is His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And this is a blessed remembrance﴾ and ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the remembrance, and indeed, We are its guardians﴾.

The cause of the tranquility of their hearts through this is their knowledge that there is no sign greater than it, and for this reason they do not demand the signs that others demand. The shift to the present-tense form serves to convey the continuity of the tranquility and its renewal in accordance with the renewal of what is sent down of the remembrance.

﴿Unquestionably, by the remembrance of God﴾ alone ﴿hearts find rest﴾. (28) That is, in God alone, not in other matters of worldly things toward which souls incline. If all the miracles are intended, then the restriction (*qasr*) is in terms of the fact that they, with respect to one who has not witnessed them, do not match the Glorious Qur'an in conveying tranquility, for it is a miracle remaining until the Day of Resurrection, which everyone witnesses, and by which all hearts find rest. In it there is an indication that the disbelievers have no hearts, and their hearts are hollow, since they did not find rest in it and did not count it a sign, though it is the most manifest and most dazzling of signs.

It has been said that there is an omitted genitive (*mudaf muqaddar*) in the speech, meaning: so that their hearts may find rest through the remembrance of His mercy and forgiveness, after anxiety and agitation from fear of Him, as in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of God﴾. This is suitable according to what is in *al-Kashf*, regarding turning in repentance to Him, the Exalted, and the verbal noun (*masdar*) in that case is in construct with the agent.

It has been said that by the remembrance of God is meant His signs, glorified be He, which indicate His oneness, exalted and majestic be He, and the tranquility is from the anxiety of doubt and hesitation. This is suitable to the mention of disbelief and its occurrence in opposition to it.

It has been said that by His remembrance is meant intimacy with Him and devotion to Him, glorified be He. Then by guidance is meant its continuance and persistence. It has been said: this is also suitable to the newness of disbelief, because when God the Exalted alone is mentioned, the hearts of the disbelievers recoil. The verbal noun in both opinions is in construct with the object. The first opinion is more harmonious with the structure of the verse, especially in view of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾, where the verbal noun carries the sense of the passive participle.

Among the strange things is what is transmitted in the *Tafsir* of al-Khazin, that this refers to swearing by God, because when a believer is sworn to by God, his heart is calmed. Something similar is narrated by Abu al-Shaykh from al-Suddi. Imposing that meaning here is not suitable to the context. As for what is narrated from Anas, that (ﷺ) said to his companions when this verse was revealed: "Do you know what its meaning is?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "Whoever loves God and His Messenger and loves my companions." Similar to it is what is narrated from Ali, may God honor his face, that when it was revealed, (ﷺ) said: "That is whoever loves God and His Messenger, and loves my family, truthfully and not falsely, [p. 150] and loves the believers, present and absent." The intent of this is not to explain the meaning of the remembrance of God, but to state that those described by what is mentioned are those whom God and His Messenger (ﷺ) love, etc. And that is so, since the separation between these attributes can hardly be realized. So let this be considered. There is no contradiction between this verse, on all its aspects, and His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿When God is mentioned, their hearts tremble﴾, because the meaning there is that they tremble from awe of Him, the Exalted, and from magnifying Him, may His majesty be exalted.

The Imam mentioned, in explaining the tranquility of the heart through His remembrance, several aspects. He said: Existent things are of three kinds: an influencer that is not influenced; an influenced thing that does not influence; and an existent that both influences and is influenced. The first is God, the Exalted. The second is the body, for it has no property except acceptance of contrary effects and differing attributes. The third is the spiritual existents, for when they turn toward the divine presence, they become receptive to the effects that overflow upon them from it, and when they turn toward the bodily realm's signs, they long to act upon them, because the world of spirits governs the world of bodies. When this is known, the heart, whenever it turns to contemplating the world of bodies, experiences agitation, unease, and strong inclination to dominate it and act upon it. But when it turns to contemplating the divine presence, and the eternal lights are realized in it, there it remains still and tranquil. Also, the heart, whenever it reaches something, seeks to move from it to something else higher than it, because there is no happiness in the world of bodies except that above it there is another rank. But when it attains felicity through divine knowledge and holy lights, it is firm and settles, and it is never able to move from that, because there is no higher and more perfect degree of happiness beyond it. Also, when a single particle of the elixir falls upon a copper body, it turns into gold that endures through the passage of ages and is patient under the melting caused by fire. So the elixir of God's light, when it falls into the heart, is more deserving of turning it into a pure, enduring, luminous substance that does not accept change or alteration. For these aspects He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Unquestionably, by the remembrance of God hearts find rest﴾. End of quotation.

The more appropriate view is to say that the cause of tranquility is a light which God, the Exalted, pours forth into the hearts of the believers through their remembrance of Him, so that the anxiety, loneliness, and the like within them is dispelled. There is room for debate concerning what he mentioned, and what resembles that will come, God willing, in the chapter on *ishara* (allusive interpretation).

[p. 151]

﴿Those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the hearts," meaning: the hearts of those who believed. The more evident view is that it is a substitute of the whole (badal al-kull), because the hearts mentioned first are the hearts of the believers who find rest. The same applies if "heart" is generalized, in the sense that the hearts of these noble people are all hearts, since the disbelievers' hearts are hollow (hawa'). As for taking it as a substitute of a part (badal al-ba'd) so that "heart" is generalized without the aforementioned consideration, and deriving this meaning from the substitute, that is far-fetched. As for its possibility as a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), although al-Tibi approved of it, it is rejected. Or it may be a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is the supplicatory clause according to interpretation, namely His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Ṭūbā lahum﴾ (blessedness is for them), meaning it is said to them thus. Or there is no need for interpretation, and the clause is informative. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, or it is put in the accusative by way of praise, so ﴿Ṭūbā lahum﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara), and the governing elements in it are the two verbs.

Some of the careful scholars (al-mudaqqiqīn) said: Perhaps the more probable view is another one, namely that the sentence is complete at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿whoever turns back (to Him)﴾. Then it is said: ﴿those who believed and whose hearts find rest﴾, in contrast to ﴿and those who disbelieved say: "Why has not a sign been sent down…"﴾. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Surely by the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾ is a parenthetical clause (jumla i'tiraḍiyya), which conveys: how could their hearts not find rest in Him, and there is no rest for the heart in other than Him. His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿those who believed﴾ is a substitute for the first, and in it is an indication that the remembrance of God, exalted is He, is the best of righteous deeds, indeed it encompasses all of them. And ﴿Ṭūbā lahum﴾ is the predicate of the first. Thus there is a complete contrast between the two pairs: ﴿those who disbelieved say﴾ and ﴿those who believed and whose hearts find rest﴾, and between the two parts of the concluding statement (tadhyīl): ﴿He leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back﴾.

Among the people is one who claimed that the first relative pronoun is a subject and the second relative pronoun is its predicate, and ﴿Surely by the remembrance of God﴾ is a parenthetical statement, and ﴿Ṭūbā lahum﴾ is a supplication. And it is as you see. As for ﴿Ṭūbā﴾, it has been said that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) from ṭāba, like Bushrā and Zulfā, and the waw is changed from a yā', like mūsir and mūqin. Makūzat al-A'rābī read it as ﴿Ṭībā﴾ to keep the yā' intact. Abū al-Ḥasan al-Hanā'ī said: it is the plural of ṭayyiba, as they said for kayyisa, "kūsā." Abū Ḥayyān objected to this, saying that fu'lā is not among the patterns of plurals, so perhaps he meant that it is a collective noun (ism jam').

According to the first view, there are various expressions regarding the intended meaning. Ibn Jarīr and others transmitted from Ibn 'Abbās that the meaning is joy and coolness of the eye for them. From al-Ḍaḥḥāk: felicity (ghibṭa) for them. From Qatāda: a good end (ḥusnā) for them. In another narration from him: they have attained good. From al-Nakha'ī: much good for them. In another narration from him: honour for them. From Sumayṭ ibn 'Ajlān: the continuance of good for them. All of this returns to the meaning of a good life for them. In a narration from Ibn 'Abbās and Ibn Jubayr, Ṭūbā is a name for Paradise in Abyssinian, and it has been said in Hindi. Al-Qurṭubī said: the correct view is that it is a proper name for a tree in Paradise. Aḥmad, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ṭabarānī, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba'th wa al-Nushūr transmitted, and al-Suhaylī and others authenticated, from 'Utba ibn 'Abd, who said: "A Bedouin came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: O Messenger of God, is there fruit in Paradise? He said: Yes, in it is a tree called Ṭūbā, which is the girdle of Firdaws. He said: What tree of our land does it resemble? He said: It does not resemble any tree of your land, but you have come to Syria. He said: No. He said: Then it resembles a tree in Syria called the jawza, which grows on a single trunk, then its top spreads out. He said: How great is its root? He said: If you were to travel with a young camel of your family's herd, you would not go around its root until its neck breaks from old age. He said: Does it have grapes? He said: Yes. He said: How large is its cluster? He said: A month's journey for the white-spotted crow."

The reports stating explicitly that it is a tree in Paradise are very widespread. In that case there is no dispute about the permissibility of beginning a sentence with it even though it is indefinite (nakira). What justifies beginning with it is what Sībawayh held, namely that it is treated in the manner of a supplication, like their saying: "Peace be upon you." But Ibn Mālik held that it is obligatorily in the nominative by way of the subject. This was refuted by the fact that 'Īsā al-Thaqafī read ﴿wa-ḥusna ma'āb﴾ (and a good return) in the accusative. Tha'lab explained this as being coordinated with Ṭūbā, and that it is in the accusative position, and it is, in his view, a verbal noun governed by a verb (ma'mūl li-miqdār), meaning "it was good," and the lām is for clarification, as in "suqyā lahu." Some held that it means: "made Ṭūbā for them." And the author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: The estimated sense is "O Ṭūbā for them, and O the good return," so ḥusn is coordinated with the vocative noun, and it is governed by a pronoun, and the lām is inserted, as in the poet's words:

"O misery for ignorance, the harm of peoples."

For this reason the tanwīn was dropped from bu's. It is as if it were said: "O their blessedness, and O the goodness of their return," meaning: how good they are and how good their return is, just as you say: "O how good is it, a night," meaning: how good it is as a night. There is no hiding the artificiality in this. Al-Safāqisī answered Ibn Mālik by saying that it is permissible to put ḥusn in the accusative by means of an omitted verb, meaning: "and He granted them a good return," but this is far-fetched.

It was also read as ﴿ḥusnu ma'āb﴾ with a fatḥa on the nūn and a ḍamma on the mīm of ma'āb, and this was explained as: ḥusn is a past-tense verb, originally ḥasuna, with the ḍamma of the sīn transferred to the ḥā'. Its like is permissible in a verb when it is used for praise or blame, as they said: "ḥusna dhā."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 30:

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that great and mighty sending, accompanied by the dazzling miracle. It is also possible that it means like the sending of the messengers before you, ﴿We have sent you to a community﴾. In that case, his sending (ﷺ) is compared to the sending of those before him, even though they were not mentioned, because of the indication in His words, exalted is He, ﴿already there have passed before it communities﴾, i.e., have gone by, ﴿many﴾, to whom messengers were sent, upon them be peace. This was narrated from al-Hasan. It was also said that the kaf (ك, "thus") is connected to the meaning in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Say: Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills﴾ ... etc., meaning: just as We executed that, We have sent you.

[Page 152]

Something similar was transmitted from al-Hawfi. Ibn Atiyya said: "What appears is that the meaning is: just as We have made it the practice with the earlier communities that We cause to go astray and guide through revelation, not through the demanded signs, so too We did in this community, and We sent you to them with revelation, not with the demanded signs. So We cause whom We will to go astray, and We guide whoever turns back in repentance." Abu al-Baqa' said: "The estimated meaning is: the matter is thus. And the best of what we have mentioned, and what was transmitted from al-Hasan, is the most fitting."

The fi (في, "in") is in the sense of ila (إلى, "to"), as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and they put their hands into their mouths﴾. It was also said that it is in its literal sense, and that in it is an indication that he is one of them and raised among them. It cannot be in the sense of ila, because there is no need to clarify to whom he was sent. In this there is clear scrutiny. It is connected to the verb mentioned.

The words of al-Zamakhshari in interpreting the verse: "that is, We have sent a sending that has dignity and superiority over other sendings. Then he explained how He sent him by His words: ﴿to a community﴾ already there have passed before it communities, i.e., We have sent you to a community that was preceded by many communities. So it is the last of the communities, and you are the Seal of the Prophets." He did not mean that it is not connected to what was mentioned; rather he meant that the indefinite demonstrative, since what follows it is an exalting, its clarification is by the complement of that verb, so that the indefiniteness is removed. It is also possible that he intended this, so that one estimates: "We have sent you a second time," and his words "that is, We have sent you to a community" serve as a clarification of the omitted element, not as an explanation of the total meaning of the verse. This is what al-Allama al-Tibi preferred. Connection to what was mentioned is the apparent meaning. The clause ﴿already there have passed﴾ ... etc. is in the position of a qualifier for ﴿community﴾. The benefit of describing it with this, it was said, is what al-Zamakhshari indicated.

It was objected that the passing of many communities before it does not necessarily entail that there is no community to which he is sent afterward, such that it would follow that he (ﷺ) is the Seal of the Prophets, upon them be peace. Al-Shihab examined this, saying that what is meant by his sending (ﷺ) being wondrous is that his message is greater than every message, so it encompasses everything that is needed; thus it follows that there is no abrogation (naskh), since abrogation only occurs for completion, and the perfect is in the utmost perfection, not in need of completion, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾. End of quote. By my life, the objection is strong and the examination is extremely weak, since it does not follow from his sending (ﷺ) being wondrous what he claimed. And even if we grant that, it does not follow from it either that he (ﷺ) is the Seal, since his being sent confirms his perfect religion, just as many of the prophets of the Children of Israel were sent to confirm the religion of Moses, upon him be peace. This does not contradict what has been mentioned about the comprehensiveness of his message (ﷺ), nor the necessary absence of abrogation because of it, as is not hidden. Perhaps for this reason some preferred what was transmitted from al-Hasan, and said, drawing attention to the benefit of the description: that is, like the sending of the messengers before you, We have sent you to communities preceded by communities to whom messengers were sent, so your being sent to them is not novel. ﴿So that you may recite﴾, i.e., read, ﴿to them that which We have revealed to you﴾, i.e., the great Book. This description is hinted at by the mention of the described noun without being followed by a describing adjective, by attributing the verb in its clause to the pronoun of greatness, and similarly by the arrival at the exalted addressee, as indicated by what preceded it, as you have heard first. And the placing of the prepositional phrase before the object is of the type of ambiguity followed by clarification, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾. In this is what is not hidden of the soul's eagerness for what is to come and its fine acceptance of it when it arrives. The plural pronoun refers to the community according to its meaning, as the singular pronoun in ﴿passed﴾ was treated according to its wording.

﴿And they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, i.e., in the One of abundant mercy, whose blessing encompasses them and whose mercy has encompassed everything. Yet they did not thank His blessings, glorified is He, especially what He bestowed upon them by sending you to them and sending down the Qur'an, which is the source of religious and worldly benefits for them. Rather, they met His mercy and blessings with disbelief, while reason requires the opposite. The apparent expectation would have been "We" (بنا), but it turned to the explicit noun, and this name, which indicates intensity in mercy, was chosen to point out that the sending arises from it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾. The plural pronoun also refers to the community. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (حال) from the subject of (أرسلنا, "We have sent"), not from the pronoun in ﴿upon them﴾, since the sending is not for recitation to them while they are in disbelief. Some permitted that, saying that recitation to them in the state of disbelief is so that they may stand before its miraculous nature and believe in it, because of their knowledge of the varieties of eloquence. And this does not contradict his reciting it to them after their Islam. It was also permitted that the clause be a new independent sentence, with the pronoun as you have understood. It was said that the pronoun refers to those who said ﴿Why has not a sign been sent down to him from his Lord?﴾. It was also said that it refers to ﴿community﴾ and to ﴿communities﴾, and that in the verse there is consolation for him (ﷺ).

[Page 153]

From Qatada, Ibn Juraij, and Muqatil it is narrated that the verse was revealed concerning the polytheists of Mecca when they saw the treaty document on the day of al-Hudaybiyya, in which Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, had written "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Suhayl ibn Amr said: "We do not know the Merciful except Musaylima." It was also said: Abu Jahl heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "O Allah, O Merciful," and said: "Muhammad forbids us from worshipping the gods, yet he calls upon two gods," so the verse was revealed. From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that when it was said to the disbelievers of Quraysh: ﴿Prostrate to the Most Merciful,﴾ they said: ﴿And what is the Most Merciful?﴾ and the verse was revealed. All of that is weak, because it is not appropriate, since it requires that they disbelieve in this name and its application to Him, glorified and exalted is He. The apparent meaning is that their disbelief is in its referent, ﴿Say﴾ when they disbelieved in Him, glorified is He, and did not affirm His unity. ﴿He﴾, i.e., the Most Merciful whom you have disbelieved in, ﴿is my Lord﴾, my Creator, the one who manages my affairs, and who brings me to the stations of perfection. The placing of this before His words, exalted is He, ﴿There is no god but He﴾, i.e., there is none deserving of worship except Him, is an indication that the entitlement to worship is linked to lordship. The clause is included within the scope of the saying, and according to some it is a predicate after a predicate. Another group said: after He, exalted is He, censured the disbelievers for their state, which is the reverse of what reason requires, He commanded His Prophet, upon him be peace, to remind them of his own particular matter and his duty of thankfulness, and the ultimate purpose of the command is rebuke for them. So He said: ﴿Say: He is my Lord, who sent me to you and strengthened me with what He strengthened me, and I have no lord other than Him.﴾ ﴿Upon Him﴾, not upon anyone besides Him, ﴿I have relied﴾ in all my affairs, especially in seeking victory over you. ﴿And to Him alone﴾ ﴿is the return﴾. (30) i.e., my return, so that He will reward me for my perseverance and striving against you. His words, glorified is He, ﴿There is no god but He﴾, are an interjected clause (اعتراض), by which the exclusivity of reliance upon Him, glorified is He, and the committing of affairs to Him, both in this world and the next, is emphasized. Similar to it is His words, exalted is He: ﴿Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord; there is no god but He, and turn away from the polytheists.﴾ End of quote.

The author of al-Kashf (al-Tibi) went to the view that it is an interjected clause, and he interpreted the words of al-Kashshaf accordingly, where after ﴿He is my Lord﴾ he mentioned "the One exalted above partners," then said: he made it the benefit of the interjected clause "there is no god but He," i.e., this one of abundant mercy, and there is no god but He. So He is of utmost retribution, just as He is of utmost mercy, who shows mercy to me and takes vengeance for me upon you. It is also a preparation for His words: ﴿Upon Him I have relied.﴾ It was not made a predicate after a predicate, because the intent is not to inform that He, exalted is He, is singular in divinity; rather the intent is that the one singularly possessing it is my Lord, and this is conveyed by the interjected clause. As for the understanding from his words that it is a circumstantial clause, and therefore it is treated as a qualifier, that is not so, unless it is made a confirmatory circumstantial clause, and then the interjected clause does not differ much from it, but the first is fuller in benefit. End of quote. There is no hiding what is obscure in directing al-Kashshaf's words in this way, and what is said about the intent being that the one singularly possessing divinity is my Lord, rather than informing that He, exalted is He, is singular in it, let it be considered. Perhaps its basis is that what he affirmed is more fitting to the purpose that his words indicate he considered as the context of the verse, and in it is what is not hidden of exaggeration in describing Him, exalted is He, with unity.

Indeed, it was said that there is a rationale for the view of interjection, and that in that case it is not far-fetched to say: after He, exalted is He, mentioned His sending him (ﷺ) to them, and that their state is that they disbelieve in the One of abundant mercy and do not meet His mercy with gratitude so as to believe in Him and affirm His unity, He commanded him to inform them that his reliance and trust are specifically upon that One of abundant mercy, and that he returns to Him in all his affairs. This is an allusion that their persistence in disbelief does not harm him at all, that he, upon him be peace, has a praiseworthy end, and that He, glorified is He, will give him victory over them. In that is a rebuke of their opinion in persisting in disbelief and a rousing of them to follow him, which is nothing except that He, mighty is His affair, first commanded him to say: ﴿He is my Lord﴾ as a preparation for that, and the interjected clause ﴿there is no god but He﴾ was introduced for emphasis. What the soul inclines to after reflection and consideration of the style is the view of interjection. Then it is not hidden that the clauses ﴿And to Him is the return﴾ upon the reading ﴿to Him is my return in all my affairs﴾ are contrary to the apparent meaning, and that on that reading it would be like a confirmation of what precedes it. Shaykh al-Islam said in his tafsir: i.e., to Him is my repentance, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾. He (ﷺ) was commanded with that to make clear the excellence of repentance, its measure with Allah, exalted is He, and that it is an attribute of the prophets, and to urge the disbelievers to return from what they are upon in the most eloquent and subtle manner. For he (ﷺ), since he was commanded with it, while being free of any trace of committing what necessitates it of sin, however small, their repentance while they are immersed in kinds of disbelief and sins is something that is absolutely necessary. End of quote. In this is that this is only suitable to arouse abandoning sin in the most eloquent and subtle manner if the speech were addressed to other than the disbelievers, who suppose that they are doing good. Perhaps this is evident to the fair-minded. Al-Allama al-Baydawi said concerning it: i.e., to Him is my return and your return. It seems he also intended: "so He will show me mercy and take vengeance upon you." And vengeance from the Most Merciful is more severe, as it is said: "I seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He, from the anger of the forbearing one."

It was criticized that this only holds if the omitted antecedent of the pronoun is the first-person pronoun together with others, i.e., "our return," since then it would be "my return and your return" in detail. Yet no one would say that along with his saying with the kasra on the ba' (مَتَابِ), since that requires that the omitted element be the yā' (ي). Moreover, that pronoun does not suit what precedes it. Perhaps al-Allama considered that there is an ellipsis (اكتفاء) in the verse, as it has been said: i.e., "my return and your return," or that the speech implies it by necessary inference (التزام). This is better, as has been said, so consider it carefully.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 31 (part 1 of 2)]

﴿And if there had been a Qur'an﴾, i.e., a Qur'an of any kind, and what is meant is its linguistic sense. The noun of *anna* (its subject) is ﴿by which the mountains were set in motion﴾, and the predicate is His words, exalted be His majesty: ﴿by which the mountains were set in motion﴾. The response to *law* (the conditional particle "if") is omitted because the context leads to it, as in his saying:

*So I swear, if any messenger had come to us other than you, but we found no way to repel you.*

The purpose is either to show the great rank of the Noble Qur'an and the corruption of the opinion of the disbelievers, in that they did not appreciate its worth, did not count it among the signs, and proposed other things instead; or to show the extent of their obstinacy and defiance and their persistence in error and corruption. The meaning according to the first view is: if a book had been such that the mountains were set in motion by its being sent down or by its recitation, and were shaken from their places, as was done to the mount (*al-Tur*) for Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿or the earth was split asunder by it﴾, i.e., it was cleft and made into rivers and springs, as was done with the stone when Musa, peace be upon him, struck it with his staff; or it was made into fragments that split apart; ﴿or the dead were spoken to by it﴾, i.e., someone spoke to the dead by it, by bringing them to life through its recitation so that they then spoke with him, as the raising of the dead happened for Isa, peace be upon him. Then ﴿that would have been this Qur'an﴾, because it is the supreme extreme in containing the wonders of the traces of God's power, exalted be He, and His awe-inspiring majesty, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of God﴾. This was said by some of the verifiers (*al-muhaqqiqun*). It was also said, as a rationale, that it is the supreme extreme in inimitability (*i'jaz*) and the ultimate in admonition and warning.

This was objected to: there is no place for inimitability in these effects, and admonition and warning are specific to the rational; moreover, there is no connection between that and speaking to the dead, and taking into account the flow of intellects to them undermines the intended exaggeration. It was examined: what was mentioned first, namely the greater containment of the wonders of the traces of God's power, is a matter that returns to awe, and awe too is something that does not entail speaking to the dead; rather, it may even prevent that, for since it requires the shaking of mountains and the splitting of the earth, then all the more it requires the death of the living, not the reviving of the dead after which speaking takes place, which is more fitting. Yet there is something to consider in this.

The *ba'* (preposition "by") in the three places indicates causation, and it was permitted for the third of them to be a relative clause (*sila*) of what is after it, and the fronting of the prepositional phrase over the noun in it is for the purpose of creating suspense, and then the explanation for the sake of further affirmation, as was mentioned more than once before.

The *aw* ("or") in the two places is for preventing the absence of all options, not for combining them. The masculine form in ﴿was spoken to﴾ is for giving precedence to the masculine among the dead over others. And although the thing being proposed is connected merely to the appearance of such wondrous deeds at the hand of the Prophet ﷺ, and not to their appearance through the Qur'an, nevertheless, since that was based on their supposition that it contains no marvels, the appearance of such marvels was attached to it, to exaggerate its containing them, and that it is worthy of being the source of every marvel, and to expose the feebleness of their opinion regarding its exalted status. It is as if it were said: if the appearance of the likes of what they proposed were among the requirements of wisdom, then its place of manifestation would be this Qur'an, which they did not count as a sign. In this there is an exaltation of its noble status and a description of them with feebleness of intellect, which is not hidden. So said some of the eminent scholars, and it is very fine.

According to the second view: if a Qur'an had been such that these wondrous deeds were performed upon it, they would still not have believed in it, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels and the dead had spoken to them﴾ and so on. According to what al-Shihab (i.e., al-Alusi) favored, the statement under both interpretations is a real (*haqiqa*) statement by way of supposition, as in his saying:

*Had any hoofed creature flown before her, she would have flown, but none did.*

He considered it, under the first interpretation, to be a figurative expression (*tamthil*) like the verse mentioned there, but he said this has no basis. Al-Zamakhshari's use of it as an illustration is to show that the Qur'an entails the utmost fear. The practice of many of the verifiers clearly favors the first interpretation.

In *al-Kashf*: If you reflect on this noble surah with due reflection, you will find that its discourse is built upon the truth of the glorious Book and its containing what is good for both abodes, and that the fortunate, wholly fortunate, is one who holds fast to its rope, and the wretched, wholly wretched, is one who turns away from it toward his own desire. For He said, first: ﴿And that which was sent down to you from your Lord is the truth﴾. Then He marvelled at their denial of that, saying, glorified be He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why has no sign been sent down to him?"﴾. Then He said: ﴿To Him is the call of truth﴾, thereby affirming its truth by argument. Then He said, exalted be He: ﴿He sends down water from the sky﴾, which is a parable for the truth that is the Qur'an and for those who benefit from it, according to what the verifiers have explained. Then God, exalted be He, stated the result of all of that with clear proof in His saying, glorified be He: ﴿Is then one who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾. Then He, exalted be His majesty, repeated His words ﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾, indicating their denial at the very first coming to them and after the firmness of their knowledge of its truth; so they persist in denial. Then He returned to explaining the truth in what we are dealing with, and exaggerated with an exaggeration beyond which there is no equal, whether it is taken as within the scope of the saying or taken as a fresh utterance from Him, exalted be He, as a concluding statement (*tadhyil*). The latter is more eloquent, so that it is intended in itself for the stated benefit, and affirms the entirety of what His words ﴿Thus We have sent you﴾ indicated: the magnification of the Messenger, upon whom be prayer and peace, and what was sent down to him, and the intensity of their denial and obstinacy, in addition to the fact that nothing remained but reliance upon God and patience in striving against you, since there is nothing beyond this Qur'an that I could bring so that you might submit.

Then He glorified it and reproached them for their obstinacy with His words, exalted be He: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic judgment﴾. And He confirmed the truth of the Book concerning the one upon whom it was sent down at the end of the surah with His words, exalted be His majesty: ﴿Sufficient is God as a witness﴾, up to His words, glorified be He: ﴿and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾, as a reminder that, despite the clarity of its matter in conveying the gnostic truths and the faith-based dispositions, the true reality of what is in it is known only by the One who alone has it and by whose sending it down, blessed and exalted be He.

As for the occasion of revelation, you will know it shortly, God willing, and it supports the second view, though the apparent meaning accords with the first. We indicated earlier that the verse under the first view is connected to His words, exalted be He: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why has no sign been sent down to him?"﴾, and under the second view it is connected to His words, glorified be He: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, as an explanation of their firmness in disbelief and their denial of the signs and of the one who brought them, not of that (the Qur'an), since the target is distant without necessity.

[p. 156]

His words, exalted be He: ﴿Rather, to God belongs the entire affair﴾, i.e., to Him belongs the affair upon which the sphere of existences revolves, in existence and non-existence; He does what He wills and decrees what He desires, according to what the profound wisdoms require. It was said: this is a turning away (*idrab*) from what the conditional sentence entails of the sense of negation, not according to its explicit wording but in terms of its implication and what it leads to. That is: if a Qur'an had been made to undergo what was mentioned, that would have been this Qur'an; but God, glorified be He, did not do so, rather He did what is the current state of affairs, because the whole matter belongs to Him alone. Thus the turning away is not directed at the matter belonging to God, exalted be He, but at what that does not lead to, namely that the state of affairs would be as it is according to what wisdom requires.

It was also said: the upshot of the turning away is that the setting in motion of the mountains is not with the Qur'an together with what was mentioned, but would come about by something else that God, exalted be He, desires, since the whole affair belongs to Him, glorified be He. Some claimed that the better reading is a conjunction with an implied element, i.e., "You have no share in the affair at all; rather, the whole affair belongs to God."

As for His words, glorified be He: ﴿Have not those who believe despaired?﴾, the meaning is: have they not known? It is, as al-Qasim ibn Ma'n said, the dialect of Hawazin. Ibn al-Kalbi said it is the dialect of a tribe of al-Nakha'. They cited as evidence the verse of Suhaym ibn Wuthayl al-Rabahi:

*I say to them at the mountain pass when they took me captive: did you not know that I am the son of the knight Zahdam?*

And the verse of Rabah ibn 'Adi:

*Did the peoples not know that I am his son, even though I am far from the land of my clan?*

Thus the denial of al-Farra' of this and his claim that no one from the Arabs was heard saying "I despaired" in the sense of "I knew" is not in its proper place, and the one who has memorized it is evidence against the one who has not. The apparent view is that the use of *al-ya's* (despair) in this sense is literal. It was also said that it is figurative, since it implicitly contains knowledge, for one who despairs of something knows that it will not happen. It was objected that despair in this case requires attaining knowledge of non-existence, whereas it is used for knowledge of existence. It was answered that since it implies knowledge of non-existence, it implies knowledge in general, and so it is used for it.

What supports the intention of knowledge here is the recitation of 'Ali, may God ennoble his face, and Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may God be pleased with them, and 'Ikrimah, and Ibn Abi Mulaykah, and al-Jahdari, and Abu Yazid al-Madani, and a group: ﴿Have not those who believe clarified (*yatabayyan*)?﴾, from *tabayyantu kadha*, meaning "I knew such-and-such." This recitation (*qira'ah*) is traced back to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and it does not contradict the written text, since they wrote *yay'as* without the shape of the hamza. As for the statement of one who said: "The scribe wrote it while drowsy, and he levelled the teeth of the *sin*," this is the word of a heretic, a godless apostate, according to what is in *al-Bahr*. Accordingly, the narration of this as found in *al-Durr al-Manthur* from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, is not authentic. Some claimed that it is a recitation of tafsir (explanatory reading), but this is not so.

The *fa'* ("then") is for conjunction with an implied element, i.e., "they were heedless of the fact that the whole affair belongs to God, exalted be He, so they did not know." ﴿That, had God willed, He would have guided all of mankind﴾: here *anna* is lightened (*mukhaffafa*), with its noun being the dummy pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), and the conditional clause (*al-jumla al-imtina'iyya*) is its predicate, and *anna* and what follows it fill the position of the two objects of the verb "to know." The meaning is: by the manifestation of the likes of those great signs, He would have guided all people.

The denial in this case is directed at all of the conjoined elements together, or the meaning is: "Have they known that the whole affair belongs to God, exalted be He, yet not known what that knowledge requires of what was mentioned?" In that case it is directed at the sequence of the conjoined element after the element it is conjoined to, i.e., the failure of the second knowledge to follow from the first.

Whichever it is, the denial is a denial of occurrence, not of the thing that occurred, and the basis of the denial is not merely their ignorance of the content of the conditional sentence, but their ignorance of the non-occurrence of its antecedent. It is as if it were said: "Have they not known that God, exalted be He, had He willed their guidance, would have guided them, and that He, glorified be He, did not will that? And that is because of what was related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, that the disbelievers..."

[p. 157]

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 31 (part 2 of 2):

When they asked for signs, the believers wished that God Most High would make them manifest, so that they would all gather together upon faith. This is according to the first interpretation. As for the second interpretation, the turning away (idrab) is directed at what was previously mentioned of their demands, together with their obstinacy as has been explained. The meaning is: "So that is not for them; rather, the command belongs entirely to God Most High. If He wills, He brings what they have proposed; and if He, glorified is He, wills, He does not bring it, according to what His dazzling wisdom requires, without anyone having any right or demand upon Him, majestic is His majesty."

The word yaʼs (despair) is in the sense of qunut (despondency), as is commonly used in its meaning. That is: "Have those who believed not known their present state, and so did they not despair of their faith, to the point that they wished for their proposed signs to appear?" So the rebuke is directed at the two coordinated clauses. Or: "Have they known this, and so they did not despair of their faith?" In this case it is directed at the occurrence of the second coordinated element after the first, i.e., at the failure of despondency to follow the mentioned knowledge. The rebuke under these two interpretations is a rebuke of what actually occurs, not of the occurrence itself, for their not despairing of that is something that cannot be averted.

The words of the Most High, ﴿that if God willed﴾ to the end, are the object of a deleted verb of knowing (ʿalimā), which stands as an object of purpose. That is: "Have they not despaired of the faith of the disbelievers, knowing that if God willed He would have guided all people together, and that He did not will that?" It may also be said that the knowing is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), i.e., "knowing this." Tadmin (the sense of one verb implied in another) was not considered because it is remote.

It is also permissible that it be connected to "believed," with the preposition (bi) understood, i.e., "Have those who believed and affirmed not despaired, that if God willed He would have guided all people together," in the sense of "Have these believers not despaired of the faith of these disbelievers, by the content of this conditional statement and by its non-realisation, which is understood from their obstinacy, as the word (law) indicates?" Thus the described attribute is among the motives for denying their despair. By what we have indicated, the objection is resolved that was raised: that the connection of faith to the content of the conditional statement, and singling it out for mention, implies that this has a bearing on despair of faith, whereas the matter is the reverse, because God's power to guide all people requires hope in their faith, not despair of it. This is because knowledge of the non-realisation of the content is also considered.

Some have answered this objection: the reason for singling out faith in this way is that the faith of these obstinate disbelievers is, as it were, impossible, being tied to what cannot be, since it depends on God Most High's will to guide all people, and that does not happen by agreement. This is in the sense of what has been indicated.

Abu Hayyan mentioned another possibility regarding the verse: that the speech is complete at His words, glorified is He, ﴿Have not those who believed despaired﴾, and this is an affirmation, i.e., "The believers have indeed despaired of the faith of these stubborn ones." And ﴿that if He wills﴾ ... etc. is the answer to an implied oath, i.e., "I swear, if God willed, He would have guided all people together." The existence of an (an) with (law) indicates an implied oath, as in his saying:

"By God, that if I were free, and you were neither free nor a freedman..."

And in his saying:

"So I swear that if we met, and you, there would be for us a day of darkened evil."

Sibawayh mentioned that (an) comes after an oath, and Ibn ʿUṣfur considered it a link between the oath and the sentence sworn upon. End of quotation. In this there is much strain that is not hidden.

Some people have made the turning away absolutely independent of what the particle (law) contains of the meaning of negation, in the sense of: "Rather, God Most High is able to bring what they have proposed, but His will has not been directed to that, because He, glorified is He, knows that their obstinacy does not yield to Him." It is not hidden that this is evident under the second interpretation. As for the first interpretation, it has been said: the intention to magnify the status of the Qur'an does not conflict with the rejection of the two proposals. The side of rejection is supported by what Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from al-Sha'bi, who said: "The Quraysh said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: 'If you are a prophet as you claim, then move these two mountains of Mecca, Akhshabayha, away for a distance of four or five days, for it is narrow, so that we may plant and graze in it. And raise for us our fathers from the dead so that they may speak to us and inform us that you are a prophet. Or carry us to Syria, or to Yemen, or to al-Hira, so that we may go and come in a single night, as you claimed you did.' Then this verse was revealed."

And Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas that they said: "Make the mountains move by the Qur'an, cut the earth by the Qur'an, bring forth by it our dead." Then it was revealed. According to this there is no need for an apology regarding the attribution of the aforementioned acts to the Qur'an, as was needed in what preceded. According to the report of al-Sha'bi, the cutting of the earth is intended as crossing it by travel. The interpretation we presented first is supported by what Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il and others transmitted from the hadith of al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, that: "When the verse ﴿And warn your nearest kinsfolk﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of God ﷺ shouted upon Abu Qubays: 'O family of ʿAbd Manaf, I am a warner!' Then the Quraysh came to him, peace be upon him, and he warned them and admonished them. They said: 'You claim that you are a prophet to whom revelation comes, and that Sulayman had the wind and the mountains subjected to him, and that Musa had the sea subjected to him, and that ʿIsa used to revive the dead. So call upon God Most High to move these mountains away from us and to make the earth flow with rivers for us, so that we may make fields, plant and eat. And if not, call upon God Most High to revive our dead for us, so that we may speak with them and they may speak with us. And if not, call upon God Most High to make this rock beneath you gold, so that we may cut from it and be spared the journey of winter and summer, for you claim that you are like them.' The report continues: and in it: then there was revealed ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them﴾ up to the completion of three verses, and there was revealed ﴿And if a Qur'an had been such that the mountains were moved by it...﴾ this verse."

And from al-Farra' that the answer to (law) is placed first, and it is His words, Most High: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, and what is between them is a parenthetical clause. This is based, as has been said, on the permissibility of placing the answer of the conditional before it, and some grammarians hold this. It is not hidden that the wording is remote from this, because that clause is a nominal sentence joined with a waw; and for this reason al-Samin indicated that his meaning is that this clause is the evidence of the answer, and the estimate is: "And if a Qur'an had been such that such and such were done to it, they would have disbelieved in the Most Merciful." And you know that there is no difference between this and the estimate "they would not have believed" in meaning. It is also permissible to make (law) concessive (wasliyya) with no answer for it, and the clause is circumstantial, or conjoined to an implied element.

﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by what they have done﴾ — from the people of Mecca, according to what is related from Muqatil — ﴿a calamity for what they did﴾, i.e., because of what they did of disbelief and persistence in it. Its vagueness is either for the purpose of magnifying it or of condemning it. This is an explicit statement of what the construction of the judgment upon the relative clause, with the reason of the relative clause, implies, together with what the form of the verb "they did" carries of the indication of their firm establishment in that. ﴿A calamity (qari'a)﴾ is from qar' (striking), whose origin is striking one thing against another with force. From it is his saying:

"When we struck the sapling against the sapling, some of it against some, its branches refused to be broken."

What is meant by it is the disaster that strikes the heart of its possessor, and here it is what befell them of various kinds of afflictions and calamities, such as killing, captivity, plunder and despoiling. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the subject is, as has passed more than once, for the purpose of explanation following vagueness, for the sake of added confirmation and firmness, together with what it shows: that the source of the striking is from their side, the effect of one who has an effect. ﴿Or it descends﴾ that calamity ﴿near﴾ — a near place — ﴿to their home﴾, so they are frightened by it and its sparks spread to them. He likened the calamity to an enemy advancing upon them, so he ascribed striking to it at one time and descending at another, so there is metaphor by way of allusion, imagery, and nurturing. ﴿Until the promise of God comes﴾, i.e., their death or the Resurrection, for each of these is an inevitable promise that cannot be averted. In this is an indication that what befalls them at that time of punishment is more severe. Then He confirmed that with His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed God does not break the promise﴾ (31). That is, the promise, like the (mīlād) and (mīthāq) in the sense of birth and pledge. Perhaps what is intended by it is what the promise attributed to its arrival falls under, not that alone. Al-Qadi said: This verse indicates the falsity of one who permits breaking of His promise, may He be exalted. Although it was revealed concerning the disbelievers, the lesson is in the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion, and its generality includes every threat directed at sinners. Al-Imam answered that breaking the promise is one thing, and specifying a general statement is another; we do not say there is breaking, but we specify the general threats by the verses indicating pardon. You know that the well-known answer is that the verses of promise are unrestricted, and the verses of threat, although they come unrestricted, are restricted, their restriction having been deleted for greater intimidation; and the source of both matters is the greatness of mercy and the utmost generosity. The difference between promise and threat is too evident to be mentioned. Yes, the term "promise" may sometimes be applied to what is in reality a threat, for a reason; so reflect upon what is here according to the manner established.

And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the intended "calamity" is the expeditions (sara ya) which the Messenger of God ﷺ used to send out; they were between raids, abductions, and frightening them by attacking them in their homes. So striking and descending are then among their conditions. It was permitted, according to this, that the words of God Most High, ﴿or it descends﴾, be an address to the Messenger of God ﷺ, meaning by it the descent at Hudaybiyya; and the intended "promise of God" is what He promised of the conquest of Mecca. Al-Tabari attributed this to Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah. It is related from Muqatil and ʿIkrima. Ibn ʿAtiyya held that the intended "those who disbelieved" are the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, and he explained the calamity as what descends upon them from the expeditions of the Messenger of God ﷺ. From al-Hasan and Ibn al-Sa'ib that the intended ones are disbelievers in general, and they said: that matter persists among them until the Day of Resurrection. It cannot be made consistent according to this that by the calamity is meant the expeditions of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him; rather, by it is meant then what was mentioned first. You know that if the disbelievers in general are intended, it does not follow that what was previously mentioned descends upon all of them.

Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr read (aw yahulla), with the ya, in the third person, and it was explained that the pronoun returns to the Messenger, peace be upon him. They also read (min diyarihim), in the plural, upon

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 13, verse 32:

﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked, but I gave respite to those who disbelieved﴾ means: I left them for a period (*milawa*), that is, a long span of time, and from this root comes *al-malawan* (the two long spans, night and day), in security and ease, just as a beast is left to graze. This is a consolation to the Beloved (ﷺ), may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for what he encountered from the polytheists: their mockery of him, their denial of him, their disregard for his signs, and their demands for other signs. All of this, in meaning, is both mockery and a warning to them. The meaning is that this is not specific to you. Rather, it is a constant matter that was done to many great messengers before you, and I gave respite to those who did it to them. The shift in the relative clause (*silah*) to the description of disbelief is not because those who were given respite were other than those who mocked, but to indicate that this mockery is itself disbelief, as has been said. In *al-Irshad* (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary), it is said that the purpose is to combine the two descriptions: that is, I gave respite to those who disbelieved, in their disbelief together with their mockery, not only for their mockery. ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My punishment?﴾ (32). That is, My punishment of them. The intent is to express wonder at what befell them, and in it is evidence of its severity and terribleness that is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 33:**

﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in account of what it has earned﴾, i.e., watching over it and guarding it, whatever it may be, ﴿for what it has earned﴾, whether good or evil, nothing of that is hidden from Him, and nothing escapes Him of the recompense each deserves, and He is God, exalted is His majesty. As for what al-Qurtubi relates from al-Dahhak, that what is meant by this are the angels assigned to the children of Adam, it is among things one hardly turns to here. ﴿Man﴾ (مَن) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning: ﴿like one who is not so﴾. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is then he whom God has opened his breast to Islam, so that he is upon a light from his Lord﴾. The omission is made good by the contrast (muqabala), and it has come expressed many times, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Is then he who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind?﴾, and other examples. The hamza (ء) is for the rhetorical question of denial (istifham inkari), and the entry of the fa' (ف) is said to be for directing the denial toward the supposition of equality in what is known from what He, glorified is He, has done to the mockers, of respite and seizure, and from the fact that the whole affair belongs to Him, glorified is He, and that the guidance of all people is contingent upon His will, exalted is He and high, and from the continual calamities upon the disbelievers until His promise, exalted is He, comes. It is as if it were said: The matter is so; so how can one whose state is this be like what is not in the category of things, that they should associate others with Him? Thus the denial is directed at the consequence of the conjoined clause, namely the supposition of equality, upon the conjoined-to clause that is implied, namely the state of the matter as mentioned, and not at both conjoined clauses together. In al-Kashf it is stated that within this sequence there is an escalation (tarraqi) in denial, meaning: there is no wonder at their denial of Your manifest signs despite their clarity; the only wonder, the utmost wonder, is their making the One capable of sending them down the one who recompenses them for their turning away from pondering their meanings and their parables with calamities following one another, one after another, which they see with their own eyes, drawing them toward the abode of ruin and its terrors, like one who cannot possess for himself harm or benefit, let alone one who has taken Him as Lord, hoping from Him for repelling or procuring. Some have claimed that the fa' is for sequence in mention (al-ta'qib al-dhikri), meaning: after what has been mentioned, I say: this is the matter; but that is not right. ﴿And they have set up partners for God﴾ is a resumptive clause (jumla mustaʼnafa), and it contains an indication of the omitted predicate. It is permitted that it be conjoined to ﴿has earned﴾, on the assumption that ﻣﺎ (ما) is a verbal-source particle (maşdariyya) and not a relative pronoun, with the returning pronoun omitted, and then the two matters need not be combined so that each soul is restricted to the polytheists. And one who said that it is conjoined to ﴿mocked﴾ is further off the mark.
