It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: ﴿Is then He whose attributes are these like one who is not so, when they have set up partners for Him, not a single partner?﴾ The author of Hall al-'Aqd said: The meaning on the circumstantial reading is: ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in account of what it has earned﴾ existent, while the state is that they have set up partners for Him. This is like your saying: "Is He who is generous, who gives people and makes them rich, existent, while I am deprived?" Some permitted conjoining to the clause ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in account of what it has earned﴾ with ﴿like one who is not so﴾, because the rhetorical question of denial has the sense of negation, so it is declarative in meaning. Others posited the predicate as: "they did not make Him one" (lam yuwahhidu-hu), and conjoining was made to it, meaning: ﴿Is then one whose state is this, they did not make Him one, and they have set up partners for Him?﴾ The apparent sense of their statement is that conjoining to the predicate is restricted to this estimate and not to the estimate "like one who is not so." Al-Badr al-Damamini said: The reason for this restriction has not become clear. Al-Fadil al-Shamni explained it by saying that the achievement of the suitability (munasaba) between the conjoined and the conjoined-to, which is the condition for accepting conjunction with waw, is only on the last estimate and not the first estimate. This is indicated by the statement of the people of the science of meanings: "Zayd writes and composes poetry" is acceptable, but "gives and composes poetry" is not. Al-Shihab criticized this, saying that it stems from lack of reflection, for their intention is that on the first estimate the rhetorical question is of denial in the sense of not being, by way of denying resemblance; so if ﴿they have set up partners for Him﴾ were conjoined to it, it would require that He was not, and that is not correct. On the last estimate the rhetorical question is one of reproach (tawbikh), and the denial in it means "why was it," and the non-unification and the setting up of partners is what is reproached and denounced, so conjoining to the predicate becomes evident. As for what was mentioned about the question of suitability, it is a heedlessness, for the suitability between comparing God, glorified is He, with other than Him and polytheism is complete. And on the last aspect, non-unification is itself association, so it is not a place for conjunction according to the people of the science of meanings, as he mentioned. Hence it needs another explanation.

Some of the verifiers chose the first estimate. In that omission there is exaltation of the statement and disparagement of one who slanders with that state. In shifting from the explicit noun in ﴿Is then He who stands﴾ there is a magnificent glorification, by means of the hidden ambiguity in presenting it as a relative clause, together with confirming that standing is occurring and that they are verifiers. In placing the noble name in the position of the pronoun returning to ﻣَن (man), there is a clear specification of His oneness, exalted is He, in essence and name, and an alert to His being singled out for the right to be worshipped, together with the clarification after ambiguity. Perhaps the reason for the said placement is something not restricted to one estimate over another. Some restricted it to what requires the pronoun in ﴿Say: Name them﴾ as a rebuke following a rebuke, meaning: name them, who they are and what their names are. In al-Bahr it is stated that the meaning is that they are not among those who are mentioned and named; rather, only one who benefits and harms is mentioned and named. This is like someone being told that a person is honored and magnified, while in your view he does not deserve that, so you say to the one who mentions him: "Name him, so that I may show you his falsehood and that he is far from deserving that." Close to this is what is said: that this is said only of a despised thing which reaches such baseness that it is not mentioned and no name is given to it; so it is said: "Name it," meaning: it is too base to be mentioned and named. "But if you wish to give it a name, do so." It is as if it were said: name them "gods" by way of threat, and the meaning is: whether you name them thus or do not name them, they are so base that no sensible person should turn to them. It has also been said that the threat here is like the threat to one forbidden to drink wine, and then it is said to him: "Name the wine after this," which is contrary to the apparent sense. It has also been said that the meaning is: mention their attributes and consider whether there is in them anything by which they deserve worship and are fit for partnership. ﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth?﴾, i.e., rather, do you inform God, exalted is He, of partners deserving worship whom He, glorified is He, does not know? The intent is to negate them by negating their necessary consequence, by way of metonymy (kinaya), for since He, glorified is He, does not know them, He to whose knowledge not an atom's weight escapes in the earth or in the heaven, then they have no reality at all. The specification of the earth in mention is because the polytheists only claimed that He, glorified is He, has partners in it. The pronoun resting in ﴿He knows﴾ on this interpretation refers to God, exalted is He, and the returning pronoun to ﻣﺎ (ma) is omitted, as we have indicated.

It is permitted that the returning pronoun be the pronoun of ﴿He knows﴾, meaning: do you inform God, exalted is He, of the partnership of idols which do not at all possess knowledge? The negation of knowledge is mentioned in the earth because the earth is the abode of the idols; so if their knowledge is negated in the place in which they are, then its negation in the lofty heavens is more fitting. Al-Hasan read ﴿do you inform Him﴾ (أتُنْبِئُونَهُ) with lightened pronunciation, from inba' (informing).

﴿Or with an apparent statement﴾, i.e., rather, do you name them partners with an apparent statement, without any realized meaning in the reality of the matter, like naming a black man "Camphor"? Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is their saying with their mouths﴾. It is narrated from al-Dahhak and Qatada that the apparent statement is the false statement from it. They cited for this the poet's saying:

"Did you reproach us for their milk and their meat, and that is a shame, O son of Rayta, evident?"

The word "apparent" (ظاهر) is also used for what is passing away, as in his saying:

"The watchers reproached me that I love her, and that complaint—its shame is removed from you."

Whoever wanted that here has over-exerted himself. It is narrated from al-Jubba'i that what is meant by "apparent statement" is the apparent book which God, exalted is He, sent down, and by which He named the idols "true gods." The sum of the verse is the negation of rational proof and transmitted proof for the validity of worshipping them and taking them as gods. It is permitted that ﴿or﴾ (أم) be connective, though disconnection is the apparent reading. There is no concealing what the verse contains of argumentation and wondrous methods, which proclaims with a free and sharp tongue that it is not the speech of humans, as al-Zamakhshari stated. Sahib al-Kashf explained this: since His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Is then He who stands﴾ was sufficient to demolish the foundation of polytheism by the prior branching and the realization through the subsequent attribute, together with the subtleties it contains, and it was a refutation from the side of truth, it was appended by refuting it from the side of the opposite, meaning: would that when they associated, they had associated with one who may not be associated, they had associated one about whom even the slightest supposition might arise. It observed that the partners have no names, let alone a named referent, by way of indirect allusion (kinaya ima'iyya). Then it was exaggerated by saying that they are not fit to be asked about their state, given the manifest corruption of them. In it the path of allusive metonymy was taken, by negating knowledge through negating what is known, and then from that by negating fitness. The interrogative hamza included in it indicates reproach and confirmation that they wish to inform the Knower of the secret and the hidden of what He does not know; this is an impossibility upon an impossibility. In making their taking partners and their disputing with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) a subtle point, indeed subtle points... Then he turned away from that. And it has been said: it has made clear the sun to one with two eyes, and that naming is nothing but an apparent statement without any substance beneath it, and it is nothing but an empty sound. Whoever reflects on it with due reflection ought to acknowledge that it is speech free from artifice, issuing from the Creator of powers and measures, before whose depths the understandings of humans fall short.

Al-Zamakhshari concluded his statement with: "So blessed is God, the best of creators." This, as in al-Insaf, is a word of truth by which falsehood is intended, by one who is devoid of the adornment of fairness. This is the end of it.

﴿Rather, the plotting of those who disbelieved has been made attractive to them﴾. It is a turning away from arguing against them, and the relative pronoun is placed in the position of the pronoun as a censure of them and a recording against them of disbelief, as if it were said: leave this, for there is no benefit in it, because it has been made attractive to them ﴿their plotting﴾, i.e., their scheme to deceive by their polytheism, or their embellishing of falsehoods, so they undertook to place them in imagination without reality, and then after that they assumed them to be something, because of their persistence in error. According to this meaning, their plotting is against themselves; according to the first, it is their plotting against others. The idafa of "plotting" (مَكْر) to their pronoun is an idafa of the verbal noun to its agent. It is permitted on the second that it be idafa to the object, but that is remote.

Mujahid read ﴿has made attractive﴾ (زَيَّنَ) with the active form and ﴿their plotting﴾ (مَكْرَهُم) in the accusative. ﴿And they were turned away from the way﴾, i.e., the way of truth; its definiteness is for a known referent, or for what is other than it, as if it were not the way. The agent of the turning away is either their plotting and the like, or God, exalted is He, by His sealing upon their hearts, or the devil by his seduction of them. The last two possibilities apply also to the agent of the making attractive. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿and they turned away﴾ (وصَدُّوا) with the active form, and it is like the first from "sadda-hu sadda" (he turned him away), so the object is omitted, meaning: they turned people away from faith. It is also possible that it is from "sadda sudud" (to turn away), with no object. Ibn Wathhab read ﴿and they were turned away﴾ (وصِدُّوا) with a kasra on the sad. Some said he read so in al-Mu'min, while the kasra here is for Ibn Ya'mar. The verb on this reading is passive, with the vowel of the middle radical transferred to the first radical, treating it as a hollow verb. Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿and a turning away﴾ (وصَدٌّ) with tanwin, in coordination with "their plotting." ﴿And whomever God leads astray﴾, i.e., He creates misguidance in him because of his bad disposition, ﴿for him there is no guide﴾ (33), who grants him success toward guidance and brings him to what contains his salvation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 34:

﴿For them is a torment﴾ severe ﴿in the life of this world﴾ by killing, captivity, and all the other calamities that befall them. For these come upon them only as a punishment from God Most High for their disbelief. As for such things befalling the believer, they come by way of reward and the raising of ranks. ﴿And the torment of the Hereafter is more severe﴾ than that, by reason of its intensity and its perpetuity. ﴿And they have no protector from God﴾, that is, from His punishment, glorified is He, ﴿from any defender﴾. (34) That is, no guardian who would preserve them from it. So the first "min" is connected to "wāq" (defender), and the second "min" is redundant, for emphasis. And there is no harm in the fronting of the object of the prepositional phrase before it, because the redundant element has no grammatical effect.

It is also permitted that the first "min" be an established adverbial phrase (ẓarf mustaqirr) placed as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "wāq", with its complement omitted, and the meaning would be: "They have no defender or guardian from the torment of God Most High, the defender being from His direction and His mercy." On this reading, "min" is for specification (tabyīn). It is also permitted that it be superfluous (laghw), connected to what is in the adverbial phrase, namely "lahum" with the sense of a verb, and it is for the beginning of the source (ibtidā'). The meaning would be: "What has come to them of the mercy of God Most High is no defender from the torment."

[p. 163]

*The likeness of Paradise* means its description and attributes, as Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ikrimah. It is in accordance with what is in *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*, the *Oceanic Sea*, a tafsir by Abu Hayyan), from *mathalt al-shay'* (I likened the thing), meaning I described it and brought it closer to understanding. From the same usage is ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾, that is, the highest attribute. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) denied this and said: "Interpreting *mathal* as *sifa* (attribute) is not linguistically sound, and it is not attested in that sense. Its meaning is *al-shabih* (the resemblance)."

Some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqin*) said: "It is used in three meanings. It is used in the sense of *tashbih* (comparison), which is the original linguistic meaning; in the sense of *qawl al-sa'ir* (the well-known saying, proverb) that is familiar in common usage; and in the sense of the *sifa gharibah* (remarkable attribute). The last is a figurative meaning (*majaz*) derived from the common usage by the relation of strangeness (*alaqat al-gharabah*), because a *mathal* only circulates among people due to its strangeness." Most of the exegetes interpret it here as the remarkable attribute. In that case, according to Sibawayh, the predicate (*khabar*) of the subject (*mubtada'*) is omitted, meaning: in what is recounted and recited to you, is the attribute of Paradise ﴿which the righteous have been promised﴾, that is, those who keep away from disbelief and sins. The predicate was placed first because the subject is long, and so that it would not be separated from what is semantically connected to it.

His saying, ﴿Beneath which rivers flow﴾, is an explanatory clause (*jumla mufassira*), like His creating him from dust in His saying, ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust﴾. Or it is a resumptive explanatory clause (*istinaf bayani*), or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the omitted returning pronoun in the relative clause, meaning *allati wa'adaha* (which He promised it). It was also said that it is the predicate, in the manner of your saying: "The affair of Zayd: people come to him and honour him." This was objected to on the grounds that it does not make sense semantically, because it implies that the rivers are in the attribute of Paradise, whereas they are in Paradise itself and not in its attribute. Also, it involves the feminine pronoun referring to *mathal* by considering its meaning. It was said that this is ugly, but it was answered that this is interpreted as "it flows," so the meaning is: the likeness of Paradise is the flowing of rivers; or that the clause is in the sense of a singular noun, so no pronoun returns from it to the subject; or that what is meant by the attribute is what is said about it: "This is it when it is described," so there is no need for a pronoun, as in the predicate of the pronoun of the affair (*damir al-sha'n*).

Al-Tibi said: "The feminine pronoun is because it refers to Paradise, not to *mathal*. This is permissible because what is intended by the annexed noun is the same as the annexed-to noun, and it was mentioned as a preparation for it. It is not like *ghulam Zayd* (the servant of Zayd)." Al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) criticized all of that, saying: "It is a worthless, forced statement, because interpreting a clause as a verbal noun without an intermediary particle is rare, and likewise the interpretation that the attribute refers to its wording (*lafzuha*) being described by it, while there is nothing in the wording that indicates this; it is a figurative usage upon a figurative usage, and its artificiality is not hidden. Its analogy to the pronoun of the affair is an analogy with a difference. As for the return of the pronoun to the annexed-to noun rather than the subject in such a case, it is weaker than the spider's house." Therefore, the sound course is to disregard this view.

From al-Zajjaj: the predicate is omitted, and the mentioned clause is an attribute of it, and the meaning is: the likeness of Paradise is a Paradise in which rivers flow, to the end of the verse. Thus He, glorified is He, has made us know the Paradise we have not seen through what we have witnessed and observed of worldly matters. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) criticized this, as reported in *al-Bahr*, saying: "It is not valid according to the meaning of attribute, nor according to the meaning of resemblance. The Paradise that he assumed is a body (*jutha*), and a body cannot be an attribute. And resemblance is an expression for the similarity between two things, which is an event (*hadath*), so it is not permissible to predicate it with 'Paradise,' the body." It was answered: "What is meant by *mathal* is the *mathil* (the like) or the *shabih* (the resemblance), so there is no difficulty in the predication." It was also said: "The comparison here is figurative (*tamthili*), its aspect derived from several matters of the observed gardens, such as the flowing of their rivers, the lushness of their branches, the intertwining of their boughs, and the like. The saying, ﴿its provision is eternal, and its shade﴾, is an explanation of the excellence of those gardens and their distinction from these observed gardens." It was also said: "This is an explanation of the state of the gardens of this world by way of supposition, and that in what was mentioned there is generality and sufficiency in the comparison with merely the flowing of rivers, which does not suit the Qur'anic eloquence. And it is, as you see, far-fetched."

It is reported from al-Farra' that the clause is also a predicate, except that *mathal* in the sense of *shabah* (resemblance) is superfluous (*muqhim*). The sense is: "Paradise which the righteous have been promised: rivers flow beneath it, to the end." The superfluity of this word in this sense is known, and from it is His saying, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. Abu Hayyan objected that the superfluity of nouns is not permissible. It was answered that it is common in their speech, such as *tham ism al-salam 'alaykuma* (there is the name of peace upon you both), and *la sadaqata illa 'an zahri ghina* (no charity except from surplus wealth), and other examples. After all this discussion, the preferable view is the first one, for it is free from artificiality, along with what it contains of conciseness, generality, and detail. Apparently, what is meant by the eating is what is eaten in it. The meaning of its being eternal is that it never ends. Ibrahim al-Taymi said: "Its pleasure is lasting; it is not increased by hunger, nor tired by satiety." This is contrary to the apparent meaning.

*[p. 164]*

Some explained the eating as the fruit. It was said: "Its aspect is that there is nothing else in the Paradise of this world, although in the promised one there are other foods." It was deduced that this is because of its being annexed to the pronoun of Paradise, and foods are not described as the eating of Paradise; but there is some hesitation in this. The shade, originally, is the opposite of sunshine (*al-dahh*). According to al-Raghib, it is more general than *al-fay'* (shade cast after noon), for one says *zill al-layl* (the shade of the night) but not *fay'uhu*, and everywhere the sun has not reached is called *zill*, while *fay'* is only said of what the sun has left. In the *Qamus* (al-Fayruzabadi's dictionary), it is "the sunshine," or "*al-fay'* is in the morning, and *al-fay'* in the evening." Its plural is *zilal*, *zulul*, and *aziyal*. It is also used to express might and protection, and comfort. The well-known explanation here is the first meaning, and it is a predicate omitted from the subject: *wa-ukuluha kadhalika*, that is, "its eating is likewise, eternal," and the clause is conjoined to the clause before it. The meaning of its eternity is that it is not abrogated (*la yunsakh*), as is abrogated in this world by the sun, since there is no sun there, according to the prevalent view among the people of the transmitted tradition (*ahl al-athar*); or because it has no effect, as was said. It is permissible in my view that by the shade is meant might or comfort, and also that the first meaning is intended, and the statement is taken as a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the permanence of rest.

Kharijah ibn Mus'ab disbelieved, as Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from him, in the one who held that Paradise is not eternal, as is related of Jahm and his followers, based on this verse. The judge (al-Baydawi) used it to argue that it has not yet been created, because if it were created, its eating would have to perish and cease, due to His saying, ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾. But its eating does not cease or perish, by the verse mentioned; therefore it must not yet be created. Then he said: "We do not deny that there may now be many gardens in the heavens in which whomever Allah wills of the prophets, martyrs, and others take their enjoyment. But we say that the Garden of Eternity (*jannat al-khuld*) is only created after the resurrection." Al-Imam (al-Razi) answered this by saying: "Their proof is composed of two things: His saying, ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾, and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿its provision is eternal﴾. So when we introduce a specification into one of these two pillars, the proof falls. Therefore we specify one of them by the proofs indicating that Paradise is created, such as His saying, ﴿And a Garden whose width is like the width of the heaven and the earth, prepared for those who believed﴾." End of quote.

It may be objected to the argument that it is of shared implication (*mushtarak al-ilzam*), because the word "thing" in His saying, ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾, means existing things absolutely, as in His saying, ﴿Creator of all things, and He is Knowing of all things﴾. The meaning is that whatever exists at any time becomes perishing after its existence. So it is valid to say: if Paradise existed at some time, its eating would have to perish, in order to realize the generality. But its perishing is invalid, due to His saying, ﴿its provision is eternal﴾. Therefore its existence at any time is invalid. It was answered that perhaps what is meant by the existing thing is that which exists in this world, for it is the abode of perishing, not that which exists in the Hereafter, for it is the abode of permanence; and this suffices for the non-sharing of the implication. In this there is the objection that if it is meant that the meaning of "thing" is what exists in this world, then this is manifestly invalid. And if it is meant that the intention is that, by the indication of its being judged as perishing, which can only occur in this world because it is the abode of perishing, then we say: this is a specification by a verbal indication, so we specify it by other than Paradise, by His saying, ﴿prepared for the righteous﴾ and ﴿its provision is eternal﴾. Thus the argument is not complete.

Other than al-Imam answered that the intended meaning is customary permanence, which is the absence of the coming of non-existence for a period of time specified by it, and this does not negate the coming of non-existence upon it, nor its cessation for a moment. Moreover, perishing does not necessitate annihilation; rather, mere departure from the intended benefit suffices. And even if it were conceded, it is permissible that what is meant is that every contingent thing is perishing in its own essence, in the sense that contingent existence, in relation to necessary existence, is as nothing. It was also said in the answer: the intended meaning of permanence is the true meaning, namely the absence of the coming of non-existence absolutely; and the intended meaning of the permanence of the eating is the permanence of the kind (*dawam al-naw'*), and of perishing is the perishing of individuals. It is permissible that the kind never ends at all, even with the perishing of individuals, namely that the perishing of each specific individual of the eating occurs after the existence of its like. This is based on the view of the majority that Paradise is not subject to non-existence, even for a moment. But as for the view that it is subject to it for a moment, it is not complete, for it would necessarily entail the cessation of the kind with certainty, as is not hidden.

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read *mithal al-jannah* (the example of Paradise). In *al-Lawami'* from al-Sulami: *amthal al-jannah* (the examples of Paradise), that is, its attributes. ﴿That﴾, the Paradise described by what was mentioned, ﴿is the final destiny of those who kept away﴾ from disbelief and sins, that is, their outcome and the end of their affair. ﴿And the final destiny of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾. (35) Not other than these, as the definiteness of the predicate indicates, and the interpretation of *ittiqa'* (keeping away) as keeping away from disbelief and sins, because the context is one of encouragement. On this basis, the disobedient are left unmentioned. It may also be interpreted as keeping away from disbelief by the contrast in the context, so the disobedient enter among "those who kept away," because their end is Paradise, even if they are punished.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 36:

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ were revealed, as al-Mawardi said, concerning the believers among the People of the Book, such as ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, Kaʿb and their likes from the Jews, and those among the Christians who embraced Islam, such as the well-known eighty: forty men in Najran, eight in Yemen, and thirty-two in Abyssinia. So by "the Book" is meant the Torah and the Gospel. ﴿who rejoice at what has been sent down to you﴾, since it is the Book promised in what they were given. ﴿And among the factions﴾, that is, among their factions, namely their disbelievers who banded together against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in enmity, such as Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, al-Sayyid and al-ʿAqib, the bishops of Najran, and their partisans. The root of the word is the plural of ḥizb (faction), with a kasra and a sukun, meaning a group that has banded together for some matter, such as enmity, war, or other things, and it may be used to refer to a specific group from among them by means of the covenant. ﴿of them are those who deny part of it﴾, namely that which does not agree with their books of legislation that are newly introduced, whether as new enactment or abrogation. As for what agrees with their books, they do not deny it, even if they do not rejoice in it. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd that it was revealed concerning the believers among the Jews only; so by "the Book" is meant the Torah, and by "the factions" their disbelievers. It is also reported from Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah that the relative pronoun refers to all the People of the Book, for they used to rejoice at what agreed with their books. So by "what has been sent down to you" is meant a part of it, namely that which agrees (with their books). It has been objected that this is precluded by the contrast with His words, glorified is He: ﴿and among the factions are those who deny part of it﴾, since denial of a part is common to them all. It has been answered that by "the factions" is meant those whose portion is only the denial of a part of it, and who have no share in rejoicing at any part of it, due to the intensity of their hatred and enmity; whereas those (others) rejoice at the part that agrees with their books. It has also been said: the apparent meaning is that among them are those who rejoice at a part of it when it agrees with their books, while some of them do not rejoice at that part but are grieved by it even when it agrees with them, and they deny the agreement so that none of them will follow his Law (ﷺ), as in the story of the stoning. You know that both answers are worthless. According to the interpretation of the relative pronoun as all the People of the Book, some explained "some of it" as that which does not agree with what they have distorted, and clarified this by saying that among them are those who rejoice at what agrees, and among them are those who deny it, out of their obstinacy and severe corruption, and their denial is of the divergence of the distorted, by speech but not by heart, since they know it; or it refers to those who did not distort it. Perhaps mentioning their denial is more suitable to the context than mentioning their distortion, as is not hidden from the reflective. It has also been said: the relative pronoun refers to all Muslims, and "the factions" to the Jews, the Christians and the Magians.

Ibn Jarir reported this from Qatadah. So by "the Book" is meant the Qur'an, and the meaning of ﴿rejoice﴾ is the continuation and increase of their joy. A group said: by "the factions" are meant the factions of the Jahiliyyah among the Arabs. Muqatil said: they are the Banu Umayyah, the Banu al-Mughirah and the family of Abu Talhah.

﴿Say﴾ (openly proclaiming the truth, not concerned with the denier of some of what has been sent down to you): ﴿I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him﴾.

That is, anything at all, or I do not commit association with Him, glorified is He. The apparent meaning is that the intent is to restrict the command to the worship of Allah, exalted is He, alone, and this is what the words of the Imam require, where he said: "Indeed ﴿innama﴾ is for restriction, and its meaning is: I have not been commanded except to worship Allah, exalted is He." This indicates that there is no obligation, command or prohibition except with that. It has also been said: its meaning is: I have only been commanded to worship Him, exalted is He, and to affirm His oneness, not what you are upon.

In Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim it is stated that the meaning, as a binding argument against the deniers and a rejection of their denial, is "I have only been commanded..." to the end, and the intent is to restrict the command to worship to Allah, exalted is He, not to restrict the command absolutely to His worship, glorified is He. That is: say to them: I have been commanded, in what has been sent down to me, to worship Allah, exalted is He, and to affirm His oneness. It is clear that you have no way to deny it, since all the prophets, peace be upon them, and the Books agree upon it, by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Come to a word that is common between us and you: that we worship none but Allah, and that we associate nothing with Him﴾. So why do you associate with Him ʿUzayr and al-Masih, peace be upon them both? It is not hidden that this interpretation is based on the factions being the disbelievers of the two groups of People of the Book, and that this statement is a binding argument against them. It has been objected that some of them deny the Oneness and the agreement of all the prophets and Books upon it, such as the Trinitarians among the Christians. It has been answered that they, with their Trinity, claim Oneness and do not deny it, as their saying indicates: "in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God." You know that this is not something requiring response, and the objection arises from heedlessness of the intended meaning. It may be said: the meaning is: I have only been commanded to worship Allah, exalted is He, and not to associate anything with Him, and that is a matter which sound minds approve and which the signs of the horizons and of the souls clearly attest. And in everything there is a sign indicating that He is One.

Denying it is a proof of foolishness and a witness of ignorance; no intelligent person should pay heed to it. The same applies to the rest of the interpretations of the "factions."

Abu Khulayd, from Nafiʿ, read ﴿wa-la ushriku﴾ with a raised vowel (damma), as a resumptive clause: "and I do not associate." It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (ḥal), meaning: to worship Allah without associating with Him. It has been said: this is preferable, since the resumptive reading lacks the indication that what is commanded is the restriction of worship to Him, exalted is He. There is discussion of this.

﴿To Him﴾, that is, to Allah, exalted is He, alone, in the manner mentioned of Oneness, or to what I have been commanded of Oneness, ﴿I call﴾ people, not to other than Him, nor to anything else that the divine Books and the prophets, peace be upon them, do not confirm. So what is the basis of your denial? This is also said in Irshad.

It is preferable to return the pronoun to Allah, exalted is He, like its earlier counterpart, and likewise the following one in His words, glorified is He: ﴿and to Him is my return﴾, that is, to Allah, exalted is He, alone, ﴿(36)﴾: that is, my place of return for recompense. Al-ʿAllamah al-Baydawi restricted himself to this, though he had added "and your return" in what preceded, which is not far off. It was objected that he should have added it here too; rather, this context is more suitable to generalization, so as to indicate the establishment of resurrection in general, and this is what is reported from Qatadah. The Imam made this verse comprehensive of all that a person needs to know of the origin and the return: His words, glorified is He, ﴿Say: I have only been commanded to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him﴾, encompass everything for which obligation has come; His words, exalted is He, ﴿To Him I call﴾, point to his prophethood, peace be upon him; and His words, majestic and high is He, ﴿and to Him is my return﴾, are an indication of the Gathering, the Resurrection and the Last Day. Al-Shihab answered this by saying: Al-Zamakhshari's words "to Him and not to other than Him is my return, and you say the like of it, so there is no sense in your denial" are an explanation of the wisdom of the restriction, namely that they deny it either in reality or in ruling; so there is no need for what is said: there is no need to mention it, since the words of the Exalted ﴿That is the final home of those who are mindful of Allah, and the final home of the disbelievers is the Fire﴾ indicate it. End of quotation.

This, as you see, is not so; and perhaps the more evident view is that the indication of the statement here is not like its indication there, since the context of the verse there is for warning, which is fitting to consider, whereas its context here is for another matter, and restricting oneself to that suffices for it.

You know that there is no barrier to considering it, and the meaning of the verse would be: Say in reply to them: indeed Allah, exalted is He, has commanded me only with what is among the highest of matters, and to Him I call, time after time, and to Him is my return and your return, so He will reward me for what I am upon and will take vengeance on you for your denial and your failure to follow my call; or then the truth of all that has been sent down to me will become manifest, and the corruption of your opinion in denying any part of it will become clear. It may also be said, on the view of not considering it, along the lines of what was said before: the meaning is: Say, in response to their denial: indeed Allah, exalted is He, has commanded me with what He commanded me, and to Him I call, and to Him is my return in what befalls me concerning the matter of the call and otherwise; so I do not care for your denial, for He, glorified is He, suffices for whoever returns to Him. Perhaps this meaning here is more suitable, since there it is a pure establishment of a new point; al-Irshad confined itself to making the statement a binding argument, and made it the wisdom of His command, ﷺ, to address them with this, and mentioned that the words of the Exalted:

This is the commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 37:

﴿And thus We have sent it down as a judgment (hukm), in Arabic.﴾ This begins the response to their denial of the subsidiary rulings of the sharia (shara'i'), whether they were revealed initially or as replacements for abrogated (mansukh) laws, by explaining the wisdom behind that. The pronoun refers to what was sent down to you, and the demonstrative refers to the source of ﴿We have sent it down﴾ or ﴿it was sent down to you﴾. That is, like that revelation, which is unique and comprises fundamentals on which there is consensus and subsidiary rulings that branch out into agreement and disagreement, as the requirement of wisdom dictates. We sent it down as a judgment (hakim), which judges disputes and events with truth and judges by it in the same way. Mentioning this designation, although some of it is not a judgment, is to emphasize the obligation to observe it and the necessity of preserving it. The mention of it being Arabic, that is, translated into the language of the Arabs, is to indicate that this is one of the points of difference with previous scriptures. This is also what wisdom requires, since through it its understanding and the perception of its inimitability become easier, meaning for the Arabs. As for others, the wisdom may be that it encourages the learning of the sciences upon which the aforementioned depends. Some have limited the revelation to including the fundamentals of the religions on which there is consensus, as indicated by the view on His saying: ﴿Say: I have only been commanded﴾ to the end of the verse. This has been objected to on the grounds that it is contradicted by the mention of following their desires and the hadith of erasure and affirmation, and that ﴿for every term there is a Book﴾. For what is agreed upon does not admit of being followed or made to follow. It has also been said that the reference is to the revelation of the earlier books to the prophets, peace be upon them, and the meaning is: just as We sent down the books to those before you, We sent down this Book to you, because His saying ﴿And those to whom We gave the Book﴾ includes His sending down that. And this which We sent down is in the language of the Arabs, just as the earlier books were in the language of those to whom they were sent: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, to make clear to them﴾. This is the view of al-Imam and Abu Hayyan. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the meaning is, just as We made these easy for joy and those for denial of some, We sent it down as a judgment, to the end. Would that what was said were so. The more eloquent of the possibilities we have indicated is the first. ﴿A judgment﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the object of ﴿We sent it down﴾. If it is meant as "judging," then there is a metaphor in the attribution, as is clear. ﴿In Arabic﴾ is also in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, either of the pronoun in ﴿We sent it down﴾, like the first circumstantial qualifier, making it a parallel circumstantial qualifier (hal mutaradifa), or of the concealed pronoun in the first, making it an embedded circumstantial qualifier (hal mutadakhila). It may also be a descriptor of ﴿judgment﴾, which would be a preparatory circumstantial qualifier (al-hal al-muwatti'a), the rigid noun that serves as a circumstantial qualifier while its description is by a derived noun, which is in reality the circumstantial qualifier. The first is preferable, because ﴿judgment﴾ is intended here as a circumstantial qualifier, and the preparatory circumstantial qualifier is not intended in itself.

Al-Tabarsi chose that the meaning of ﴿judgment﴾ is wisdom, as in His saying: (And We gave him judgment and prophethood). This is one of the aspects mentioned by al-Imam, and he also put it in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, so do not be heedless.

The Mu'tazila used the verse to argue that the Qur'an is created (muhdath), in several ways. First, He described it as being sent down (munazzal), and that is only fitting for something created. Second, He described it as Arabic, and "Arabic" is a conventional matter (wad'i), and what is so is created. Third, it indicates that it was a judgment in Arabic only because Allah made it so, and what is made is created.

Al-Imam answered that all of this only indicates that what is composed of letters and sounds is created, and there is no dispute about this

(page 168)

meaning between the Mu'tazila and the Ash'ari. Otherwise, the Hanbalis, as is well known from them, hold that the spoken word (al-kalam al-lafzi) is eternal. We have already presented a precious discussion on the question of speech in the Introductions, so return to it. Do not let the clamor of the opponents of the early community (salaf) alarm you.

﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ which they call you to, such as praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis after the qibla was changed to the Ka'ba, and abandoning the call to Islam, ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, the knowledge of great stature that is poured upon you from that Arabic judgment, or the knowledge of its content, ﴿you would have from Allah﴾, from His mighty presence, exalted be His majesty, ﴿no protector﴾. The shift from first person to third person and the mention of the exalted name are to cultivate awe, from a guardian who manages your affairs and helps you against those who seek to harm you with calamities, ﴿nor any shield﴾. (37) A shield who protects you from the places of evil. Since denying a helper against the enemy does not necessarily imply denying a shield from his harm, he introduced the negative particle into the conjoined item for emphasis, like your saying: "I have no dinar nor dirham," or: "You have no helper or shield against the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, if you follow their desires after the truth has come to you." Such stern admonitions are only to cut off the hopes of the disbelievers and to stir the believers to steadfastness in the religion, not for the Prophet (ﷺ), for he, peace and blessings be upon him, is in a station where he needs no motivator or stimulant. From here it has been said that the address is to someone other than the Prophet (ﷺ). The lam in ﴿la'in﴾ is a preparatory particle, the second ﴿min﴾ is an added particle, and ﴿ma laka﴾ takes the place of the answers of both the conditional and the oath.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 38:**

﴿And We certainly sent messengers﴾ many, existing ﴿before you, and We gave them wives and offspring﴾, i.e., women and children, just as We gave them to you. It is narrated from al-Kalbi that "the Jews reproached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'We see no concern in this man except women and marriage. If he were a prophet as he claims, the matter of prophethood would have occupied him away from women.' So this was revealed," as a reply to them, since it includes that marriage does not contradict prophethood, and that combining the two has occurred among many messengers before him.

It is mentioned that Sulayman (peace be upon him) had three hundred free wives from the Mahriyya tribe and seven hundred concubines, and that Dawud (peace be upon him) had a hundred wives. And He, exalted is His majesty, did not address their saying, "We see no concern in this man except women," in order to indicate that it does not deserve an answer, since it is evident that he (peace and blessings be upon him) was not occupied by the matter of women from anything of the matter of prophethood. And in his (ﷺ) fulfilment of both matters in the most perfect manner there is evidence, and what evidence, of the increase of his perfection in being both angelic and human. And among what clarifies this is that he (ﷺ) would go hungry for days until he tied a stone upon his noble belly, yet despite that he would visit all his wives in a single night, and that did not prevent him from this.

In his (peace and blessings be upon him) having many wives there are abundant benefits. Even if there were nothing in it but the knowledge of the evenness of his secret and his public conduct, that would suffice. This is because it is in the nature of women that they cannot keep any secret whatsoever. So if he had done something in private that contradicted what was public, they would have become aware of it despite their number, and if they had become aware of it, they would have disclosed it, acting according to the disposition of women, especially co-wives.

Whoever examines the reports and comprehends what has been narrated from those pure women will know that they left out none of his hidden affairs except that they mentioned it. Consider what has been narrated: "The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) disagreed about penetration without ejaculation, whether it requires ghusl (the major ritual bath) or not. So they asked 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), and she said, without any shame regarding religion: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did this with me, and we both performed ghusl.'" And it is narrated that they (the disbelievers) criticised his prophethood on account of his marriage and his not bringing the signs they proposed. So this was revealed, along with His saying, ﴿And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by the permission of Allah﴾, i.e., it is not valid nor proper, and it was not within the power of any messenger of the earlier messengers to bring to those to whom he was sent a sign or miracle that they propose to him, except by Allah's facilitation and His will, which is based on the wisdoms and interests upon which the affairs of creation depend. The sign may also mean the written revelation descending with the ruling in accordance with the wish of those to whom it is sent, and this is more fitting with what follows. It is also permissible that both meanings are intended, on the basis of the general scope of the metaphor, i.e., that which indicates in an absolute sense, or on the basis of using the word in both its meanings, according to the permissibility of this, and the turning (of address) to what has preceded, and for confirming the content of the sentence by alluding to the cause.

﴿For every term﴾, i.e., for every time and period of the times and periods, ﴿there is a decree﴾. (38) A specific ruling that is written for the servants according to what wisdom requires. For all the laws are for the reform of their conditions in the beginning and the return. And part of this matter is that they differ according to their changing conditions, as the changing of times changes things, like the difference of treatments according to the differing conditions of the sick over time. According to some, this is a response to what they denied of him (peace and blessings be upon him) regarding the abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by another) of some rulings, just as what precedes it is a response to their criticism regarding not bringing the proposed miracles.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 39 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah erases what He wills﴾, i.e., He abrogates (naskh) whichever rulings He wills to abrogate, according to what wisdom requires in accordance with the time. ﴿And establishes﴾ in its place what wisdom requires, or leaves it as it is, unabrogated; or He establishes whatever He wills to establish absolutely, which is more general than both of these and includes the initiation (inshaʾ) of something from the start.

ʿIkrimah said: He erases by repentance all sins and establishes good deeds in their place, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Except for those who repent, believe, and do righteous work; for those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾. Ibn Jubayr said: He forgives whomever He wills of the sins of His servants and leaves whomever He wills without forgiveness. And he said: He erases, from among those whose term (ajal) has come, whomever He wills, and establishes, among those whose term has not yet come, whomever He wills. ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, said: He erases whomever He wills from the generations (qurun), according to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾, and establishes from them whomever He wills, according to His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿Then We brought into being after them other generations﴾. al-Rabiʿ said: This is concerning the souls during sleep, which Allah the Exalted takes back to Himself. So whoever He intends to die suddenly, He withholds his soul and does not release it; and whoever He intends to remain alive, He releases his soul. Its explanation is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾, the verse.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak: He erases from the register of the recording angels (hafazah) what is neither a good deed nor an evil deed, because they are commanded to record every word and action, and He establishes what is either a good deed or an evil deed. It has been said: He erases some of the creatures and establishes others, among humans, all animals, plants, and trees, and their attributes and conditions. It has been said: He erases the world and establishes the Hereafter. al-Hasan and a group said: This concerns the terms (ajal) of the children of Adam, which Allah, Glorified is He, writes on the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr). It has been said: on the night of the middle of Shaʿban He writes the terms of the dead, so He erases some people from the register of the living and establishes them in the register of the dead. al-Suddi said: He erases the moon and establishes the sun. Its explanation is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So We erased the sign of the night and made the sign of the day as a means of seeing﴾.

In a report from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: Allah the Exalted erases what He wills of the affairs of His servants and establishes, except for happiness (saʿadah), wretchedness (shaqawah), and terms (ajal), for these have no erasure in them. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from him as a marfuʿ report. It has also been said: it is general regarding provision, term, happiness, and wretchedness, and it is attributed to a group of the Companions and the Successors (tabiʿun), who used to beseech Allah, the Exalted, to make them among the happy. Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf and others transmitted from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: No servant has ever made these supplications except that his livelihood was expanded for him: "O Possessor of kindness, upon whom no kindness is bestowed; O Possessor of majesty and honor; O Possessor of bounty, there is no god but You, refuge of those who seek refuge, protector of those who seek protection, and security of the fearful. If You have written me in Your presence in the Mother of the Book as wretched, then erase from me the name of wretchedness and record me in Your presence as happy. And if You have written me in Your presence in the Mother of the Book as deprived, with my provision restricted, then erase my deprivation, ease my provision, and record me in Your presence as happy and granted success in good, for You say in Your Book which You have sent down: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and establishes, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and others transmitted from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said while circumambulating the House: "O Allah, if You have decreed for me wretchedness or sin, then erase it and make it happiness and forgiveness, for You erase what You will and establish, and with You is the Mother of the Book."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Shaqiq Abi Wa'il that he used to frequently make these supplications: "O Allah, if You have written us as wretched, then erase us and write us as happy; and if You have written us as happy, then establish us, for You erase what You will and establish."

Ibn Saʿd and others transmitted from al-Kalbi that he said: "Allah the Exalted erases from provision and increases it, and erases from the term and increases it." It was said to him: "Who related this to you?" He said: "Abu Salih, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Riʾab al-Ansari, from the Prophet (ﷺ)." Abu Hayyan said: If anything of that is authentic, its interpretation must be sought. For it is known that happiness, wretchedness, provision, and term do not change in any respect.

Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah) adopted the generalization. After quoting many opinions he said: "The most fitting is to generalize each of the erasure and the establishment so that it encompasses everything, and this includes the objects of denial (mawarid al-inkar) by primary inclusion." He also mentioned what Ibn Jarir transmitted from Kaʿb, that he said to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "O Commander of the Faithful, were it not for one verse in the Book of Allah the Exalted, I would inform you of what will occur until the Day of Resurrection." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah erases what He wills﴾, the verse." It hints at that. And you know that erasure and establishment, if they are relative to what is in the hands of the angels and the like, then there is no difference between happiness, wretchedness, provision, term, and other things in that each accepts erasure and establishment. And if they are relative to what is in knowledge, then there is likewise no difference between those matters and others in that each does not accept that, because knowledge has only been related to them as they are in reality; otherwise it would be ignorance. And what is in reality is not conceivable to undergo change or alteration. How could the evenness of four, for example, change and turn into oddness while four remains four? This does not occur at all, and I do not think you doubt this. The general evidences indicating that whatever Allah the Exalted wills comes to be do not contradict this, because will follows knowledge, and knowledge of a thing follows what the thing is in reality; so He, Glorified is He, wills only what the thing is in reality. It has been said: That what is in knowledge does not change is also indicated by His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾. (39) This is based on the Mother of the Book being knowledge, because everything that is written in the scrolls of the angels and others does not come to pass wherever it comes to pass except in conformity with what is established in it. So it is its mother, that is, its origin. It is as if it were said: He erases what He wills to erase and establishes what He wills to establish of what is inscribed in the books, and with Him is the eternal knowledge, by which nothing occurs except in accordance with what is in it. The interpretation of the Mother of the Book as the knowledge of Allah the Exalted is what ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir transmitted from Kaʿb, may Allah be pleased with him. The well-known view is that it is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). They said: It is the origin of the books, since nothing among what passes away or what remains is not written in it as it is.

The apparent meaning is that what is intended by what passes away and what remains is what relates to the world, not what relates to both the world and the Hereafter, because of the rational proof for the finitude of dimensions absolutely, and the textual proof for the finitude of the Tablet in particular. It has been reported that it is made of white pearl, having two covers of ruby, and its length is the distance of five hundred years. The impossibility of a finite thing being contained within an infinite thing is self-evident. Perhaps whoever holds that what passes away and what remains is general would hold to the view of summary (ijmal) where detail is impossible. Some have gone to interpret the Mother of the Book as the well-known view and held that what is in it does not change, and that change is only in other books. This speaker holds that what is in knowledge does not change, as you have learned and seen in a copy belonging to one of the virtuous scholars, which was with me and was lost in the incident of Baghdad, composed on this question, in which it is stated that there is nothing that cannot be changed and altered, even the eternal decree (al-qada' al-azali). It was argued for this by several matters, among them that it is authentically reported from his supplication

صفحة 171

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 39 (part 2 of 2):

The Prophet (ﷺ) said in the qunut (the supplication in prayer): "And spare me the evil of what You have decreed." This contains a request for protection from the evil of the primordial decree, and if its alteration were impossible, it would not be valid to ask for protection from it. Among the evidence is what is authentically reported in the hadith of the tarawih (the voluntary night prayers in Ramadan), concerning his (ﷺ) excuse for not going out to them when people had gathered waiting for him, out of their great eagerness for them, when he said: "I feared that it would be made obligatory upon you and you would be unable to perform it." There is no sense in this fear if the eternal decree could not change. For if the decree had already preceded that it would be made obligatory, then it must become obligatory; and if the decree had preceded that it would not be made obligatory, then it is impossible for it to become obligatory. Moreover, it is reported in the hadith about the obligation of prayer on the night of the Ascension (mi'raj), after what is clear in showing that the decree had preceded that they would be five obligatory prayers and no more, what is the meaning of the fear after knowledge of that, unless there were knowledge of the possibility of change and alteration?

Among the evidence is what is authentically reported that he (ﷺ) was troubled in his noble state on a night of violent wind, to the extent that he would not sleep, and he would say concerning that: "I fear that the Hour may be established." There is no sense in this fear either, given Allah the Exalted's report that before it there are signs that had not yet occurred at that time, such as the appearance of the Mahdi, the emergence of the Dajjal (Antichrist), the descent of 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj (Gog and Magog), the beast of the earth, the rising of the sun from its west, and other things whose realization requires a long time. If he (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, did not know that the decree could be changed, and that what has been decreed of its signs could be altered, he would not have feared that.

Among the evidence is that those who were given the glad tidings of Paradise were among the most fearful of people of the Fire, to the extent that some of them would say: "Would that my mother had not given birth to me." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "If a caller were to call out that all people are in Paradise except one, I would think that I am that one." This is not fitting for him, given the report of the Truthful One (ﷺ) and his giving him glad tidings of Paradise, and the knowledge that the decree does not change.

Among the evidence is that if the possibility of change were not present, supplication (du'a') would be pointless, since what is asked for either has been preceded by the decree that it will be, in which case it must be, or it has been preceded by the decree that it will not be, in which case it is impossible for it to be. Requesting what must be or what is impossible is vain. Yet the command to supplicate has been given. And the claim that its purpose is merely to show servitude and dependence upon Allah the Exalted, and that this suffices as a benefit, is refuted by the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿Call upon Me; I will respond to you﴾.

Also, al-Hakim reported and declared authentic, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Caution does not avail against the decree, but Allah the Exalted erases by supplication whatever He wills of the decree." Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir reported from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Allah erases what He wills﴾ and so on. He (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said to him: "I will certainly gladden your eye with its explanation, and I will gladden the eye of my community after me with its explanation: charity given in its proper manner, kindness to one's parents, and performing good deeds, which transform misery into happiness, increase lifespan, and protect against evil deaths." This can hardly be understood if the decree does not change. There is in the reports and traces, of that which clearly indicates the possibility of change, what cannot be counted in its abundance, and perhaps among it is the supplication previously mentioned from Ibn Mas'ud.

Furthermore, the conditional decree (al-qada' al-mu'allaq) ultimately returns, according to the one who affirms it, to the definitive decree (al-qada' al-mubram). Therefore, attaching oneself to it benefits nothing regarding what befalls one, nor in repelling what comes upon him. As for the objection to the view of change, that it entails change in the Essence of Allah the Exalted, because it leads to a change in knowledge, and that this necessitates change in His Essence from one attribute to another, or it entails ignorance, this is derived from the doubt that the majority of the philosophers (falasifa) raised in denying Allah the Exalted's knowledge of particulars that change. They said: If He, the Exalted, knows, for example, that Zayd is in the house now, and then he leaves it, then either that knowledge disappears and He, glorified be He, no longer knows that he is in the house, or that knowledge remains as it is. The first necessitates change in His Essence, glorified be He, and the second necessitates ignorance, and both are deficiencies from which Allah the Exalted must be declared free. They responded to this doubt with what is mentioned in al-Mawaqif (of al-Iji), and its commentary: denying that change necessarily occurs in Him, the Exalted; rather, change is only in relations (idafat), because our knowledge is a specific relation and a connection between the knower and the known, or it is a real attribute that has relation. On the first view, the knowledge itself changes; on the second, only its relations change. On both views, no change occurs in an existing attribute, but only in a conceptual, relational notion, and this is permissible.

Many of the Ash'aris and the Mu'tazilah answered that knowledge that a thing has existed and knowledge that it will exist are one and the same. For whoever knows that Zayd will enter the city tomorrow, then when tomorrow comes, he knows by that same knowledge that Zayd has entered the city now, provided that his knowledge remains constant without a distracting heedlessness. Rather, one of us needs another, renewed knowledge by which he knows that Zayd has entered now, because of the occurrence of heedlessness regarding the first. But the Creator, the Exalted, is free from heedlessness. So His knowledge, glorified be He, that a thing has come into existence is the very same as His knowledge that it will come into existence. Thus, change in the known does not entail change in the knowledge. The conclusion of his speech on this matter is that what is in Allah the Exalted's knowledge may change; otherwise, He, glorified be He, would be necessitated to act or to refrain. In this there is a restriction upon Him, majestic is His majesty, that is not hidden. And this change entails nothing but change in the connections (ta'alluqat), which does no harm.

It has been objected that according to this view, no reliance remains upon any of the unseen reports, such as the resurrection and gathering. Likewise, no reliance remains upon the report that he (ﷺ), may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, is the Seal of the Prophets, because it is possible that Allah the Exalted knew that at the time He reported it, then His knowledge became connected to its opposite, yet He did not report that. There is no defect in the first report, because it is a report about what was the object of knowledge at that time. Moreover, this entails either the negation of reality itself, or the negation of the knowledge's connection being in its proper state, and both negations, as you see, leave the answer to what he relied upon unaffected. Its answer is clear in some respects, but in others it requires reflection, so reflect.

Some of the Shi'ah who permit bada' (the notion of a change of divine intention, or apparent change of knowledge) upon Allah, glorified be He, have also used the verse as evidence, and in that there is what there is. Here ends this discussion.

It occurs to me regarding the verse a meaning that I have not seen anyone mention. It is that by His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿Allah erases what He wills and establishes﴾ is meant what we mentioned first, before recounting the opinions. It is what al-Bayhaqi reported in al-Madkhal and others from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Jarir from Qatadah. This is to be restricted to the legal rulings of practice (al-ahkam al-far'iyyah), and by "the Mother of the Book" (umm al-kitab) is meant the fundamental rulings (al-ahkam al-asliyyah), for these are not subject to abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one), and they are the root of every book, in that the practical rulings contained in it are valid only from the one who brings them. However, the transmitted view from the early generations (al-salaf) does not support this, though it is suitable to the context, as is not hidden.

Al-Dahhak and al-Farra' claimed that there is an inversion (qalb, transposition of words in a sentence) in the verse, and the original is: "For every book there is a term (ajal)." This was criticized on the ground that claiming inversion is not permissible except in cases of poetic necessity, and furthermore there is no need for it here; rather, it may even be claimed that it corrupts the meaning. Whatever the case, the definite article in "al-kitab" (the Book) is generic (lil-jins), so it encompasses many, and for this reason more than one commentator explained it as the plural.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited: (wa-yuthabbitu) [the verb with doubled "ba'", meaning "and He establishes"].

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 13, verse 40:

﴿Whether We show you﴾. Its original form is *in nurīka*, and *ma* (*mā*, an extra particle added to emphasize the meaning of the conditional) is redundant. For this reason the *nūn* (the energetic nūn, a verbal suffix for emphasis) was attached to the verb. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "If *in* (the conditional particle) stood alone, attaching the *nūn* would not be permitted." This contradicts the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's statement. Ibn Kharuf said: Sibawayh permitted using *mā* and omitting it, and using the *nūn* with *mā* and omitting it. The seeing (*al-irā'a*) here is visual, the *kāf* is the first object, and His statement, glorified is He, ﴿some of what We promise them﴾, is the second object. The intended meaning is some of what We promised them of the descent of punishment upon them. The shift to the present tense (*al-muḍāri'*) either narrates a past situation or indicates a renewed promise, as wisdom requires, namely warning following warning. The mention of "some" (*al-ba'ḍ*) is said to be an allusion to showing you some of what was promised. ﴿Or We cause you to die﴾ before that, ﴿then upon you is only the conveyance (*al-balāgh*)﴾, that is, conveying the rulings of what We have sent down to you and what it contains of promise and threat, not bringing about the fulfillment of the threat contained therein. The restricted element is the conveyance, and for this reason the predicate was placed first. This restriction is derived from *innamā* (the particle of restriction "only"), not from the word order, since otherwise the meaning would be reversed. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And upon Us is the reckoning﴾. (40)

The apparent view is that it is coordinated with what is within the scope of (*innamā*), so the meaning becomes: "Upon Us alone is the reckoning of their evil deeds and the taking them to account for them, not compelling them to follow you, or the sending down of the signs they have demanded of you." Al-Zamakhshari, however, considered its coordination with the clause "upon you is only the conveyance," so the meaning becomes: "And upon Us, not upon you, is the reckoning of their deeds." It was said: this is the apparent view, preferring the explicit meaning (*al-manṭūq*) over the implicit meaning (*al-mafhūm*) when two indicators of restriction coexist.

The overall meaning of the verse: however the situation turns out, We either showed you some of what We promised them of worldly punishment, or We did not show it to you. In either case, that is Our concern, and your only duty is conveyance. So do not be anxious about what lies beyond that, for We will suffice you in it and complete what We promised you of victory. Its delay should not trouble you, for that is because of hidden wisdoms that We know. In al-Bahr (*al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*) it is reported from al-Hawfi that two conditions have preceded in the verse, *nurīyannaka* and *natawaffayannaka*, because what is coordinated with a conditional is itself a conditional. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿then upon you is only the conveyance﴾ cannot serve as the response (*jawāb*) to the first condition or to the second, because it does not follow from either of them, which is evident. So it requires interpretation, which is that for each condition there is supplied what is suitable to be a consequence following from it. Thus it is said, and God knows best: "Whether We show you some of what We promise them, that is your cure against your enemies and proof of your truthfulness. Or whether We cause you to die before it befalls them, then there is no blame upon you and no reproach." The statement, exalted is He, ﴿then indeed﴾ ... and so on, is evidence for both of them. The one that actually occurred of the two conditions is the first, as at Badr.

Then Allah, glorified is He, consoled His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, with the first signs of victory, and said, exalted is His majesty: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?﴾ ... and so on. The interrogative is for denunciation, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied clause that the context requires, meaning: Did they deny the descent of what We promised them, or did they doubt it, or did they not look into this and see ﴿that We come to the land﴾, that is, the land of the disbelievers, ﴿reducing it from its outlying parts﴾, from its sides, by conquering it little by little and joining it to the abode of Islam, and taking away its people by killing, captivity and expulsion? Is this not a preface to that?

Similar to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts? Are they then the victorious?﴾ This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, 'Atiyyah, al-Suddi and others. It was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hakim transmitted it from him and declared it sound, that the reduction of the land is the death of its nobles and great ones and the departure of its scholars. In another narration from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, only the latter is mentioned. It is also narrated from Mujahid. Thus the meaning of "land" is its genus, and "outlying parts" as it has been said means "nobles." Such usage is reported from Tha'lab, and al-Wahidi cited in support the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"And ask about us and you, when the nobles of every tribe come forth from me, who is restrained?"

Close to this is the saying of Ibn al-A'rabi: "al-Taraf and al-Tarf are the noble man," and the saying of some: "The taraf of everything is its best." From this they took the saying of 'Ali, may Allah honour his face: "Knowledge is valleys; whichever valley you take from them, you lose. So take from every thing its taraf." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: he meant by it, may Allah honour his face, "its best." And you know that the more apparent is "its side." Al-Wahidi claimed that interpreting the verse in the previous manner is the most fitting, and al-Imam criticised him, saying that it is possible to say the second is fitting too, and the verse's construction upon it is: Do they not see that We bring about in the world, through differences, ruin after prosperity, death after life, humiliation after honour, and deficiency after perfection? These are changes perceived by the senses. So what assures them that Allah, exalted is He, will not reverse the matter against them, making them abased after they were honoured, and overpowered after they were the conquerors? And this, as you see, [is far-fetched]. It has also been said: "its reduction" is the destruction of those nations that perished before Quraysh, and the ruin of their lands; that is, did they not see the destruction of those before them and the ruin of their dwellings? So how can they feel safe from such befalling them? The first is also more suited to the context than this. And there is no hiding what is in the expression "coming" (al-ityan), which indicates the great dominance, of grandeur, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾. In the Shihabi marginal notes it is stated that the meaning is: Our command and Our punishment comes to it. The clause ﴿reducing it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (ya'ti) or from its object. Al-Dahhak read (nunaqqisuha), intensified, from naqasa, making it transitive by doubling, from the intransitive naqasa, as in al-Bahr.

﴿And Allah judges﴾ whatever He wills as He wills, and He has decreed for you and your followers honour and ascendancy, and against your enemies and opponents subjugation and humiliation, as those with insight witness from the signs and traces. In the shift from the first person to the third person, and in building the judgment upon the noble Name, there is what indicates grandeur, cultivates awe, and establishes the content of the statement by pointing to the cause, which is not hidden. It is a parenthetical clause brought to confirm the meaning of what precedes it. And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿There is no one to repel His judgment﴾ is also a parenthetical clause, to show the exaltedness of His judgment, exalted is He. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, as if it were said: Allah, exalted is He, judges, His judgment being binding, just as you say: "Zayd came, without a turban on his head or a cap," meaning bare-headed. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari. It is said: he interpreted the nominal clause as a single word because its being devoid of the waw when it occurs as a circumstantial clause is not eloquent in his view. But it is not hidden from you that making it a parenthetical clause is better and loftier. The mu'aqqib is one who turns back upon a thing and nullifies it; its essence is one who follows up a thing to annul it. From this, one who seeks a right from another is called mu'aqqib, because he follows his debtor and pursues him for settlement. Labid said:

"Until he abandons the departure, and the seeking of the wronged one's right by the pursuer drives him away."

It is also said that the procrastinator is a mu'aqqib, because he postpones every demand with a refusal. From Abu 'Ali: "'aqabani haqqi," meaning, he delayed me over my right. It is said of searching into a thing: ta'aqqaba. Al-Raghib allowed that this meaning be intended here, so that the statement is a prohibition to people from delving into the search for His judgment and wisdom when these are hidden from them, and this would be akin to the prohibition against delving into the secret of predestination. ﴿And He is swift in reckoning﴾. (41) So, before long, He will call them to account and requite them in the Hereafter, after having punished them by killing, captivity and expulsion in this world, as He sees fit. It is as if it were said: Do not be impatient for their punishment, for it is coming without doubt, and everything that is coming is near. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is swift in retribution.

**Page 175**

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 13, verse 42:

﴿And indeed those who were before them plotted﴾ the disbelievers ﴿who came before them﴾, that is, before the disbelievers of Makkah, against their prophets and against the believers, just as these (disbelievers) have done. This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that their plotting is of no consequence and has no effect; rather, it does not exist in reality. Allah, glorified is He, did not state this explicitly, relying instead on the indication of restriction (*qasr*, the limiting of a predicate to a subject) derived from His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So to Allah belongs all plotting﴾, meaning the entire category of plotting, ﴿all of it﴾. Their plotting has no existence whatsoever, since it is the conveying of harm to another from a direction he does not perceive. And since all that they do and leave undone is by His knowledge and power, glorified is He, what they have is merely the *kasb* (acquisition, the Ash'ari notion that humans "acquire" actions created by God) without any act or effect, as His statement, exalted is He, clarifies: ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾. Among the consequences of this is the protection of His friends, glorified is He, and the punishment of those who plot against them, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned. It becomes clear that their plotting, in relation to those against whom they plot, has neither substance nor effect, and that all plotting belongs to Allah, exalted is He, since He takes them to account for what they have earned of the various kinds of sins, among which is their plotting, from a direction they do not reckon. This is what Shaykh al-Islam said.
