He (may his secret be sanctified) went to great lengths in this matter, and he interpreted *kasb* according to what is common among the Ash'ariyyah (the Ash'ari school of theology), while Allah, exalted is He, does not distinguish between it and action (*fi'l*), and neither does His Messenger (ﷺ), nor the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), nor the Successors, nor the linguists. It has also been said: the reason for the restriction is that the plotting of any other than Allah, glorified is He, is not taken into account, because He, glorified is He, is the One who is able in Himself to bring about the intended harm, and anyone else, if he is able to do so, it is by Allah's enabling and permission; so everything returns to Him, majestic and exalted is He.

In *al-Kashshaf* it is stated that His statement, exalted is He, ﴿He knows what every soul earns﴾ … and so on, is an explanation of His statement, glorified is He, ﴿So to Allah belongs all plotting, all of it﴾, because whoever knows what every soul earns and prepares its recompense for it, then to him belongs the plotting, since it comes upon them from a direction they do not know, while they are heedless of what is intended for them. It has also been said: the speech contains an elided *mudaf* (omitted genitive construction), meaning: "So to Allah belongs the recompense of plotting." It has also been permitted that the *alif-lam* (the definite article in *al-makr*) be for prior reference (*'ahd*), meaning: to Him, exalted is He, belongs the plotting which they all undertook, not to them, in the sense that this is not plotting by them against the prophets, but is in fact plotting by Allah, exalted is He, against them, while they are unaware, since "the evil plot does not encompass anyone except its own people." ﴿And the disbelievers will know﴾ when the punishment comes upon them ﴿to whom belongs the final home (*'uqba al-dar*)﴾. (42)

That is, the praiseworthy outcome for both groups, even if this was unknown before. It has been said: the *sin* (of *sa-ya'lamu*, "will know") is for emphasizing the occurrence of that and their knowledge of it at that time. The word "disbeliever" (*al-kafir*) here refers to the genus, so it includes all disbelievers. This is the reading of the two Harams (the reciters of Makkah and Madinah) and Abu 'Amr. The rest of the seven readers recited ﴿*Wa-sa-ya'lamu al-kuffar*﴾ in the form of the broken plural (*jam' al-taksir*).

Ibn Mas'ud recited ﴿*al-kafiruna*﴾ in the form of the sound masculine plural (*jam' al-salamah*). Ubayy recited ﴿*alladhina kafaru*﴾ ("those who disbelieved"). And one reading is ﴿*al-kufr*﴾ ("disbelief"), meaning its people. Janah ibn Hubays recited ﴿*wa-sa-yu'lamu*﴾ in the passive voice from *u'lima*, meaning "will be informed," and the *lam* (in *li-man*) is for benefit. It is also permitted that the *lam* be for possession, in the sense of "the disbelievers will know who will possess the world in the end." 'Ata' interpreted *al-kafir* as referring to the mockers, who were five, and the swearers, who were twenty-eight. Ibn 'Abbas said: by *al-kafir* he means Abu Jahl. What preceded is the apparent meaning, and perhaps what has been mentioned is by way of illustration (*tamthil*).

[p. 175]

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger."﴾ It is said: this was said by the leaders of the Jews.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "A bishop from Yemen came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he (ﷺ) said to him: 'Do you find me in the Injil as a messenger?' He said: 'No.' So Allah revealed the verse." According to this, what is meant by "those who disbelieve" is this man and whoever agreed with him and approved of his statement. The use of the present tense (*yaqulu*, "say") is to bring before the mind the image of their shameful utterance, to express astonishment at it, or to indicate that this is repeated and continuous among them.

﴿Say: "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you."﴾ For He, may He be exalted, has manifested, in proof of my messengership, such evidence and arguments that there is no need for the testimony of any other witness. Calling this "testimony" although it is an action, while testimony is a statement, is a metaphor, since it serves the same purpose as testimony and is even stronger than it.

﴿And whoever has knowledge of the Book.﴾ (43) That is, the knowledge of the Qur'an and of its inimitable composition. It is said: if "testimony" means bearing it, then the matter is clear; if it means delivering it, then the one referred to by the relative clause is the one characterised by that title, namely whoever has abandoned obstinacy and believed.

In *al-Kashshaf* (by al-Zamakhshari) it is said: the meaning is that this world is sufficient as a witness between me and you, and it does not follow from its sufficiency as a witness that it must give testimony. Whoever gives it is a trustworthy witness, and whoever does not give it is a traitor. There is in this an eloquent implication that if they were fair, they would bear witness. It is also said: by "the Book" is meant the Torah and the Gospel, and by "whoever has knowledge of it" is meant those among the People of the Book who embraced Islam, such as ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and his like, for they bear witness to his description (ﷺ) in their books. This is the view of Qatada. ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said regarding the verse: "There were among the People of the Book people who bore witness to the truth and recognised it, among them ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, al-Jarud, Tamim al-Dari and Salman al-Farisi." It has also come from Mujahid and others, and it is a narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, that what is meant is ʿAbdullah alone, and they did not mention anyone else.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the chain of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr from Jundub, who said: "ʿAbdullah ibn Salam came until he took hold of the two doorposts of the mosque, then said: 'I adjure you by Allah, do you know that I am the one about whom this was revealed: "And whoever has knowledge of the Book"?' They said: 'O Allah, yes.'" Ibn Jubayr denied this. Sa'id ibn Mansur and a group narrated from him that he was asked: "Is this 'the one who has knowledge of the Book' ʿAbdullah ibn Salam?" He said: "How, when this surah is Meccan?" Al-Shaʿbi denied that any part of the Qur'an was revealed concerning him.

[p. 176]

This is not to be relied upon, for one who has memorised (the narration) is a proof against one who has not. Ibn Jubayr's objection has been answered by saying that they may say: the surah is Meccan but some of its verses are Medinan, so let this be one of those. But you know that this requires a transmission.

In *al-Bahr* (by Abu Hayyan) it is said that what has been mentioned is only consistent if this verse is Medinan, whereas the majority hold that it is Meccan. It has been answered that this does not contradict the verse being Meccan, by its being a report about what will bear witness to it. You may also say: if the meaning is as in *al-Kashshaf*, and it does not follow from the sufficiency of the one mentioned as a witness that he must give the testimony, then the verse being Meccan does no harm, nor does ʿAbdullah ibn Salam's not having embraced Islam at the time of its revelation, nor even his not being present. There is no obstacle to the verse being Meccan while "those who disbelieve" means the people of Mecca, and "whoever has knowledge of the Book" means the Jews and Christians, as Ibn Jarir narrated through al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas. The result of the answer on this basis would be: you are not People of a Book, so ask its people, for they are in your neighbourhood.

Shaykh al-Islam said: the verse is Medinan by consensus. It seems he was unaware of the disagreement.

It is also said: by "the Book" is meant the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh*, the celestial record of all things), and "whoever" (*man*) is an expression for Him, exalted is He. This was narrated from Mujahid, al-Zajjaj, and from al-Hasan: "No, by Allah, He means only Allah, exalted is He." The meaning, as in *al-Kashshaf*, is: sufficient is He who deserves worship, and He who alone knows the knowledge of what is in the Preserved Tablet, as a witness between me and you. With this interpretation, the conjunction (*ʿatf*) becomes like the verse of the poet:

*To the lordly king, and the son of the brave one, and the lion of the battalion in the crush.*

There is therefore no problem with the conjunction. The restriction (*hasr*) is either from outside the text, since knowledge of that belongs exclusively to Him, exalted is He, or it arises from taking the adverbial phrase as a predicate placed first, which gives the restriction. The oath of al-Hasan is for emphasis, in rejecting what they claimed, as has been said. In *al-Kashshaf* it is said: al-Hasan only emphasised because of what we have already mentioned, namely that the noble surah is built upon what it is built upon, and makes the earlier part like the closing part, and because of the point in the conjunction. For this reason al-Zamakhshari explained it with his words "sufficient is He who..." etc. He conjoined it as one essence to another essence, to indicate that each of the two attributes has independent sufficiency as a witness, without regard to the other. He who deserves worship has borne witness through what the Book is filled with of the call to worship Him, and through what He has strengthened His servant with, the one who has knowledge of it, by various kinds of support. He who alone knows the knowledge of what is in the Preserved Tablet, that is, the knowledge of everything, has borne witness through what the Book contains of knowledge, and through sending it down in a style that surpasses what is customary. This view is supported by the fact that ʿAli (may Allah honour his face), Ubayy, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, Ibn Jubayr, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra, al-Dahhak, Salim ibn ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Mujahid, al-Hakam and al-Aʿmash read: "*wa-min ʿindihi ʿilmu al-kitab*" (*min* here being a preposition), with the prepositional phrase as the fronted predicate and *ʿilm* as the postponed subject.

ʿAli (may Allah honour his face) also read, as did Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ and al-Hasan according to one report: "*wa-min ʿindihi*" with the preposition, and "*ʿulima al-kitab*" (the Book is known), taking *ʿulima* as a passive verb and *al-kitab* as its deputy subject. The pronoun in "*ʿindihi*" in both readings refers to Allah, exalted is He, as in the previous reading according to that interpretation. The original principle is the agreement of the readings.

It is also said: by "the Book" is meant the Preserved Tablet, and by "whoever" is meant Jibril (peace be upon him). Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Jubayr an interpretation of "*man*" in this way. But it is, as you see, far-fetched.

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya and al-Baqir said, as in *al-Bahr*: by "*man*" is meant ʿAli (may Allah honour his face). The apparent meaning in that case is that by "the Book" is meant the Qur'an. By my life, that with him (may Allah be pleased with him) is the complete knowledge of the Book, but it is apparent that what is meant is not that he (may Allah honour his face) is intended.

The apparent meaning of "*man*" in the reading of the majority is that it is in the genitive position by conjunction with the word of the Majestic Name (Allah). This is supported by the fact that in the irregular (*shadhdh*) readings the preposition *bi* is repeated. It is also said that it is in the nominative position by conjunction with its (grammatical) position, since the *ba'* (preposition) is superfluous.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said:

[p. 177]

It is possible that it is in the nominative position as a subject, with the predicate omitted, its estimated form being "is more just," or "more binding in speech," or something similar of what the word "*shahidan*" (witness) indicates, and what is meant by it is Allah, exalted is He. In this there is much remoteness, as is not hidden.

The knowledge in the reading in which "*ʿindahu*" occurs is the relative clause's complement of a nominative noun elided within the adverbial phrase. Therefore it is the subject, because when an adverbial phrase occurs as a relative clause, it takes on the character of a verb due to its reliance on the relative pronoun, and so it operates as a verb does. Like your saying: "I passed by the one who is in the house, whose brother…" so "his brother" is the subject, just as you say: "by the one who is settled in the house, his brother." This is what al-Zamakhshari said. But it is not obligatory, for when an adverbial phrase or similar occurs as a relative clause, or as an adjective, or as a circumstantial clause, or as a predicate, or when a negative particle or an interrogative particle precedes it, it is permitted for the apparent noun after it to be nominative as the subject, and this is the better option. It is also permitted for it to be the subject, with the adverbial phrase or its equivalent in the position of the predicate, and the nominal sentence as a relative clause, adjective, circumstantial clause or predicate. This is based on the active participle: just as this is permitted with it, although it is better to make it operate on the apparent noun, so too it is permitted with what stands in for it, namely an adverbial or prepositional phrase. Sibawayh explicitly permitted this in the example "I passed by a man, whose face is good" (*hasanun wajhuhu*), where he allowed "*hasanun*" to be nominative as a fronted predicate. Some have wrongly thought that when the active participle relies on any of the things mentioned, its operation on the apparent noun becomes obligatory, but that is not so. Al-Hufi parsed "*ʿindahu ʿilmu al-kitab*" as a subject and predicate within the relative clause of "*man*", but this is a leaning towards the weaker option.

In the verse, according to both readings with *min* as a preposition, there is an indication that the ennobling of the servant with the sciences of the Qur'an is one of Allah's beneficence towards him and His granting him success. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to honour us with those sciences, to grant us success in standing upon the secrets of what it contains of the explicit and the implicit, and to make us among those who hold fast to its firmest handle and are guided by its guidance, so that we neither go astray nor are wretched, through the blessing of the Prophet (ﷺ).

* * *

This (and from the category of allusion in the verses):

﴿Those who fulfil Allah's covenant and do not break the pledge.﴾ It is said: the covenant of Allah with the believers is to stand before Him, glorified is He, in servitude, in ease and in hardship. ﴿And those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined.﴾ They join with their hearts His love, and with their inner secrets the witnessing of Him, glorified is He, and nearness to Him. ﴿And they fear their Lord﴾ at the manifestation of the attributes in the station of the heart, so they witness the majesty of the attribute of greatness, and awe and fear necessarily fall upon them. ﴿And they dread the evil reckoning﴾ at the manifestation of the acts in the station of the self, so they look upon the seizing and the punishment, and fear necessarily falls upon them.

Ibn ʿAta' was asked what the difference is between *khashya* (awe) and *khawf* (fear). He said: *khashya* is fear of falling from the ranks of nearness, and *khawf* is fear of reaching the levels of hatred and estrangement. Some of them said: *khashya* is more subtle and *khawf* is more solid. ﴿And those who endure, seeking the face of their Lord﴾: they endure in turning away from what is other than Allah, through Allah, glorified is He, for the unveiling of the lights of His noble Face; or they endure in travelling His path, glorified is He, away from what is habitual, seeking His pleasure. ﴿And establish prayer﴾: the prayer of witnessing, or they occupy themselves with purification through bodily acts of worship. ﴿And spend of what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾: they benefit from what We have bestowed upon them of states, stations and unveilings, and they refined the aspirants until what they attained became manifest and hidden to them; or they occupy themselves with purification through acts of worship involving wealth as well. ﴿And repel evil with good﴾: the good obtained by them from the manifestation of the sublime divine attribute ﴿the evil﴾ which is the attribute of the self. Some of them said: they associate with people with good character, so if anyone treats them with harshness, they respond with loyalty. ﴿Those will have the good final abode﴾: lasting after passing away, or the praiseworthy outcome. ﴿Gardens of Eden which they will enter, and whoever was righteous among their fathers, spouses and offspring﴾: it is said: they enter the Garden of the Essence, and whoever was righteous among the fathers of spirits; they enter the Garden of the Attributes through the hearts, and they enter the Garden of the Acts, and whoever was righteous among the spouses of the souls and the offspring of the faculties; or they enter the gardens of nearness, witnessing and union, and whoever was righteous among those mentioned follows them. And for the sake of an eye, a thousand

ʿAyn tukramu (...). [The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing the commentary on the words of the verse.]

﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final abode of the Home!﴾ The people of might and dominion (al-jabarut wa'l-malakut) will enter upon them from every gate of the attributes, greeting them with the salutations of the luminous illuminations and the holy divine outpourings. Or, the angels who accompanied them in this world will enter upon them from every gate of obedience, greeting them after they have settled in their abodes, just as the friends of a absent person greet him when he returns home and settles in it. ﴿Those who believe﴾ with the knowledge-based faith in the unseen, ﴿and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of God﴾. They said: the remembrance of the self is by the tongue and by reflecting on blessings; the remembrance of the heart is by reflecting on the malakut and contemplating the attributes of beauty; the remembrance of the innermost (sirr) is by intimate converse; the remembrance of the spirit (ruh) is by witnessing; the remembrance of the hidden (khafa') is by tender communion in love; and the remembrance of God Most High is by annihilation in Him. ﴿Verily, in the remembrance of God do hearts find rest﴾. This is because the self is agitated by the manifestation of its qualities and its discourses, and it becomes restless, so the heart changes and varies accordingly; but when it reflects on the malakut and contemplates the lights of beauty and majesty, it settles and is at rest. All other kinds of remembrance occur only after this tranquility. Al-Hazjuri said: The hearts of the friends of God are at rest and do not constantly move, out of fear that God Most High may manifest Himself upon them suddenly and find them not marked by courtesy. ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: emptying (takhliyah) and adorning (tahliyah). ﴿Blessed is theirs﴾ by reaching the primordial nature (fitrah) and the perfection of attributes. ﴿And excellent final return﴾ by entering the Garden of the heart, which is the Garden of the attributes. Or: ﴿Blessed is theirs﴾ now, since nothing is found in them that contradicts the good pleasure of their Beloved; and ﴿excellent final return﴾ in the Hereafter, where they find from their Beloved nothing contrary to what they hope for.

﴿Is then one who stands over every soul in what it has earned﴾, i.e., according to its earning and its requirement; that is, just as its acquired qualities and states, which arise in accordance with its readiness, require, He bestows upon it the recompense. ﴿Say: I have only been commanded to worship God and not to associate anything with Him.﴾ God, glorified be He, did not remove anyone from servitude, not even the master of the free ones of creation, God bless him and grant him peace. Abu Hafs interpreted it as abandoning every dominion and persisting in what is commanded.

Al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, said: No one ascends in the degrees of servitude until he establishes between himself and God Most High the initial beginnings, which are the obligations, the duties, the sunnahs, and the litanies; and the steeds of grace are the resolute matters. Whoever firmly establishes this upon himself, God Most High bestows upon him what comes after it.

﴿And We have certainly sent messengers before you and given them wives and offspring﴾. In this, according to what has been said, is an indication that when God Most High honours a person with His guardianship (wilayah), the direct engagement with human affairs, such as family and children, does not harm him, and the spreading of worldly provision for him is not a defect in his guardianship. His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by God's permission﴾ contains a prohibition against seeking miracles (karamat) from the shaykhs or proposing them.

﴿For every term there is a Book﴾: for every time there is a written matter that occurs in it and does not occur in another. From here it has been said: affairs are bound to their appointed times. It has also been said: God Most High has specifics in times, places, and persons.

﴿God effaces what He wills and establishes﴾. It has been said: He effaces from the tablets of intellects the forms of thoughts and establishes in them the lights of remembrances; He effaces from the leaves of hearts the sciences of occurrences and establishes in them the divine knowledge of gnosis. It has also been said: He effaces from the gnostics through the unveiling of His majesty, and establishes them at another time through the subtlety of His beauty. Ibn 'Ata said: He effaces their attributes and establishes their secrets, for these are the locus of witnessing. It has been said: He effaces what He wills from the particular tablets, which are the celestial souls, of the engravings fixed in them, so He annihilates from the matters and passes away, and establishes what He wills in them, so He brings into existence.

﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾: the eternal knowledge subsisting in His essence, glorified be He. It has been said: it is the tablet of the preordained decree (lawh al-qada' al-sabiq), which is the Universal Intellect, and in it is all that has been and will be, eternally and everlastingly, in the universal manner, exempt from effacement and establishment. They mention that the tablets are four: the tablet of the preordained decree, exalted above effacement and establishment, which is the tablet of the First Intellect; the tablet of destiny (qadar), which is the tablet of the universal rational soul, in which the universals of the first tablet are detailed, and which is called the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz); and the tablets of the particular celestial souls, in which everything in this world is inscribed with its form, configuration, and measure, and which is called the lowest heaven, and which is in the position of the world's imagination, just as the first is in the position of its spirit and the second in the position of its heart; then the tablet of prime matter (hayuli), receptive to forms in the world of witnessing. Ended. This is a philosophical discourse.

﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its extremities?﴾ It has been said: this refers to the passing away of the people of guardianship through whom the land is inhabited. It has been said: the allusion is that We come to the land of the body at the time of old age, reducing it from its extremities by the weakening of the outward and inward limbs and powers, little by little, until death occurs; or We come to the land of the self at the time of spiritual journeying, reducing it from its extremities: first by annihilating its actions through Our actions, second by annihilating its attributes, and third by annihilating its essence in Our essence.

﴿None can avert His judgment﴾: none can repel or alter whatever He has decreed. We ask God Most High to decree for us what is better and more excellent in the Hereafter and in this world, by the sanctity of the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, and by his nobility, greatness, and generosity.
